22806-the-bronze-hand-1897:
The Bronze Hand is a mystery story dated 1897, built around a woman's voice that arrests its listener with sudden, extraordinary emotion. The catalog record names no author. Tales of the 1890s loved an object with a secret, and a bronze hand promises one: a relic, a clue, or a token from a buried past.

Any words from those lips, the narrator says, would have drawn my attention. But this utterance carried such marked emotion that curiosity woke in me at once, and interest with it. Curiosity is the detective story's true engine, and this one starts it early. The story proceeds in the era's manner: respectable people, a strange inheritance or summons, and the past reaching, literally, into the present.
arxiv-2511-20297:
Kirtania, Biyani, Gupta, and Bajpai improve computer-using agents by writing down what they learn. Their 2025 paper introduces BREW for language agent optimization. Weight-tuning agents with reinforcement learning is costly and opaque. Learned policies resist inspection and piecemeal fixes. Experience could be stored as readable knowledge.

BREW builds a structured knowledge base from agent runs. Memory splits into concept-level documents for clean retrieval. Task graders and behavior rubrics judge each attempt. Insights are distilled from graded successes and failures. State-space search hardens the lessons against noisy wording. The knowledge base stays modular and editable by design. Benchmarks included OSWorld and SpreadsheetBench suites. A tau-bench for tool agents joined the tests. Task precision rose by ten to twenty percent. Tool and API calls fell by ten to fifteen percent. Compute costs stayed near the base model's level.
arxiv-2511-20497:
Tran, Liu, Li, and Feamster show fake internet traffic can betray real users. Their 2025 paper measures privacy leakage from synthetic network traffic. Generators create fake traffic to replace scarce, sensitive recordings. Many assume such data is safe to share by default. The authors built metrics to test that assumption.

Their toolkit combines membership tests and data extraction attacks. Network IDs and attributes get their own measures. Four modern generators and five datasets were tested. Membership attack success ranged from zero to eighty-eight percent. In the worst cases every network ID could be recovered. Up to one hundred percent of IDs leaked from fake traffic. How varied the training data was strongly swayed attack success. Overfit models leaked markedly more. Noise-based defenses were tested with their trade-offs. The guidance: treat fake traces as security-sensitive data. Stronger protection costs realism, and that cost must be accepted.
arxiv-2511-20697:
Congren Dai and a large team introduce in 2025 MSU-Bench, a test of whether AI models can read complete musical scores. Reading a score means reasoning about pitch, rhythm, harmony, and overall form at once. Earlier benchmarks mostly probed short fragments or multiple-choice answers. MSU-Bench asks open questions about whole works by Bach, Beethoven, Chopin, Debussy, and others. Each score appears both as text-based ABC notation and as PDF images.

The benchmark holds 1,800 human-curated question-answer pairs in four levels of difficulty. Levels run from basic onset information through notes, then chords and harmony, and finally texture and form. The team evaluated more than 15 leading language and vision-language models, as shipped and after fine-tuning. Scores in the two formats differed sharply, and success at one level often failed to carry higher. Fine-tuning improved results markedly in both formats while leaving general knowledge intact.
arxiv-2511-20797:
Emma Daggett, Libai Huang, and many co-authors review in 2025 the push to entangle many solid-state quantum emitters at once. The emitters are defects and nanostructures releasing photons on demand: colour centres in wide-bandgap crystals, quantum dots, molecules, and defects in two-dimensional materials. Trapped atoms pioneered quantum information, but solid-state platforms can be miniaturised and wired onto chips.

The review organises the field around engineering interactions between emitters, through shared photonic modes or direct dipole coupling, to build graph and cluster states for computation, superradiant emission, and emergent quantum phases. It explains the ground rules, like photon indistinguishability, tested by the Hong-Ou-Mandel dip when two photons meet at a 50:50 beamsplitter. The central enemies are inhomogeneity, no two emitters alike, and decoherence from the solid environment. The authors survey strategies for beating them, arguing robust many-body coherence on chip is nearing reach.
arxiv-2511-21097:
Geetanjali Sharma and colleagues present in 2025 CLRecogEye, an iris-recognition system built to survive the messy conditions of checkpoints. Iris matching is prized for border control and citizen identification, but rotation, scale changes, reflections, and blur trip it up, and most systems compare distance scores. CLRecogEye instead slices each iris image into sub-images and feeds them to a 3D convolutional network, which learns patterns across space and slices.

Training follows a curriculum, easy examples first, and combines triplet loss with ArcFace loss to force distinctive embeddings. Trained on half of one dataset, it was tested across seven iris databases. On CASIA-Iris Lamp V3, with 783 subjects and 20 samples, it reached an equal error rate of 0.35 percent in closed-set tests, with true-match rates above 99 percent. In open-set testing its error rate fell to 0.23 percent with a correct recognition rate of 99.87 percent, showing generalisation to unseen devices.
arxiv-2511-21497:
Andrew Golightly, Sarah Heaps, Chris Sherlock, Laura Wadkin, and Darren Wilkinson fuse two statistical workhorses into a better inference engine in 2025. State-space models track a hidden process through noisy observations, and the ensemble Kalman filter follows the hidden state efficiently by shifting an ensemble of guesses. Estimating fixed parameters is harder: the usual trick of stapling parameters onto the state forces an unrealistic linear-Gaussian story on them.

Golightly and his coauthors instead nest the Kalman filter inside the SMC-squared algorithm, a sampler that normally nests particle filters. Parameter candidates are weighted by the likelihood the Kalman filter computes, then refreshed by a resample-move step aimed at the true parameter posterior. Extensions add a delayed-acceptance shortcut to the refresh step and support nonlinear observation models. Several case studies illustrate the method, aimed at high-dimensional systems where particle filters collapse from weight degeneracy.
arxiv-2512-00097:
Proving olympiad geometry theorems by computer has long been a test of machine reasoning. Boyan Duan and a team of co-authors present a method for International Mathematical Olympiad level problems in 2025. Their solver is described as reaching gold-medal level while running entirely on ordinary CPUs.

The method relies on efficient heuristic choices of auxiliary constructions, the extra lines and points that unlock a geometry proof. It avoids neural network inference altogether. A fast CPU-only prover could make theorem proving cheaper and easier to inspect. Each step follows explicit geometric reasoning rather than a learned model's guesses. Geometry proofs are a demanding test because one wrong construction ruins the whole argument.
arxiv-2512-00297:
Checking whether several automata can accept one common input sounds simple, but it can be surprisingly hard. Michael Wehar revisits lower bounds for this intersection non-emptiness problem in 2025, for deterministic finite automata. The aim is unconditional results about time and space complexity.

Earlier conditional bounds, from Kasai and Iwata in 1985, tied the problem's difficulty to algorithms for nondeterministic logarithmic space. Wehar first strengthens those conditional time bounds as a step in the argument. Lower bounds matter because they tell algorithm designers when to stop hunting for faster methods and design around the hardness instead. The problem is also called DFA intersection, a staple of automata theory courses.
arxiv-2512-00497:
The EPR paradox challenges whether quantum mechanics completely describes reality, through entangled particles measured far apart. Henryk Gzyl reexamines the paradox for systems with finitely many levels in 2025. The analysis emphasizes the connection between measurements and conditional probabilities.

When a measurement is performed, the quantum state and the probability distribution become functions of the observable being measured. That observation reframes parts of the paradox in the language of chance. Finite-level systems are the ones actually built in laboratories, so sorting out the paradox there keeps the base of quantum theory tied to practice. Finite-level systems include the qubits and qudits of real quantum devices. Conditional chance is the language in which test outcomes are in fact reported. For a reader new to the field, the gain is a fresh eye. Old rifts are recast in terms of what a test can show, and what it can not show.
arxiv-2512-00597:
Medical vision-language models promise one system for many clinical imaging tasks, but volumetric CT remains hard. Thuraya Alzubaidi, Farhad Nezami, and Muzammil Behzad introduce MedCT-VLM in 2025, a parameter-efficient framework for adapting large CT foundation models. They use cross-modal low-rank adaptation.

Foundation models show strong zero-shot ability across image domains, yet their use in volumetric medical imaging is limited. Low-rank adaptation updates only a small set of added parameters, keeping adaptation cheap enough for hospitals. Efficient clinical models could bring foundation-model assistance to radiology departments without supercomputing budgets. Volumetric scans are three-dimensional, so adapting flat-image models is not straightforward. Low-rank updates are small enough to share between hospitals for comparison. For scan teams in small towns, the gain is reach. A big model can be trimmed to fit their kit, and still read chest scans with care and speed.
arxiv-2512-00697:
Amichai Lampert, Andrew Snowden, and Tamar Ziegler work on a classic problem in number theory in a 2025 paper. Birch's theorem, from 1957, says that a set of polynomial forms of odd degree always has a nontrivial zero, if there are enough variables. A zero is an input, other than all zeros, that makes every form vanish.

Birch's proof gave no clear bound on how many variables are enough. Lampert and his coauthors prove polynomial bounds for that threshold, over any number field. Explicit bounds turn a pure existence result into something other mathematicians can use and check.
arxiv-2512-00797:
Nan Sun and five coauthors propose a new shape for robot intelligence in a 2025 paper. Foundation models now unify perception and planning in robotics, promising one model that sees, thinks, and acts. Real service work, though, is spread out, fast changing, and shared among people and robots.

Vision-language models read scenes well but lack a body-aware sense of action and lean on hand-crafted skills. The authors turn a single monolithic model into an embodied multi-agent architecture. Several agents split the cognitive work and coordinate with people. A team design like this may fit messy real workflows better than one giant model.
arxiv-2512-00897:
Kfir Eliaz and Ran Spiegler model a data monopolist in a 2025 economics paper. Imagine one firm that curates a database for users who want to learn a changing parameter. Some users, nowcasters, want the parameter's current value. Others, forecasters, care about its long-run value.

Storing data costs the firm a constant amount per unit. The monopolist designs a menu of contracts, each pairing a fee with a level of data access. The paper studies what menu a profit-maximizing firm would offer, a practice the title calls monopolistic data dumping. The results speak to pricing and access in today's data markets.
arxiv-2512-00997:
Param Biyani and four coauthors introduce IndiMathBench in a 2025 paper on machine-checked math. Autoformalization turns worded math problems into formal statements a theorem prover can check. Even with strong language models, doing this reliably is hard, and good training data is a major bottleneck.

Expert annotation takes deep skill in both math and theorem proving. IndiMathBench is a human-verified benchmark for evaluating mathematical theorem proving. It was curated with an AI-powered, human-assisted pipeline that formalizes natural language problems in the Lean language. A trusted benchmark shows whether autoformalization tools are ready for real mathematical work.
arxiv-2512-01097:
Zachary Terner, Alexander Petersen, and Yuedong Wang present Smart Bayes in a 2025 statistics paper. Classification can be generative, modeling how each class produces data, or discriminative, learning the class boundary directly. Naive Bayes is the classic generative method, while logistic regression is the classic discriminative one.

Smart Bayes bridges the two. It feeds ratio-based features from the first approach into a logistic-style classifier. From the first side, it relaxes Naive Bayes's fixed unit weights, letting the data set the weights on ratio features instead. The hybrid could keep Naive Bayes's stability on small data while gaining the sharper boundaries of the second.
arxiv-2512-01197:
Yuzuru Inahama studies random paths that jiggle with long memory. In his setup, noise comes from fractional Brownian motion. That noise keeps a trace of its past, unlike plain random steps. The paths that result are called fractional diffusion paths.

Inahama asks what those paths look like when they must end at a set point. A path forced to hit a fixed end is called a bridge. He builds the math for these fractional bridges. Such bridges help in fields where a random path must be tied to a known start and end, like in finance or physics.
arxiv-2512-01297:
Shruti Rastogi and Vaibhav Vaish study the intersection complex of a threefold as a motive. The intersection complex is a tool that tracks the shape of singular spaces. Morel's work framed it through weight cuts. That frame drives the new work.

The pair build a new object in the world of motivic sheaves. It is made for set schemes and weight profiles. Their object aims to capture the intersection complex in motive terms. Work at this level helps unify how singular spaces are counted and compared across geometry fields. A motive-level form also lets the complex be moved and compared across base changes, which older forms did not allow with ease.
arxiv-2512-01797:
Cheng Gao and co-authors hunt for neurons tied to hallucinations in language models. Models often state false facts with full confidence. Past work blamed data or training goals at a broad level. Neuron-level causes stayed largely unexplored until now.

The team finds a set of neurons linked to hallucination acts. They study the impact and origin of those neurons. If a small set drives many false claims, targeted fixes become feasible. Neuron-level insight could lead to monitors that flag risky outputs as they form. Hallucination neurons may cluster by fact type, which would let monitors watch the riskiest sets during high-stakes use like medicine.
arxiv-2512-02097:
When particles collide slowly, the rules of quantum mechanics demand that probability is never created or destroyed, a constraint called unitarity. Marcos Flores and Kalliopi Petraki build in 2025 a tidy scheme for non-relativistic scattering that respects that demand while joining elastic and inelastic channels.

Inelastic channels, where collisions change the particles' internal state, secretly shape the elastic ones through the optical theorem. The authors show those effects can be deduced consistently, leading to non-local separable potentials and a compact unitarization scheme. Getting unitarity right matters for effective theories of dark matter and nuclei, where scattering calculations must not leak probability.
arxiv-2512-02297:
Fifth-generation mobile networks are becoming software systems, with the radio access network steered by small applications called xApps. Philip Rodgers and Paul Harvey propose in 2025 an xApp Store, a framework for bringing such apps on board and deploying them in open RAN networks.

The app-store model invites third-party developers into an ecosystem that was once closed to a few vendors, much as phone apps once did. Onboarding needs vetting, packaging, and deployment machinery that telecom lacks today. A working store framework could diversify who builds the intelligence inside future mobile networks.
arxiv-2512-02397:
Clusters in data can be judged by how their points spread in space and by how the mass is shared among them, and the two views need not agree. Emanuele Bossi, C. Tyler Diggans, and Abd AlRahman AlMomani introduce in 2025 the Boltzmann-Shannon Index, a normalized measure of density balance across clusters.

The index compares a geometry-based distribution over clusters with a frequency-based one, quantifying how similar the clusters' densities are. A single balance score helps analysts compare clusterings and spot lopsided groupings. Clustering underlies customer segmentation, image grouping, and exploratory science, so better quality measures propagate widely.
arxiv-2512-02797:
Sebastian Zieglmeier and four co-authors schedule data driven control across the working range of a nonlinear system. Data enabled predictive control steers a system using recorded behavior instead of a physics model. One global dataset struggles when the system behaves differently in different regimes.

Their gain scheduled version splits the range of a measurable scheduling variable into regions. Each region gets its own Hankel matrix, built from rich recorded data. Control then blends these local descriptions as conditions change. The approach suits engines, robots, and processes whose dynamics shift with speed or load. Local charts for each zone keep the math lean, since each chart need span just its own small patch of work.
arxiv-2512-03397:
Robots and drones need to know where they are without GPS. Seungwon Choi, Dong-Gyu Park, Seo-Yeon Hwang, and Tae-Wan Kim present Surfel-LIO in this 2025 work. It is a LiDAR-inertial odometry system, blending laser scans with motion sensors.

Recent advances in map structures have made such systems faster. Surfel-LIO pre-computes surfels, small surface patches, and uses a hierarchical voxel hashing scheme. Fast, accurate tracking matters in tunnels, warehouses, and disaster sites. The design aims for real-time speed without losing precision. Pre-computed surfels shift work ahead of time, which frees the live system for speed.
arxiv-2512-03697:
Rafael Machado and colleagues report, candidly, how hard it is to measure energy efficiency honestly on supercomputers. Their 2025 paper tests synthetic benchmarks and the Gromacs molecular dynamics package on two German clusters, Fritz and Alex. Intel and Nvidia hardware both came under the meters.

Runs used full sockets with MPI parallelism while Likwid and vendor profiling tools recorded power and performance. The metrics those tools return hide pitfalls the team hit repeatedly, from sampling quirks to attribution traps. Results are presented alongside the mistakes, deliberately. Their closing best practices aim to save the next efficiency study from the same misreadings.
arxiv-2512-03797:
Placing an ordinary superconductor against a magnetic topological insulator may create an exotic state that hosts Majorana modes, particles prized for quantum computing ideas. Daniele Di Miceli and colleagues model that proximity effect analytically in a 2025 superconductivity preprint. Their film has finite thickness, and a conventional s-wave superconductor sits on top of it.

Treating the tunnelling between the two layers as a small perturbation, the authors derive the leading correction to the anomalous Green's function. From it they extract how the induced pairing varies with position, spin, and momentum across the film. One formula gives the decay length of the pairing at zero momentum directly. Stronger magnetisation, they show, boosts spin-polarised triplet pairing and p-wave contributions. The results clarify how topology, magnetism, and superconductivity interact in such films, guiding attempts to realise Majorana modes in real devices.
arxiv-2512-03897:
Gibbs measures describe the statistical state of a system in equilibrium, and a log-Sobolev inequality for such a measure controls how fast the system settles down. Guopeng Li, Jiawei Li, and Leonardo Tolomeo examine that inequality for a Gibbs measure built from the focusing Schrödinger equation, in a 2025 analysis preprint. The measure dates back to Lebowitz, Rose, and Speer in the late nineteen eighties.

The answer splits at an exponent threshold. When the power in the equation sits between two and four, the authors show the measure does satisfy a log-Sobolev inequality. Above four, they prove a lower bound on the curvature of the potential. That bound shows standard techniques for proving such inequalities cannot work for this measure. The note maps where a widely used analytical tool succeeds for this classic measure, and where new ideas are needed.
arxiv-2512-03997:
Not every scholarly paper announces a discovery; some exist to dispute one. Dmitry Shatilov writes such a comment in a 2025 accelerator physics note, aimed at a design study for the future FCC-ee collider. The original article proposed monochromatisation optics for producing Higgs bosons directly in the s-channel, a scheme that narrows the collision energy spread.

Shatilov divides the original work into two parts, parameter choices and optics design, and addresses only the first. His charge is blunt: the proposed parameters do not look realistic, and they raise many questions. Space limits him to the most important objections. The comment is a reminder that flagship collider designs are stress-tested in public, parameter by parameter, before metal is cut. Readers get a compact list of the points the original authors would need to defend or revise.
arxiv-2512-04097:
Genetic algorithms breed solutions by mixing and mutating a population, but they need a starting population, and for language tasks nobody knew whose words should seed it. Isabelle Diana May-Xin Ng and colleagues answer: sample several large language models at once. Their MultiGA framework, presented in a 2025 preprint, treats different models' outputs as the gene pool.

Each parent model generates candidate solutions, and a neutral fitness function scores them without favouring any source. An iterative recombination loop mixes and refines the generations until an optimal answer emerges. The authors report high accuracy across multiple benchmarks. Their framing suits tasks where picking a single pretrained model in advance is unclear or suboptimal, since the population hedges across models' strengths. They position the work as a foundation for combining multiple language models in evolutionary search.
arxiv-2512-04197:
Error-correcting codes can be drawn: valid codewords are the independent sets of a confusion graph, far apart by design. Yuting Li, Ryan Gabrys, and Farzad Farnoud exploit that picture in a 2025 information theory preprint. Their move is to build codes through distributed graph colouring, borrowing algorithms from the LOCAL model of computing.

Computing one vertex's colour, via a modified version of Linial's algorithm, yields an efficient encoder and decoder. The harvest is broad. The authors construct uniquely decodable codes that fix any fixed number of errors, whatever their kind, at twice the Gilbert-Varshamov redundancy. A hypergraph labelling extension gives list-decodable ones. They add an incremental synchronisation scheme, plus the first asymptotically optimal codes for bursts of unbounded-length edits. Compared with syndrome compression, they claim more flexibility and no reliance on a good base code.
arxiv-2512-04397:
Zeeshan Ahmad, Shudi Bao, and Meng Chen compare six ready-made deep learning models on the task of spotting disease in chest X-rays. Training a big model from scratch for medical scans is rarely practical. Transfer learning solves that by reusing a model trained on general photos, then tuning it for the new task. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests how far that shortcut goes for disease detection.

The team fine-tuned AlexNet, three sizes of ResNet, VGG16, and InceptionV3 on a custom chest X-ray set. Each model sorted scans into disease classes from image features. InceptionV3 came out ahead in their runs. The study reports the full comparison across accuracy and related scores. For clinics and labs with modest compute, such head-to-head results help pick a starting model with care. The work also maps the limits of off-the-shelf models on medical data.
arxiv-2512-04597:
Tao Wu, Chuhao Zhou, Guangyu Zhao, and co-authors argue that robots answering questions in real spaces should sometimes say they do not know. Embodied question answering sends an agent to look around a scene and reply. Old benchmarks assume every question has an answer. Their 2025 arXiv paper starts from a study of five hundred human queries. A third of those queries lacked key context.

From that study and from theories of human talk errors, the team names five cases that call for silence. They cover tasks the agent cannot do, vague references, taste-based choices, missing information, and false premises. They then extend the OpenEQA benchmark with questions reshaped to hit those cases. Leading agents were graded on whether they abstain when they should. The results expose how often current systems guess instead. Honest silence is a safety trait for home robots and guides.
arxiv-2512-04797:
The SIMA team at Google DeepMind, with Adrian Bolton, Alexander Lerchner, and many co-authors, introduces SIMA 2, a generalist agent that plays and works inside many three-dimensional virtual worlds. Built on a Gemini foundation model, it goes well past the first SIMA, which followed only simple commands. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents an agent that reasons about high-level goals, chats with its user, and follows complex instructions given in words or images.

Across a diverse portfolio of games, SIMA 2 closed much of the gap with human performance. It carried its skills into worlds it had never seen, while keeping the base model's reasoning intact. The team also shows open-ended self-improvement: Gemini itself proposes fresh tasks and hands out rewards, letting the agent practice without human trainers. Such agents point toward game partners and testers that learn new worlds on their own.
arxiv-2512-04897:
Samuel Poncé and Xavier Gonze ask what small correction standard theory misses when it adds up the total energy of a solid. Most calculations first freeze the atomic nuclei in place and solve for the electrons alone, then add the nuclei's motion back in afterward. That split, dating to Born and Oppenheimer, works well, but tiny leftovers matter when researchers must tell apart crystal forms whose energies differ by a hair.

The authors sort out the versions of the split, write an exact form for the total energy, and list the extra terms order by order. One grouped set, the part due to electrons and vibrations acting together, shows up partway through the list, and in diamond it proves small but too big to ignore. They also check that every computed term behaves consistently as the system grows.
arxiv-2512-04997:
Raphael Maggio-Aprile, Maxime Rambosson, Christophe Coreixas, and Jonas Latt present LEDDS, an open-source framework for simulating grains and fluids together on a single graphics chip. The coupled method pairs a lattice scheme for the fluid with a particle scheme for the grains, and such codes are usually hand-built for one brand of hardware. LEDDS instead writes every step — neighbor search, collision checks, and the fluid-grain handshake — as standard building-block operations that any modern platform can run.

Benchmarks cover colliding spheres and stretched grains, wall friction, a settling particle, a tumbling grain in shear flow, and grain-laden streams. Despite the high-level style, LEDDS matches the speed of hand-tuned code written for one vendor's chips, while staying readable and portable. The authors offer it as a blueprint for multiphysics tools that need not be rewritten each time hardware changes.
arxiv-2512-05097:
Kirsten Knudsen and ten co-authors peer at one of the faintest known galaxies from the universe's first billion years, magnified by a gravitational lens. The galaxy, cataloged as A383-5.1, had been flagged by the Webb telescope as a Little Red Dot, a puzzling new class of early object. Using the ALMA observatory, the team measured a spectral line from doubly ionized oxygen, complementing an earlier carbon line detection.

The oxygen line is strikingly strong next to the carbon line, a ratio that points to gas poor in heavy elements and dust. True to that picture, ALMA sees no dust glow at all. The team argues the galaxy is bathed in a strong ultraviolet field that dust cannot blunt, letting its light escape to help ionize the space between galaxies. The result adds a clue about what Little Red Dots are and their role in cosmic reionization.
arxiv-2512-05397:
Rachel Poonsiriwong and eight co-authors test whether meeting your future self changes the decisions you make today. Life choices are hard partly because people cannot picture how their older selves will live with the outcome. The team built digital twins: personalized avatars aged thirty years, with progressed faces, cloned voices, and language-model dialogue. The twins have seemingly lived through the scenarios a participant is weighing. The team used them in a randomized study with young adults facing real binary decisions.

Participants imagined alone, or consulted avatars presenting one option, both even-handedly, or three including a generated alternative. One-sided avatars pulled choices toward the option shown. Balanced ones moved people in both directions. The invented third option won real adoption, suggesting such twins can expand choice by surfacing unseen paths. Participants valued reasoning and meaning-making over vividness, sharpening questions about autonomy in deciding.
arxiv-2512-05797:
Ronen Brilleslijper and Oliver Fabert lay groundwork for carrying Floer theory from mechanics into field theory. In symplectic geometry, Floer theory is the sharpest tool for proving that Hamiltonian systems have periodic solutions. Its engine is a link between gradient lines of an action functional and special surfaces that elliptic methods can handle. Field theory needs a bigger home, called multisymplectic geometry, where time becomes a surface or volume.

For the two dimensional case, the authors build a multisymplectic framework to keep that engine running. They prove a Darboux theorem, the local flatness result every such framework needs. Then they show the gradient lines of their action functional are again special objects: pseudo-Fueter curves, defined through a compatible almost hyperkähler structure. It means the analytic machinery that powers Floer theory in mechanics has a foothold in field theory, opening a path to existence results for field equations.
arxiv-2512-06097:
Emre Umucu and six co-authors teach language models bedside manner. General chatbots fail healthcare dialogue twice: wrong facts, cold tone. Their framework uses direct preference optimization, training on pairs of answers, the better one marked. Preferred responses here are supportive, plain spoken, and correct; rejected ones are prescriptive or jargon laden. No separate reward model is needed.

The tuned systems beat baselines, including Google's medical dialogue systems, on accuracy and empathy scores. The code is open. Preference alignment offers accuracy and humanity together. For exhausted caregivers, tone is not decoration. An answer that is right but brusque may not be followed; an aligned model aims to be both correct and actually heard.
arxiv-2512-06297:
Luca Di Carlo, Chase Goddard, and David Schwab resolve a puzzle about the shape of the error surface inside neural networks. Good solutions often sit in basins joined by low error paths, so one might expect training to wander along them. In practice, training stays put in one basin. The authors trace this to barriers that are not made of high error, but of high curve.

Away from a basin's floor, the surface curves more sharply, and the jitter of training turns that curve into a push back toward the floor. Their tests show this push lasts longer than plain error based barriers, and it shapes where solutions end up late in training. The picture helps explain why linked basins do not mean free roaming, and why the spot a network lands in can matter long after the error looks flat.
arxiv-2512-06797:
Gabriel Peyré surveys a family of math tools that machine learning now leans on to move and reshape clouds of data. Many tasks, he notes, come down to guiding how a spread of points changes over time. That includes drawing new samples, training the weights inside a neural network, and tracking tokens as they pass through a large language model. Different jobs, Peyré argues, share one basic shape underneath.

Two views of the same motion sit at the heart of the survey. One follows the cloud as a whole, while the other follows single particles carried along by a flow. Peyré weighs two main methods built on these views. Diffusion adds controlled randomness and powers much of modern image and text generation. Optimal transport instead seeks the cheapest way to move one spread into another, and both appear across sampling, training, and model design.
arxiv-2512-07097:
David Wang, Jiale Zhang, and Pei Zhang inspect sealed packages with nothing more than cheap radio tags. Logistics firms struggle to catch counterfeit goods, fraudulent returns, and hidden hazards without opening boxes, and present screening is slow or costly. TagLabel uses ordinary passive RFID tags, the kind already stuck on merchandise. As radio waves pass through different materials, the returning signal's strength and phase change in telling ways.

The system first works out which way the package faces, using phase differences between tags, which tags are shadowed, and antenna patterns. It then reads the contents through the most shadowed tag, where the material's fingerprint is strongest. Configurations with two or three tags were tested, with learning classifiers turning signal patterns into verdicts. Combined, the pipeline identified orientation and material with accuracy above four fifths across all facings, in realistic radio conditions.
arxiv-2512-07297:
Yingying Cai, Jiuyi Zhu, and Jinping Zhuge measure how much a solution of an elliptic equation can hide inside a flat two-dimensional domain. Unique continuation asks a sharp question. If a function vanishes on a small patch, must it vanish everywhere? The quantitative version asks how its features scale. Their setting carries a vanishing Neumann condition, a constraint on the slope at the boundary, over domains with mildly rough or convex edges.

The authors establish sharp estimates for three quantities: how many critical points the solution can have, its doubling index, and the total length of its level curves. The key maneuver is a classical duality that trades an A-harmonic function for its stream function, converting the Neumann problem into a Dirichlet one, where the theory is better understood.
arxiv-2512-07497:
JV Roig wrote this 2025 paper on how language models fail when they act as agents. An agent model uses tools over many steps to finish a job. Roig studies where that process breaks down in practice.

The evidence comes from a benchmark called the Kamiwaza Agentic Merit Index. Roig reads hundreds of execution traces from three well-known models. The tasks span file systems, text extraction, spreadsheet analysis, and databases. Instead of trusting total scores, the study inspects each trial in fine detail. Winning runs share habits of careful, grounded action across steps. Failing runs fall into four repeating shapes. Models act before checking, invent missing items to seem helpful, or chase distractors. They also break down when the workload grows heavy. Raw size does not predict sturdy agent behavior, the traces show. One model's edge came chiefly from reinforcement post-training, not scale.
arxiv-2512-07797:
Lingyao Li and six co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on chatbots and mental health. People increasingly turn to language model chatbots for emotional support. The practice carries risks around misinformation and over-reliance.

The authors gather a large crop of public posts from six social platforms. Those posts show how users discuss their chatbot use across conditions. A language-model-assisted pipeline sorts the material by sentiment and values. The lens for that sorting is Value-Sensitive Design, a human-centered framework. Clear condition-specific patterns emerge from the crowdsourced record. Neurodivergent users, including those with ADHD or autism, report strongly positive experiences. They describe practical and appraisal support from their chatbot chats. Users with higher-risk disorders show more negative sentiment in contrast.  One-size-fits-all design, the authors argue, should give way to condition-specific care.
arxiv-2512-07897:
Lucas Isenmann wrote this 2025 computer science paper on a trust problem in digital currencies. Duniter-based coins pay out a kind of universal basic income. Fake identities, called Sybil attacks, could farm that income unfairly.

Their defense is a Web of Trust built on a social graph. Graph rules, time limits, and a licence together police who may join. Isenmann studies a simplified version of those graph rules in depth. He asks how large an attack the rules can absorb at all. The answer depends on the number of attackers and the system's parameters. In pure theory, ignoring social and time limits, huge attacks can slip through. The graph rules alone cannot, in general, bar them completely. Reality is kinder than that worst case suggests. For a live Duniter currency with thousands of users, the graph rules suffice. Attacks of large size are stopped by the rules as deployed.
arxiv-2512-08197:
Jianyang Zhou, a researcher in aviation data science, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about predicting flight departure delays. A delayed incoming flight does not always delay the next departure, because airports and airlines can absorb some lateness during turnaround. Standard prediction models treat earlier delays as fixed inputs and miss that recovery process entirely.

Zhou builds a two stage machine learning framework that models absorption directly. First, a CatBoost classifier estimates the chance that a flight absorbs its upstream delay, using operational, timing, and weather features. That chance becomes a score fed into a second classifier that predicts delays over fifteen minutes. On United States domestic flight data with national weather records from summer 2023, the framework beat baseline models clearly. It also revealed which airports recover well, giving planners a practical tool for managing delay before it spreads.
arxiv-2512-08497:
Fiona H Panther and Paul D Lasky, gravitational wave astronomers in Australia, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. When two neutron stars merge, the hot remnant may collapse to a black hole at once or survive briefly, and its faint post merger gravitational waves carry that answer. Single events are too weak to claim, sitting below the detection threshold.

The authors show how to combine many such sub threshold events coherently. Counting what fraction of remnants collapse promptly, and pairing that with the mass distribution read from the louder inspiral signals, gives an indirect measure of the maximum neutron star mass. With a few dozen events, they estimate the mass of hot, rapidly spinning neutron stars to a useful precision. That, in turn, constrains the equation of state of hot nuclear matter. Compared against cold star data, it could hint at phase transitions inside these extreme objects.
arxiv-2512-08697:
Athena Psalta, Vasileios Tsironis, and Konstantinos Karantzalos ask which visible traits person re identification models really rely on. Those models match images of the same person across cameras and reach high accuracy, but their choices stay opaque. Knowing which semantic traits matter would make the systems easier to trust and improve.

Their framework, MoSAIC ReID, uses a mixture of experts, with each expert tied to a single trait such as clothing color. A router that knows the traits allows controlled tests of trait importance. The system stays competitive on two standard data sets when trait labels are given at test time. Broader analysis with statistical tools shows that common traits, such as clothing colors and personal features, matter most. Rare cues, such as accessories, contribute little. The work gives a clear method for interpretable matching systems.
arxiv-2512-08797:
Francesca La Piana introduces a variant of quantum magic squares that is based on graphs and studies when a classic theorem survives in the quantum setting. A recent result showed that a quantum analogue of the classic Birkhoff von Neumann theorem can fail for quantum magic squares in general. Questions from quantum automorphisms of graphs motivate the new graph based version.

La Piana shows the analogue already fails for the four cycle graph, giving an explicit counterexample. That small case makes the failure concrete and easy to examine. The author also shows that these objects admit descriptions by monic linear matrix inequalities. As a result, they form compact free spectrahedra, a well structured class in convex geometry and operator theory. The work links quantum symmetry questions for graphs with matrix convexity, giving both a negative result and a clean structural description.
arxiv-2512-09397:
Joshua Zahl surveys a quarter century of progress on the Kakeya conjecture, a famous problem in Euclidean geometry. A Kakeya set contains a unit line segment pointing in every direction, yet can be astonishingly small. The conjecture concerns how small such a set's dimension can be, a question tied to deep problems in harmonic analysis.

Zahl's survey emphasizes developments since the year 2000, updating the earlier accounts by Wolff and by Katz and Tao. It traces how new methods reshaped the field, including the arguments that recently settled the three-dimensional case and pushed knowledge in higher dimensions. The survey is written as an invited lecture for the 2026 International Congress of Mathematicians. For readers, it offers a single entry point into the ideas, milestones, and open ends of one of modern analysis's most watched problems, from the conjecture's statement to the current frontier.
arxiv-2512-09597:
Aymeric Lutier, Frédéric van Wijland, and Jean-Baptiste Fournier study self-propelled particles that lay down chemical trails and then steer toward those trails. Systems like slime-depositing bacteria are examples of active matter: each particle moves on a surface while leaving chemicals that bias motion through chemotaxis. When the steering is orientational, a torque turns the particle toward the chemical gradient, coupling every particle to its past path.

That self-coupling breeds an instability. A particle diffusing can abruptly switch to trajectories curled with a radius comparable to its size, becoming trapped by its own trail. The authors argue this trajectory instability happens for any strength of chemotactic coupling, not strong coupling alone. In different regimes the mechanism differs: sometimes it is a first-passage problem over a barrier, sometimes a rare-event effect. The paper isolates a mechanism behind a behavior seen across trail-laying systems.
arxiv-2512-09697:
Sheng Zhao and Peng-Bo Li propose a quantum system that realizes a three-body interaction at the level of single quanta. Three-body interactions can produce phenomena impossible with pairwise couplings, but engineering them is challenging. Their system combines a magnonic mode, a collective spin excitation in a YIG sphere, with an Andreev spin qubit and a superconducting qubit.

The Andreev qubit's spin-dependent supercurrent and circuit integration let the trio couple. Destroying a magnon excites both qubits, and the reverse process excites a magnon and the superconducting qubit when the Andreev qubit de-excites. Studies show that starting the magnon in a coherent state makes the qubit populations collapse and revive in synchrony. During the collapse periods, the entanglement reorganizes: three-party entanglement converts into two-party entanglement between the qubits and back, with the total conserved. The authors highlight this redistribution as unique to three-body coupling.
arxiv-2512-09797:
Blessed Guda and Carlee Joe-Wong present M3Net, a digital twin for computer networks. A digital twin is a virtual copy of a real network, used to predict how it will behave. New services such as self driving cars and virtual reality bring strict demands on delay and reliability, and older tools like simulators struggle to be both accurate and fast. M3Net uses a graph neural network with a mixture of experts design to estimate several performance measures at once.

Unlike earlier models that tracked one metric or used only simulated data, M3Net reads an expanded set of network state information across varied scenarios. In tests it sharpened predictions of flow delay, cutting the average percentage error noticeably. It also predicted jitter and dropped packets with solid accuracy. The authors argue the design moves network twins closer to practical use in managing fifth and sixth generation networks.
arxiv-2512-09897:
Haoye Lu, Pavan Seshadri, and Kaheer Suleman introduce SCOPE, a planner for text based environments that asks a large language model for help only once. Long horizon planning in text worlds is hard, with open ended actions and sparse feedback. Querying language models throughout training and play is expensive. SCOPE instead has the model generate subgoals at the start, drawn from example trajectories. A small student model is pretrained to plan toward those subgoals.

Skipping repeated model queries makes the system far cheaper to run. The trade off is less explainability and possibly imperfect subgoals, yet on TextCraft they gave hierarchy a strong start. SCOPE slightly beat a leading language model based agent on success rate. The dramatic gain was speed: inference time fell from well over two minutes per episode to a few seconds. One round of teacher guidance carries much of the benefit of constant supervision.
arxiv-2512-09997:
Basabendu Barman and colleagues use gamma ray data to constrain dark matter that was created by gravity itself in the early universe. Such gravitationally produced dark matter barely interacts, making it hard to test. The team uses diffuse high energy gamma rays from our galaxy, measured by the LHAASO observatory and the Fermi-LAT satellite. Four candidate particles are tested: a dark photon, a heavy right handed neutrino, a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, and a non-minimally coupled scalar.

For the first three candidates, the combined data force the interaction strength down to extremely small values for particles heavier than about a teraelectronvolt scale. The scalar is bounded less tightly but still strongly. Photon to dark photon oscillation adds further limits, closing a region of parameter space for heavier dark photons that earlier work had left open. The results narrow where gravitational dark matter can hide.
arxiv-2512-10097:
Mira Littmann and colleagues check whether a future muon collider could catch long lived particles that other searches miss. A ten teraelectronvolt muon collider would probe the energy frontier, but decaying muons flood its detector with background. Timing cuts tame that background with little loss for ordinary particles. The authors ask what those cuts do to metastable charged particles, using a supersymmetry benchmark where the stau partner of the tau lepton lives long and appears as a heavy, slow track. Nominal timing selections prove too restrictive for such particles.

Loosening the time acceptance recovers sensitivity, even to particles nearly as heavy as half the collision energy allows. The team draws concrete recommendations for tracker design and reconstruction. The stakes are general: long lived particles are a generic prediction of theories beyond the Standard Model, and a detector optimized only for prompt particles could be blind to them.
arxiv-2512-10597:
R Bailhache and H Appelshäuser review dileptons, pairs of a lepton and its antiparticle, as messengers from the quark-gluon plasma. Colliders smash heavy ions to recreate the deconfined soup of quarks and gluons that filled the early universe. Dileptons are emitted at every stage and then escape untouched, unlike hadrons, which only report on the final moments.

The pair's mass separates radiation from the hot partonic stage from later hadronic emission, opening measurements no hadron can give: how fast the plasma settles into equilibrium, its average temperature. And signs of chiral symmetry returning in the hot medium through vector meson decays. The price is a heavy background from ordinary hadron decays. The review, published in the Annual Review of Nuclear and Particle Science, gathers what colliders have learned so far and the push for more sensitive future experiments.
arxiv-2512-10897:
Thomas Borsoni and Virginie Ehrlacher prove that a quantum system in a crystal can be watched without disturbing the result. An observability inequality bounds how well measurements on part of a system reveal the whole state. And for the von Neumann equation, the law of motion for density matrices, a bound was known in free space but not in the periodic setting of a crystal.

Their proof follows the strategy of Golse and Paul: a stability argument between the quantum dynamics and its classical Liouville counterpart, with the gap measured by an optimal-transport-style pseudo-distance. The work lies in rebuilding every tool for the periodic case, using the Bloch decomposition, periodic Schrödinger coherent states, periodic Töplitz operators, and periodic Husimi densities. The resulting bound holds uniformly as the reduced Planck constant shrinks, exactly the regime where quantum and classical descriptions meet.
arxiv-2512-10997:
Anija R. and co-authors introduce a new measure of uncertainty for lifetime data, built from the Mathai Haubold entropy applied to remaining life. Entropy measures help describe how spread out or unpredictable a distribution is. The authors also define a dynamic version that changes with time and show it can pin down the underlying distribution uniquely.

Practical use needs ways to estimate the new measures from data, so they build non-parametric estimators based on smooth estimates of the survival curve. A large Monte Carlo simulation study checks how well those estimators perform. Real examples use failure times for aircraft windshields and for mechanical switches, showing how the dynamic measure can be applied to reliability questions in engineering.
arxiv-2601-06897:
Viktoriia Borovik and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with elimination ideals of plücker ideals and algebras with straightening laws. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. It is well known that the Plücker ideal defining the Grassmannian is generated by quadratic Plücker relations.

These relations form a reverse lexicographic Gröbner basis and endow the Plücker algebra with the structure of an algebra with straightening laws (ASL). Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07297:
Bo-Lun Huang and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers WISE/CatWISE constraints on dysonian Waste-Heat technosignatures in nearby galaxies facilities. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. We search for galaxy-scale ( Dysonian ) waste heat in the mid-infrared using WISE .

Starting from the 2MASS Redshift Survey , we cross-match to CatWISE2020 and AllWISE , apply standard MIR AGN/starburst vetoes (Stern. Assef R90, Jarrett), and treat W1 and W2 as stellar baselines and W3 and W4 as constraining bands. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07497:
Sergio Conti and coauthors treat sharp edges in solids with smooth fields, in a 2026 analysis preprint. Their phase-field approach targets energies set on splits of a solid, built to model grain edges in polycrystals. Grains are small crystals with different orientations inside a metal or ceramic. The variable takes values in the orthogonal group, adjusted by the lattice point group.

That adjustment reflects the crystal symmetries of the underlying lattice. Two orientations that differ by a symmetry should count as the same physical state. A good approach must respect that match while still being fit for use in math work. Phase-field models see wide use to track how small scale forms grow. This work strengthens their mathematical base for polycrystals. Applied mathematicians and materials scientists both have reason to read it. The grains are tiny, yet their edges shape how strong or weak a solid is.
arxiv-2601-07697:
Anna Shapiro sets three formulas side by side for a new polynomial tied to polymatroids. The cave polynomial is new, and it was brought in to study syzygies of polymatroidal ideals. Syzygies describe relations among the equations defining an ideal. Her 2026 preprint studies the counting links between the three formulas. Each one counts the terms of the polynomial in its own way.

As a use, she reads the Snapper polynomial through all three of them. Multiple views of one object often reveal facts that a single view hides. Polymatroids generalize matroids, a core structure in combinatorics and optimization. The paper serves those who work in algebra and counting and who use such polynomials. It also shows how a new invariant can connect older, separate lines of work. Each view is short to state, yet each one brings out facts the rest can hide.
arxiv-2601-08097: Yongliang Miao, Yangyang Liang, and Mengnan Du present AdaJudge, a reward modeling method from Emory University. Their 2026 arXiv paper addresses a core step in aligning language models with human choices. Most reward models squeeze a full sequence into one score with a fixed pooling rule. The authors list two flaws in that habit. A fixed bias can miss task-dependent preference signals, and backbone features tuned for generation may suit fine judgment poorly. AdaJudge answers with adaptive judging from multiple perspectives.
arxiv-2601-08197: A natural account of galactic magnetic fields is offered through multistate scalar field dark matter. The 2026 arXiv paper, co-authored by Miguel Alcubierre, studies fields of order microgauss seen across galaxies. The authors test whether these fields arise from a complex scalar field dark matter halo. In their setup, the halo carries charge under a local U(1) symmetry. If the mechanism works, dark matter itself could seed the magnetic fields telescopes observe. That link would tie two open problems in astrophysics into one testable story.
arxiv-2601-08397: Shohei Aoki and co-authors build empirical transit spectra of Mars from TGO and NOMAD data. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that transit spectroscopy probes exoplanet atmospheres, a powerful but tricky tool. Aerosols strongly affect spectra, and accounting for them is key to recovering atmospheric properties. Mars offers a well-characterized atmosphere to practice on. The team models its transit spectrum with petitRADTRANS and the Planetary Spectrum Generator. Lessons from Mars can sharpen how researchers read spectra of distant rocky planets.
arxiv-2601-08497: Jia-Xin He and Hung-Hsuan Chen present GraphFusionSBR for session-based recommendation. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that session-based systems must infer user intent from short click sessions. Existing models suffer from item interaction dominance and noisy sessions. The authors propose a multi-channel model that denoises across three graph views. Channels include a knowledge graph, a session hypergraph, and a session line graph. Fusing several views aims to capture intent that any single graph would miss, improving suggestions for anonymous shoppers.
arxiv-2601-08597: Aryaman Patel and Dario Weissmann stratify moduli spaces of Higgs bundles through stability under covers. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies slope-stability of reflexive twisted sheaves over a normal projective variety. The question is how stability behaves under pullback along a cover. Stability is always preserved when the cover does not factor through a quasi-etale cover. One special cover checks stability across all Galois covers, yielding a stratification of the moduli space. The result organizes Higgs bundle moduli for algebraic geometers.
arxiv-2601-08697: Nifu Dan audits how online graduate computer science students collaborate with AI. The 2026 arXiv case study notes that generative AI now shapes how students complete academic tasks. These systems offer efficiency and support for learning and coding work. Concerns persist about over-automation, diminished student agency, and unreliable or hallucinated outputs. The audit examines real collaboration in one online graduate setting. Findings can help instructors set AI policies grounded in observed student behavior rather than guesswork.
arxiv-2601-08997:
Ziqiang Guan and a large team study a nickel based stuff that splits into layers when it cools. The stuff is a three layer nickel oxide. In its wave state, charge piles in a set wave plan. The team reads that shift with slant light in the heat ray range. Light slant lets them split in plane from out of plane acts.

They find a sharp split. In plane, the stuff acts like a metal. Out of plane, it acts like a block. In the wave state, that split grows by more than ten fold. Out of plane flow all but stops. A reader in new stuffs gets a clear sign. Wave order can peel layers apart in how they carry charge.
arxiv-2601-09297:
Ioana-Claudia Lazar studies a class of shape groups built from triangle and pentagon tiles. Such groups act on spaces with a set bend rule, called CAT(0). That rule says triangles in the space are no fat than flat ones. It is a broad sign of a tame, no wild fold space. Tile groups of this kind are test cases for that tameness.

She shows a tile form of these groups has two neat local traits. It is 7-located and locally 5-large, in the terms of the field. Those traits give new cases of groups with both marks. A reader in group shape work gets fresh cases to test broad claims on.
arxiv-2601-09497:
Ritabrata Chakraborty and three co-authors probe why object detectors stumble on new datasets. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies cross-dataset object detection through the lens of setting specificity. A detector trained on one benchmark often scores far worse on another.

The authors sort benchmarks into two kinds: broad sets with varied everyday scenes, and narrow sets tied to one setting. They then run a standard detector family across all train-test pairs. The pattern of wins and losses shows how much of the drop comes from the setting itself. That diagnosis helps builders choose data that travels better.
arxiv-2601-09597:
Manish Chaudhary studies how to grow complex entanglement by letting a system leak in a controlled way. His 2026 arXiv paper treats dissipative state engineering with Markovian dynamics. Highly entangled states shared among many parties are key resources for quantum computing tasks.

The target here is a cluster-state pattern of entanglement in spins coupled by Ising interactions. Instead of shielding the system from its surroundings, the method engineers the leak itself. The engineered dissipation drives the spins toward the desired entangled state. Such recipes could make delicate states easier to prepare and hold.
arxiv-2601-09697:
Jieying Chen, Jeffrey Hu, Joan Lasenby, and Ayush Tewari make camera-controlled video generation fast enough to use. Their 2026 arXiv paper combines sparse diffusion with 3D rendering for static scenes. Diffusion video models make realistic clips but can need minutes of GPU time for seconds of footage.

That cost blocks real-time uses such as embodied AI and virtual or augmented reality. The authors shift work into a 3D render, using diffusion only where it is needed. Static scenes are the target, where geometry can carry most of the image. Faster generation opens interactive applications that current models cannot serve.
arxiv-2601-09897:
Nestor Colin and four co-authors extend a classic symmetry theorem to huge surfaces. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves a Birman-Hilden result for big mapping class groups. The surfaces involved are connected, without boundary, and either infinite in type or of negative Euler characteristic.

Given a fully ramified branched covering between two such surfaces, the authors prove it has the Birman-Hilden property. That property lifts symmetries of the base to the cover. Big mapping class groups govern infinite surfaces like flute surfaces. Work of this kind gives the field shared ground rules it did not have before. Extending the theorem there strengthens tools for a fast-growing area of study, one that more and more young researchers are now choosing to enter.
arxiv-2601-10197:
Maxwell West proves that some quantum states are hard to learn on mean. Two sets of states are in play. One set is drawn flat from all states. One set comes from free fermion states. A learner sees data from a state's birth spread.

West works in the stats query model. In that model, the learner asks for rough means, not raw data. He shows the task is hard on mean for both sets. Hard here means the query count must be vast. The work marks a bound on what such learners can do. It aids the map of quantum learn tasks.
arxiv-2601-10297:
Hans-Christoph Grunau and Marius Müller find whole space best forms for a fourth order free edge task. The task is a biharmonic form of the Alt Caffarelli model. Such models trade bulk cost against the size of a set where the field is live.

The team study forms that span all space. Half space forms win for the two sided case. They do not win in the one sided case. The team find a next class of best forms too. All forms in that class have a flat Laplacian. The work sorts which shapes can be global bests.
arxiv-2601-10397:
Genki Shimizu and Taro Toyoizumi build a theory of fast, linked change at nerve joins. A join can grow or shrink for a short span based on use. That fast change is named short term plasticity. It was seen as a pre side sieve for spikes. The post side was thought to play no role.

Fresh tests show the change can link both sides. It rests on pre and post fires at once. The team give a rule based theory for that link. Their theory rests on how much fact a join pass can carry. It shows why a linked form would aid a net.
arxiv-2601-10697:
Manuj Mukherjee, Sagnik Chatterjee, and Alhad Sethi study how parties can cook up a shared secret key from shared randomness. Nitinawarat and Narayan built a perfect scheme for the pairwise independent network model. That model's backbone is a graph, and the scheme leans on how many spanning trees the graph packs. The new work swaps the graph for a hypergraph.

In a hypergraph, one edge can join many parties at once. The authors push toward perfect key schemes that use the hypergraph's own structure. Perfect keys leak nothing to an eavesdropper. Extending the graph results would widen the networks where such strong secrecy is possible by design, not by extra hardware.
arxiv-2601-10797:
Alice Crafford and co-authors, with the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration, probe a weak point in photometric redshift work. Most science from the LSST survey will rest on photo-z estimates, distances inferred from galaxy colors. Training sets from spectroscopy anchor those estimates. If the training set is incomplete or skewed, bias creeps into every distance.

The authors diagnose how such training set flaws hurt photo-z performance. Knowing the failure modes lets survey teams correct or at least bound the bias. Distance bias would ripple into maps of dark matter and dark energy. This groundwork helps LSST keep its cosmology honest from the start.
arxiv-2601-10897:
Boris A. Malomed, Gennadiy Burlak, Gustavo Medina-Ángel, and Yuriy Karlovich study light from quantum nanoemitters set in a lattice of conducting nanorings. The emitters sit in a periodic array where plasmon polaritons, waves that mix light with electron motion, are excited. The team investigates the semiclassical dynamics of the optical field the emitters produce.

The focus falls on dynamical correlations and chimera-like states. In a chimera, some parts of a system move in sync while others drift apart. Seeing such states in a nano-optical lattice would link two lively fields. The results may guide devices that steer light at the nanoscale with patterns no uniform array could make.
arxiv-2601-11397:
Emma Hart, Bas Peters, Julianne Chung, and Matthias Chung infer hidden states with paired nets. Their 2026 preprint builds a latent space inference framework. Inverse problems ask what hidden cause made the seen data. Mismatches between observations can wreck classic solvers.

The frame uses two autoencoders trained as a pair. One net encodes the parameter space of the problem. The other encodes the observation space in matching form. Learned maps join the two latent spaces to each other. Inference then runs in the small latent world, not the raw one. That shift can absorb gaps between data sources. It offers a data-driven path to steadier inverse answers.
arxiv-2601-11497:
Yamato Fujii and five coauthors check a hidden error in reaction cross sections. Their 2026 preprint deals with alpha-particle activation measures. Below the Coulomb barrier, such reactions are faint and rare. Secondary neutrons in the setup can fake part of the signal.

The test reaction makes 195m Pt from natural platinum. Alpha hits drive it, but stray neutrons can drive it too. The team characterized the secondary neutron field first. They used the PHITS particle transport simulation code. Neutron-driven yields were then estimated from library data. The JENDL-5/A library gave the neutron cross sections used. Knowing the fake share keeps the true cross section honest.
arxiv-2601-11597:
Martin Rivas asks if one point can describe an electron in this preprint. His 2026 answer to the title question is yes. The point is not the whole electron in his view. It marks the location of the electron's center of charge.

Rivas reads the geometry of smooth curves in 3D space. That reading yields a system of differential equations. The system is of fourth order for the moving point. The point moves at the speed of light at all times. Such a picture gives the electron a sharp trajectory. It stands apart from the cloud views of standard theory. The claim invites fresh debate on what an electron is.
arxiv-2601-11797:
Tenghao Li, Neha Sangwan, Xiaxin Li, and Arya Mazumdar study group testing when counts are noisy. In group testing, pools of samples are tested at once to find the few bad ones. The quantitative form asks how many bad ones sit in each pool.

They study three cases: no noise, added Gaussian noise, and a one-way noisy channel. For each case they test two methods. One scores links in a linear way, and one uses least squares fits. The work maps how well each method does as noise grows, which guides test design in labs.
arxiv-2601-12197:
Bihan Chatterjee, Siva Theja Maguluri, and Debankur Mukherjee refine the wait time spread in a classic queue. The M/G/1 queue has Poisson arrivals and general service times. In heavy traffic, the sojourn time tends to an exponential spread, a known limit.

They seek higher-order terms that hold before that limit. They use Stein's method to build those terms. Better finite-traffic forms help size real service systems. Call centres and cloud queues both need such pre-limit tools.  Stein terms add shape past the known limit form.  Pre limit forms are what real queues need, since no queue is at the limit.
arxiv-2601-12597:
Ron M. Adin, Eli Bagno, and Yuval Roichman study how to turn one cyclic permutation into another. Their moves are conjugations by adjacent transpositions, swaps of neighboring items lifted into the permutation. The target is the canonical cyclic permutation, a standard reference form. They ask how many steps the hardest case can take.

They prove upper and lower bounds on that maximal step count. They also bound the diameter of the underlying Schreier graph. Diameter is the longest shortest path in that graph of states. Sorting time questions of this kind sit in combinatorics and computer science. Tight bounds tell us the true cost of sorting by such restricted moves.
arxiv-2601-13097:
Elena Bruches and a large team present a small reward model for tests that need no run. Their tool scores unit tests that code models write on their own. Running each test can be slow, costly, or unsafe, so a run free score has clear worth.

The model is named RM-RF. It is kept light, so it can score many tests fast. A reward model of this kind can rank tests by how good they look. That rank can then steer a code model to write better tests. For teams that use AI to draft code, a fast test score helps pick which drafts to keep, run, or drop.
arxiv-2601-13497:
Jiayi Chen, Ming Lu, and Shiquan Ruan build a bridge of two rings, a Hall algebra and a ring of double symmetric functions. The Hall side comes from the Jordan quiver, the most plain quiver with one node and one loop. Its derived form counts how modules grow.

The next side holds symmetric sums in two sets of count less vars. Each set is held fixed by its own swaps, and a parameter t marks the ring. The team proves the two rings are the same in form. Such a bridge lets results proved on one side cross to the next. For algebra staff, a new bridge is a tool in its own right.
arxiv-2601-13597:
Shyam Agarwal, Hao He, and Bogdan Vasilescu ask how AI coding tools change real software work in 2026. Some tools sit in the code editor and suggest lines as a person types. Newer agents act on their own, writing code and sending pull requests to merge it. The true effect of agents on live open-source projects is still not clear.

The team tracks agent use over time in many open-source code stores. They match projects that took up agents with like projects that did not. They then use a staggered diff-in-diff method to judge cause, not just links. The work aims to show what agents change, for good or ill.
arxiv-2601-13897:
Ankita Joshi and co-authors build an AI method to trace white matter fibers in the brain in 2026. Tractography rebuilds fiber pathways in a non-invasive way from scans. Those maps show brain connectivity and guide precise neurosurgery. Classic methods used deterministic and probabilistic rules to trace each fiber.

Deep learning and deep reinforcement learning have improved tract reconstruction in recent years. The team's TractRLFusion uses a GPT-based multi-critic policy fusion frame. Multiple critics judge each tracing policy, and their views are fused. Better tract maps could sharpen surgical plans and brain studies.
arxiv-2601-14197:
P. G. Beck and a large team weigh a star at a key life stage with two methods in 2026. Asteroseismology gives precise masses for solar-like oscillating stars. It uses individual frequency modeling or homological scaling relations. These methods have not been dynamically validated on the main sequence.

No eclipsing double-lined binary benchmark exists for that stage. The team measures a dynamical mass for a solar-like oscillator at the main sequence turnoff. They combine Gaia astrometry with ground-based spectroscopy. A dynamical mass can test if seismic masses are as true as claimed.
arxiv-2601-14297:
Tzula B. Propp, Brandy Todd, Sara A. Metwalli, and eight co-authors issue a call to action in this 2026 paper. Their field is quantum science. The year 2025 marked one hundred years since the discovery of quantum mechanics. In that century, the field grew into a global community. It now spans academics, engineers, developers, and entrepreneurs.

The authors write for that whole community. Their title says the paper is about meeting the needs of quantum scientists worldwide. It is a position piece, not a lab report. Readers get a view of what a broad team of insiders thinks the field must do next to serve its own people.
arxiv-2601-14497:
Noam Soker examines a fading star event in this 2026 paper. The event is M31-2014-DS1, a yellow supergiant in the Andromeda galaxy that dimmed sharply. One proposed account is a failed supernova. In that scenario, most of the yellow supergiant collapsed to form a black hole. Only a weak display reached the outside.

Soker tests that scenario and finds it wanting. He argues it requires unlikely fine-tuned parameters to work, if it works at all. His title calls it the failed failed-supernova scenario. Readers get a skeptical audit of a bold claim, with the fine-tuning cost laid out in the open.
arxiv-2601-14697:
Shutong Qiao and five co-authors study generative recommendation in this 2026 paper, set for the ACM Web Conference. Semantic ID learning is a key interface in generative recommendation models. It maps items to discrete identifiers grounded in side information, most commonly via a pretrained text encoder. Those encoders are primarily optimized for well-formed natural language.

Real recommendation data are distinct. Item descriptions are often symbolic and attribute-centric, containing numerals, units, and abbreviations. The team runs an empirical study of what happens when text-as-vision meets semantic IDs in this setting. Lists there are terse and full of codes, not neat prose. A good ID is a small thing with a big job. It must hold all the facts a shop keeps on a thing. Readers get evidence on whether image-like renderings of item text serve recommenders better than raw text.
arxiv-2601-14997:
K. Punnam Chandar and Y. Ravi Kumar describe how to turn CT scans into 3D printable models. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with medical images stored in DICOM format. Building a 3D STL model from 2D scan slices helps doctors grasp a structure's shape and any deformity.

The steps start with cleaning the CT images. Contrast is raised, noise is cut, and the images are smoothed. The cleaned scans are then split into regions by a threshold rule. From the 2D contours of those regions, the team rebuilds the full 3D model.
arxiv-2601-16097:
Makbule Ozsoy works on ways to turn words in many tongues into graph queries. Her 2026 preprint deals with tools that turn plain speech into code for data stores. Such tools exist for text to SQL and kin tasks. Most past work backs speech in just one tongue, English. True use needs the same skill in many tongues at once.

Ozsoy joins small add on parts, called adapters, into one fused tool. The join uses both fixed mix rules and learned mix gates. Fused parts let one tool serve many tongues with less cost. The work aims to open graph data stores to more users. It tests if fusion beats a lone part per tongue.
arxiv-2601-16297:
Ryuichiro Kitano and Shohei Okawa link the cut off of the Standard Model to proton death. Their 2026 preprint deals with why no proton death has yet been seen. It also deals with why neutrino mass is so small. Both facts may stem from chance guards in the known model. Those guards hold as long as no death terms sit at low scale.

The pair ask how high the model can run sans new terms. That top scale is the cut off of the model. A high cut off would leave death too slow to see yet. It would also keep neutrino mass small in a plain way. The work ties two null finds to one scale.
arxiv-2601-16397:
Qianqi Yan and coauthors cite proof as they write short forms of ward cases. Their 2026 preprint deals with sums that join text and pics in care. Trust needs more than smooth text from such tools. Each claim in a sum should point to its source span. Past tools oft add cites post hoc, with weak links to truth.

The new frame cites spans and pics as text is built. It uses the gaze weights of the coder to find source spans. No fresh train is needed for the cite step. Live cites let ward staff check claims with speed. The work seeks trust in AI ward sums.
arxiv-2601-16697:
Hitomi Mori, Yuta Kikuchi, Marcello Benedetti, and Matthias Rosenkranz probe the true cost of quantum tools. Some quantum tools solve sets of linked math tasks. Such tasks sit at the core of many quantum apps. Their cost is gauged by calls to a data source. Their 2026 preprint sets a floor on that cost.

The floor turns on how sparse the task's grid is. Sparse grids have few non-null marks in each row. The team proves no tool can beat their floor. Such floors tell builders what gains are even in reach. They also show where sparse tasks stay cheap or dear.
arxiv-2601-16797:
Paulo dos Santos, João Mendes, José de Almeida, and Luís Coelho speed a key task in nano-optics. Tiny metal bits can trap light at their skins. That trap hums at a set tone for each bit shape. Labs need that tone to build sensors and light tools. Full wave sims give true tones but run slow.

Their 2026 preprint takes a leaner path for odd shapes. The path treats each bit as a set of small poles. It skips the heavy grid work of full sims. Fast tones let teams scan many shapes in a day. That pace aids design of chips that sense germs or gas.
arxiv-2601-16897:
Antesh Upadhyay, Sang Bin Moon, and Abolfazl Hashemi join four fixes for learn-by-crowd AI. Crowd learn trains one model from many phones or sites. No raw data leaves each site in that scheme. Four plagues hit it: rules, slow links, local steps, and drop-outs. Their 2026 preprint, FedSGM, treats all four in one frame.

The frame swaps steps by a switch rule as it goes. It needs no costly dual weights or sub-solves. Tight links are squeezed both ways in the frame. Part crowds can join or leave with no break. Such frames suit health and phone AI at scale.
arxiv-2601-17497:
Mohammed Barhoush, Arthur Mehta, Anne Müller, and Louis Salvail ask if top-grade security can exist for quantum functional encryption. Functional encryption lets users compute set functions on locked data. The ideal shield is simulation security. In the classical world, that ideal is known to be impossible. Those proofs, though, rest on classical steps.

Quantum rules may open or close new paths. The authors test if the ban holds in the quantum case. Their answer shapes what quantum crypto can promise. Overpromised security is a real-world risk. A firm bound tells builders what to aim for. The work sits where quantum physics meets data privacy.
arxiv-2601-17597:
Shih-Yu Chang builds spectral tools for noncommuting operators. Classical spectral theory fully describes one normal operator. It fails when operators do not commute.
