europmc-pmc2276197:
Kulich and a large team validated two symptom questionnaires in 2008 for dyspepsia, persistent upper abdominal discomfort, across six countries and languages. Reliable symptom measures are needed to manage patients and run multinational trials. In all, 853 patients completed the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale and the reflux-and-dyspepsia Quality of Life questionnaire, plus general health and mood surveys for comparison. Versions covered Afrikaans, German, Hungarian, Italian, Polish and Spanish speakers.

Internal consistency ranged from 0.43 to 0.87 for the symptom scale, and 0.79 to 0.95 for the quality-of-life questionnaire. Repeat-test reliability reached 0.82 for the quality-of-life tool. That supports its stability over time. Patient samples came from the six countries studied. The symptom scale's abdominal pain domain correlated with all quality-of-life domains in most languages. Both tools separated patients by symptom frequency and severity. The authors judge both fit for multinational trials.
europmc-pmc2361397:
Kelesidis, Kelesidis, and Mantzoros reviewed adiponectin and cancer in 2006. Adiponectin is a hormone released by fat tissue that helps the body respond to insulin. Obesity raises the risk of several cancers, and the authors asked whether this hormone helps explain why.

People with obesity tend to have low adiponectin, the opposite of most fat-made hormones. The review gathered evidence linking low adiponectin to cancers of the breast, womb lining, colon, and other sites tied to obesity. In lab work, the hormone slowed cancer cell growth and countered signals that favour tumors. The authors also set out the molecular paths that might carry these effects. They closed by listing open questions, since much of the human evidence was still indirect.
europmc-pmc2363697:
Söllner and co-authors checked whether cancer doctors spot patient distress in 2001. Between 20% and 40% of cancer patients suffer emotional distress, and the worst affected should be offered counselling. The study compared doctors' judgements with tested screening questionnaires.

They followed 298 patients starting radiotherapy, rated by eight oncologists. Agreement between doctors and the screening tools was weak, with match scores near zero once chance is removed. Doctors recognised severe distress in only 11 of 30 severely distressed patients. They missed distress more often in head and neck and lung cancer patients, and in lower-class patients. Offers of counselling tracked visible disease spread and how much patients denied problems, not measured distress. The authors called for training doctors to identify distress better.
europmc-pmc2363897:
Egrie and Browne described a longer-lasting red cell hormone in 2001. The hormone, erythropoietin, tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, and a lab-made version treats anaemia, a shortage of red cells. Studies had shown that more sugar coating on the molecule meant it lasted longer in blood, even though it gripped its target less tightly.

Acting on that trade-off, engineers built a version with five sugar chains instead of the natural three. The new protein, called NESP or darbepoetin alfa, is heavier and carries more negative charge. In animal studies it lasted about three times longer in blood than the standard version and acted more strongly. That meant fewer injections for the same effect. Human trials for anaemia were under way when the authors wrote.
europmc-pmc2408797:
The Anglian Breast Cancer Study Group tested breast cancer cases drawn from a whole defined population for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations in 2000. Faults in these two genes greatly raise breast and ovarian cancer risk, but most estimates came from high-risk families. This group instead tested 1,220 unselected cases diagnosed before age 55 in one English region.

They found eight BRCA1 carriers, 0.7% of cases, and 16 BRCA2 carriers, at 1.3% of the series, after adjusting for test failures. Rates rose sharply for women diagnosed before 35 and with more affected relatives. Still, most carriers were older at diagnosis, and few had an affected close relative. Estimated breast cancer risk by age 80 was 48% for BRCA1 carriers and 74% for BRCA2 carriers, with wide uncertainty ranges. Together the genes explained only 17% of the inherited share of breast cancer risk.
europmc-pmc2423197:
Loi and a large team built a gene-based predictor for hormone-sensitive breast cancer in 2008. These cancers carry the estrogen receptor and are treated with tamoxifen, a hormone-blocking drug. Yet 30% to 40% of such patients relapse anyway, so better forecasting tools were needed.

They trained the predictor on 255 tumor samples from women treated with tamoxifen alone after surgery. The final classifier used 181 genes grouped into 13 clusters of genes that rise and fall together. Six clusters covered cell division pathways. In an independent set of 362 patients, the classifier split women into two outlook groups with a hazard ratio of 2.01 between them. In 112 patients with spread cancer, one cluster pointing to inflammation predicted who would respond to tamoxifen. The clusters aid reading the biology, not just the score.
europmc-pmc2516597:
DiGiulio and colleagues searched for microbes in the amniotic fluid of women in preterm labour in this 2008 study. Infection inside the womb is a suspected cause of early birth, but many microbes resist standard laboratory culture. The team therefore paired culture with DNA-based tests that detect bacteria, fungi, and archaea directly.

They studied fluid from 166 women whose waters had not broken. Combining both methods found microbes in 15 percent of women and 18 kinds in total, against 9.6 percent and 11 kinds by culture alone, including uncultivated bacteria never described before. A positive DNA test was strongly linked to womb inflammation, and every woman testing positive delivered early. More bacterial DNA meant an earlier delivery.
europmc-pmc2569097:
Hansen and colleagues examined in 2008 how heat waves affect mental health in Adelaide, Australia. People with mental illness are known to be vulnerable in extreme heat, partly through behaviour and partly through medicines that disturb body temperature control. The team analysed hospital admissions and deaths tied to mental and behavioural disorders across 1993 to 2006.

Above a threshold of 26.7 degrees Celsius, admissions for these disorders rose with temperature, climbing 7.3 percent during heat waves compared with other periods. Disorders that increased included dementia, mood disorders, and stress-related conditions. Deaths tied to mental disorders also rose during heat waves. The rise hit people aged 65 to 74. It also hit those with schizophrenia and related conditions. The authors urge better care planning for the mentally ill as heat waves grow more frequent.
europmc-pmc2571997:
Pierleoni, Martelli, and Casadio introduced a prediction program called PredGPI in this 2008 paper. Many proteins sit on the outer face of the cell membrane. A GPI anchor holds them there. This fatty tether is attached after the protein is cut at a site called the omega site. Finding such proteins from sequence alone helps annotate genomes, but older predictors made too many mistakes.

PredGPI pairs two machine learning methods, a hidden Markov model and a support vector machine. It predicts both whether a protein gets an anchor and exactly where it is cut. It was trained on a carefully checked, non-redundant set of confirmed cases. In tests it beat all previous methods. It also reproduced published large-scale experiments, with a lower false positive rate. The authors offer it as a fast screen for whole proteomes.
europmc-pmc2762797:
Christensen, Griffiths, and Farrer reviewed in 2009 adherence in Internet interventions for anxiety and depression, open websites that deliver cognitive and behavioral therapy. Such sites can be effective, yet open-access versions suffer poor adherence, with almost no users finishing all modules in some reports. Understanding dropout is key to lifting their public health impact.

In randomized trials, attrition was far lower than on open sites, ranging from about one to fifty percent. Disease severity, treatment length, and chronicity predicted adherence in several studies. Very few trials asked why users dropped out, and most handled missing data poorly in their statistics. The authors call for theory-based models of adherence and deeper work on disease factors in this setting.
europmc-pmc2820097:
Domenici and a large team searched blood samples in 2010 for protein patterns that set apart depression and schizophrenia. Diagnosis of these disorders still rests on spoken symptom reports, since no blood test exists. The team profiled seventy-nine proteins at once in plasma from about two hundred forty-five depressed patients, two hundred twenty-nine patients with schizophrenia, and two hundred fifty-four healthy controls.

Single-protein tests flagged more differences than chance allows. Insulin and a tissue-cutting enzyme called MMP-9 stood out for depression, while a brain growth factor, BDNF, and several immune signals stood out for schizophrenia. Combining proteins into panels separated patients from controls better than any single marker. The authors call the panels candidate signatures needing tests in fresh groups.
europmc-pmc2826397:
Prill and colleagues assessed the DREAM3 challenges in 2010, a set of contests that grade how well computer methods can reverse-engineer biological networks. Systems biology builds models of cell networks, but claims about each method's skill rested on home-made tests. The DREAM project instead hands teams blinded datasets and scores their answers against withheld truth.

Forty teams sent in four hundred thirteen predicted networks and measurement sets across four challenges. A handful of teams clearly led, while most submissions scored no better than random guesses. Merging many teams' answers, even weak ones, sometimes beat the best single method. The authors say such blind tests give the field the context it needs to judge modeling claims.
europmc-pmc2847997:
Kosaka, Izumi, Sekine, and Ochiya asked in 2010 whether human breast milk carries microRNAs, the tiny RNA snippets that fine-tune gene activity. Milk is known to feed babies and school their immune systems with antibodies and live cells. Because microRNAs steer immune development, the team profiled which ones milk contains across the first six months of nursing.

Milk proved rich in immune-related microRNAs throughout that period. The molecules also survived strongly acidic conditions in tests, suggesting they can pass through a baby's stomach intact and be taken up as food. The authors propose that mothers hand infants ready-made gene regulators along with nutrition, a form of genetic material transfer outside reproduction.
europmc-pmc2851497:
Wu and colleagues followed survivors of SARS in 2007 to learn how long their antibodies against the virus last. SARS, the first pandemic disease of the century, could return from animal reservoirs, so knowing the protection window matters. The team tracked one hundred seventy-six patients from seven hospitals in Shanxi Province, China, testing blood at set points over three years.

Antibodies against the SARS coronavirus held at solid levels for about two years on average. In the third year, both the share of patients still testing positive and their antibody levels dropped significantly. The authors conclude that recovered patients could become open to reinfection once past roughly three years from their first exposure.
europmc-pmc2852297:
Garman reviewed in 2010 the radiation damage that X-ray beams inflict on the protein crystals used to solve molecular structures. Brighter synchrotron beams revived the problem even for crystals frozen to a hundred degrees below zero, since the beam's energy breaks bonds as it passes through. The review lays out the basic causes, the typical doses involved, and what researchers have learned about slowing the decay.

Damage grows in proportion to absorbed dose, which in these experiments runs to millions of grays. Early work on myoglobin showed a single photon can disrupt dozens of molecules, and later studies found specific weak points such as sulfur bridges breaking first. Garman weighs cryocooling, dose limits, and scavenger chemicals as partial defenses.
europmc-pmc2853097:
Tsujiura and colleagues tested in 2010 whether stomach cancer leaves a readable fingerprint of microRNAs in the blood. Stomach cancer kills heavily worldwide, and its standard blood markers miss too many early cases. The team first confirmed that microRNAs stay stable and measurable in plasma, then compared cancer patients' levels with the tumors themselves and with blood drawn after surgery.

In sixty-nine patients and thirty healthy volunteers, four microRNAs ran significantly high in patients while let-7a ran low. Levels fell after tumor removal, tying the signal to the cancer. One combined ratio, miR-106a over let-7a, separated patients from controls best. The authors propose circulating microRNAs as a complementary, needle-only route to detection and monitoring.
europmc-pmc2883597:
Bengsch and colleagues examined in 2010 why killer T cells fail against chronic hepatitis C infection. In lasting infections these cells become exhausted, wearing multiple off-switch receptors that blunt their attack. The team studied thirty-eight chronically infected patients and mapped which off-switches appeared together on virus-specific cells.

About half of the responses carried four off-switches at once, including the well-known PD-1, and those cells multiplied poorly and sat at a mid-stage of maturity. Their target virus sequences were unchanged, meaning the cells still saw their prey and kept being triggered. The other half wore few off-switches, kept an early-stage profile, and faced virus that had mutated away from them. Exhaustion deepens while the target stays visible, the pattern suggests.
europmc-pmc2890697:
Hu, Zhang, Shen, and Azhar reviewed in 2010 how steroid-making cells secure and process the cholesterol that all steroid hormones are built from. Steroids govern reproduction, salt balance, stress response, and much else, and they are made mainly in the adrenal glands and gonads. Those tissues burn through cholesterol as raw material, not just as membrane building blocks, so supply must never fail.

The review traces four supply lines. Cells make cholesterol from scratch or free it from stored droplets. They also pull it from blood particles through a docking receptor, or draw it in selectively through a second route. Inside the cell, carrier proteins shuttle the cargo to the mitochondria, where the first hormone-building step runs. Each hand-off is regulated by the tissue's tropic hormone signals.
europmc-pmc2912897:
Sorra and Dyer put in 2010 the United States government's hospital safety culture survey through a full psychometric workout. The survey asks staff to rate twelve dimensions of patient safety culture, from teamwork to management support, across forty-two items. Data came from three hundred thirty-one hospitals, over two thousand units, and more than fifty thousand respondents.

Statistical checks confirmed the survey's structure holds at the level of the individual, the unit, and the whole hospital, three lenses administrators actually use. Nearly all dimensions showed sound reliability and the expected correlations with each other. One dimension, staffing, fell slightly short on several cutoffs, yet the authors keep it for its real-world importance while flagging careful interpretation. Hospitals can benchmark their culture scores with documented confidence.
europmc-pmc2923597:
Johansson and co-authors caught in 2010 the first step of the most used animal model of ulcerative colitis, a chronic human bowel disease. The model gives mice dextran sulfate in drinking water; inflammation appears after several days, but nobody knew the opening move. The healthy colon is shielded by an inner mucus layer that bacteria cannot cross, and the team watched that shield under the chemical.

On colon tissue kept alive in dishes, the inner layer thinned within minutes and let bacteria-sized beads through. In living mice, bacteria reached the gut wall well before any inflammation could be seen. Breach comes first and inflammation follows, exactly the sequence suspected but never shown in human ulcerative colitis. Protecting or rebuilding the mucus shield becomes a rational therapeutic aim.
europmc-pmc2984397:
Dehaven, Evans, Dai, and Lawton presented a method for turning metabolomics machine output into chemical libraries in a 2010 article. Experiments that profile small molecules struggle to name what they detect without good reference collections.

Their QUICS approach builds library entries from known standards and also from unknown compounds seen in real samples, accounting for every ion in a spectrum. By correlating ion behaviour across a whole sample set, it uncovers subtle patterns pointing to hidden compounds a single spectrum would miss. Worked data from two instrument types show the entries supporting identification and measurement in later studies.
europmc-pmc3042897:
Windle, Bennett, and Noyes reviewed in 2011 the questionnaires used to measure resilience, the ability to adapt and recover after stress or trauma. Interest in resilience has grown among funders and policy makers who want programs that build it across the lifespan. The team searched widely for peer reviewed scales and judged each one on how well it was tested and whether its questions matched a clear definition.

Nineteen measures were found, including updated versions of older ones. Every scale had gaps in its testing record, and the ideas behind several were shaky. Three scales earned the best ratings for measurement quality, yet none qualified as a gold standard. The authors urge researchers to report full validation results whenever these tools are used, so readers can judge the numbers for themselves.
europmc-pmc3063797:
Su and a large Chinese team identified in 2011 the virus behind a sudden egg drop epidemic sweeping duck farms across China. Starting in spring 2010, laying ducks ate less, produced far fewer eggs, and showed diseased ovaries. The team isolated a new virus from sick flocks in several regions and used it to reproduce the same disease in healthy laying ducks, then recovered it again.

Under the microscope the virus was a small, coated RNA virus. Its genome placed it close to a mosquito carried relative first found in Malaysia, and somewhat close to another member of the same family. The authors name it a new flavivirus, a family that includes several human threats. They warn the virus could devastate the duck industry and urge close watching, since its relatives cross into people.
europmc-pmc3278097:
Julia van Gemert-Pijnen and colleagues proposed a holistic framework for designing digital health tools that people actually use, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Many eHealth technologies never become sustainable parts of care. The authors blame designs that ignore how technology, human habits, and the social and economic setting interlock, and they reviewed existing development frameworks to find a better way.

From sixty papers they distilled sixteen frameworks with practical guidance. The visions were often strong, but the link between vision, strategy, and research method stayed obscure, and none handled the stakeholder-driven style of newer web technology. Their remedy combines participatory development, in which patients and professionals co-design, with persuasive design techniques and business modeling. The result is offered as an evidence-based roadmap from first sketch to working, embedded service.
europmc-pmc3279697:
Peter Connick and colleagues gave patients with progressive multiple sclerosis infusions of their own stem cells in this 2012 open-label study in the Lancet Neurology. More than half of patients develop the secondary progressive form, marked by steadily accumulating disability, and no treatment exists for it. Mesenchymal stem cells had helped in animal models, so the team tested safety and early signs of benefit in ten patients whose visual pathways were affected.

Each patient received one intravenous dose of cells grown from their own bone marrow. No serious adverse events occurred; one transient rash and two self-limiting infections were the only notable reactions. After treatment, several vision measures improved, including visual acuity, the speed of signals along the optic nerve, and the nerve's measured area, while other measures were unchanged. The authors call the pattern suggestive of nerve protection, warranting larger controlled trials.
europmc-pmc3354997:
Patel and fellow rehabilitation specialists reviewed wearable sensors and the systems built around them. Their focus was clinical use rather than gadget design: how body-worn devices might monitor patients at home, support recovery, and flag problems earlier than clinic visits allow.

The review introduces the enabling technologies, then surveys applications in health and wellness monitoring, safety, home rehabilitation, judging whether treatment works, and early detection of disorders. It also discusses combining wearable devices with sensors placed around the home to follow older adults and people with chronic conditions. The authors close with what must improve before such systems become routine clinical tools.
europmc-pmc3367597:
Willems and co-authors traced how a drug-resistant gut bacterium, Enterococcus faecium, spread through hospitals worldwide. They compared 411 isolates, both resistant and susceptible to vancomycin, gathered from people, animals, hospitals, and the community on five continents.

One family of the bacterium, known as clonal complex-17, had gone global and kept turning up in hospital outbreaks. It also shrugged off ampicillin and carried an extra island of genes tied to disease. The authors warn that spotting this lineage early matters, because its resistance gene has already jumped into more dangerous germs, and stopping its spread is critical.
europmc-pmc3383997:
Whittle and a large team described in 2012 how a protein called BMP8B turns up heat production in brown fat. Brown fat burns energy as heat and helps balance body weight. Signals called BMPs were known for shaping fat, but not for running its furnace.

Food and cold switched BMP8B on in mature brown fat, sharpening its response to nerve signals and fat-burning enzymes. Mice missing the gene burned less energy, gained weight, and still ate less than normal. The protein also acts in the brain's appetite center, where giving it centrally fired up brown fat through nerve pathways. That two-way action makes it a tempting obesity target.
europmc-pmc3405197:
Varrin-Doyer and co-workers characterized in 2012 the T cells that attack a water channel in neuromyelitis optica, a disabling disease of the optic nerve and spinal cord. Patients make antibodies against the channel, called aquaporin 4, and such antibodies need T cell help. The team compared blood T cells from patients and healthy controls.

Patient T cells multiplied more strongly in response to the channel, especially to one standout stretch of it. That stretch closely resembles part of a transport protein from a common gut bacterium, and patient cells answered the bacterial piece too, a case of mistaken identity. The responding cells leaned toward the inflammatory Th17 style. The findings open fresh routes into how this disease begins.
europmc-pmc3429397:
Ahuja led a collaborative group that pooled individual records for more than nine thousand patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in 2012. Such tuberculosis shrugs off the two best first-line drugs, leaving longer, harsher, weaker regimens. No randomized trials existed to say which drug mixes and durations work best, so the group combined patient-level data from many centers.

Overall results were poor: only slightly more than half of patients were treated successfully. Success rose with particular treatment durations, with more likely-effective drugs in both phases, and with certain later-generation quinolone antibiotics and related drugs. The analysis, built for the World Health Organization's guideline panel, gives regimen design a firmer evidence base than study-level pooling could.

The Science of Ethics as Based on the Science of Knowledge is A E Kroeger's 1897 translation of Fichte's System der Sittenlehre of 1798. Johann Gottlieb Fichte meant his ethics to grow from the same root as his whole philosophy: the free, self-positing I. Where the Science of Rights ordered men together, this work orders the single soul.

Fichte derives duty from the I's drive to be wholly self-determined, answerable to its own law. Conscience, on his account, is the voice of that law, and it cannot err when honestly heard. The system gives the body, the scholar, and the citizen each their moral place. It crowns the great trilogy of Fichte's Jena years.
freeman-jerome-1897:
Jerome, A Poor Man came from Harper in 1897 with pictures by A. I. Keller. Freeman dedicated the novel to her father. Chapter one finds Jerome at twelve, basking in a secret hollow in a great rock ledge.

The hollow shields the boy from cold northwest wind while spring sun warms him. Peach trees bloom on a hill nearby, and a ploughman's shouts drift over the fields. Grown, Jerome stays poor until money comes to him and brings a heavy moral test. His long struggle to do right, in a town quick to condemn, makes a quiet and strong study of conscience.
frus-1861-d197:
Cassius Clay wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 June 1861. The dispatch is document 197 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Clay's first report in the file comes from his new post in Russia. He found a court that spoke warmly of the Union. His June letter began a run of good news from the north that ran through the whole war. His run of reports from Russia forms the happiest thread in the year's record. The happiest thread in the record runs north, and Clay's letters spin it.
frus-1861-d297:
Seward heard from Mr. Harvey on 25 August 1861, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 297 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the first summer of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d97:
A reply dated 14 October 1861 went from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons in Washington. The letter is document 97 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A same day answer was swift work for the age. Seward and Lyons kept a brisk exchange through that autumn, claim by claim. This reply shows the Secretary meeting British pressure with equal speed, in the hope that quick words would keep small points small. Quick answers also denied London any ground to claim its notes went unheeded. Quick words, in that season, were a form of respect that both sides prized.
frus-1862-d197:
Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 December 1861, and the letter stands as Document 197 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It came from the British legation a short walk from the State Department.

Lyons wrote while his government waited for Washington's answer in the Trent affair, the dispute over Confederate envoys seized from a British mail steamer. His manner was calm where London's first reaction had been fierce. Letters from his hand in this window show a minister trying to keep a quarrel from becoming a war. Britain's first concern in Washington was the blockade and what it cost British trade.
frus-1862-d297:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 21 July 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 297 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Late July 1862 was the war's low summer for the Union: Richmond saved by Lee. A second Confederate army gathering, and calls in Europe to end the fighting by pressure. Seward's letters to Paris pushed back with facts and resolve. This dispatch shows the Secretary's method at its plainest, steady repetition of the Union's case to the court most likely to act. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d397:
Two days after a companion instruction, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to Bayard Taylor in St. Petersburg, on 24 November 1862. The letter is Document 397 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed to accompany the President's annual message to Congress.

Short follow-up orders were the glue of Civil War diplomacy, since news crossed the Atlantic by ship and took weeks. Seward used them to correct, press, or calm his agents as events shifted. Paired with Taylor's own reports, this note helps a reader watch the Washington end of the Russian correspondence. In that quarter the Union enjoyed rare goodwill during the war.
frus-1862-d497:
On 26 April 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. It is Document 497 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Seward wrote on the day New Orleans fell to Farragut's fleet, the Union's greatest prize of the spring. News of that kind was diplomatic gold, and his orders abroad made the most of it. At The Hague the victory spoke to a trading people: the Mississippi was opening, and the Confederacy was shrinking. The instruction belongs to the confident late-April round of Seward's orders. In them he told his ministers, in effect, that the rebellion had passed its peak. Europe, he said, should take note.
frus-1862-d597:
Spain's minister of state wrote this instruction on 13 December 1861 to General Serrano, the captain general and governor of Cuba. It is Document 597 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, in an appendix of Spanish papers on Mexico.

Unlike most of the volume, this letter is not American at all: it is the Spanish government's own internal order, printed in translation. Cuba was the base and the prize of Spain's American policy, and Serrano commanded both the island and its part in the Mexican expedition. The document lets a reader see the allied move on Mexico from inside Madrid's chain of command, which is why the State Department preserved it.
frus-1862-d697: A Mr. Yrisarri wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. The letter is document 697 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, printed near the papers on Central America. The evidence names the writer and the date but does not state his post or his land, so this note claims no more than that.
frus-1862-d97:
A State Department letter of 11 July 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 97 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d197:
From Washington on 9 May 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction toward London; the catalog title garbles the envoy's name as 'Mr. Adapts,' but the letter belongs to the run addressed to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 197 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d297:
An instruction dated 19 September 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 297 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d397:
To Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this formal note on 23 February 1863. It appears as document 397 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d497:
Dated 7 May 1863, document 497 is a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d597:
Document 597, dated 27 July 1863, records a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the summer of 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d97:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams on 2 March 1863 — and wrote again, and again. Twelve letters to Adams in the volume bear this one date. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 97 in part one of the 1863 volume, the first of the dozen.

A dozen sheets in a day is a desk cleared at one stroke, most likely a set of set-piece notes on the file's live points. Each stands on its own in the printing, numbered in line. This one opens the batch. Read as a group, the twelve show Seward putting the whole London brief in order on a single March day.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d197:
President Roosevelt telegraphed Prime Minister Churchill on 8 November 1943, in personal message number 412, sent from Washington via the naval attaché in London. The whole message takes three short lines and deals with a single phrase in the Allied agreement about Turkey.

Roosevelt accepts Churchill's suggestion that the words commanders responsible be changed to the Combined Chiefs of Staff. He adds that he has already told Ambassador Harriman in Moscow and authorized him to attach the agreement to the protocol. The brief exchange closed the wording dispute that Churchill's telegram 493 had opened two days earlier.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d297: President Roosevelt sent Secretary of State Cordell Hull a short secret telegram from Cairo on 24 November 1943, a progress note from the conference. The Lebanon matter looks better this morning, he reports, though Prime Minister Churchill is being very firm, and Foreign Secretary Eden arrives in Cairo that night. The conferences are going well, Roosevelt adds, and the business with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek will finish in two or three days. Chiang will then return home, and the party will start on the next leg of the trip, toward Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d397:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull sent President Roosevelt a short telegram from Washington on 30 November 1943, questioning the President's choice of Ambassador Winant for the European Advisory Commission. It follows Roosevelt's one-line answer of the day before from Tehran.

Winant would certainly be a fine choice, Hull grants. But the American representative on the commission faces a full-time job, with much detailed drafting and discussion to come. One man, he argues, cannot combine the exacting duties of ambassador to Great Britain with those of commission member and do both jobs effectively. Hull closes by asking whether Roosevelt has any further comment or suggestions in light of that objection, or whether he still wishes Winant to hold both positions.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d497:
Admiral Ernest J. King, commander in chief of the United States Fleet, joined with Admiral Andrew Cunningham, Britain's First Sea Lord, in this memorandum of December 6, 1943. The two naval chiefs signed together on the closing day of the Second Cairo Conference. The State Department printed their paper in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

When the senior sailors of both navies signed one paper, the sea war was speaking with a single voice. Naval questions, above all the shortage of landing craft, ran through every Cairo argument about land operations. A joint King-Cunningham text shows the naval partnership at its closest. Readers get the admirals' shared view at the point where strategy met the hard limits of ships.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d97: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt on November 5, 1943, three weeks before the two men were to meet at last in Tehran. The message is Document 97 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Every exchange that month carried the nearness of the summit, even when its errand was small. The record names the date and the two leaders only. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d197:
No official minutes exist for the noon meeting of September 15, 1944, so the editors print Morgenthau's diary as the fullest account. Roosevelt, Churchill, Eden, and the Under Secretary took up the Phase Two lend-lease agreement. The president read it carefully. He added words to the clause barring export of lend-lease goods. First came "or sold," and then "for profit."

Churchill, Morgenthau wrote, was quite emotional, at one point with tears in his eyes, and thanked Roosevelt effusively once the agreement was signed. Then Churchill asked for the Ruhr minutes, which Morgenthau and Cherwell had agreed not to produce because they made too weak a case. Put out, Churchill restated his position forcefully himself and dictated the new memorandum to a stenographer.
frus-1944-quebec-d297: Writing on 18 September 1944, Prime Minister Churchill addressed his foreign secretary, Anthony Eden, in a message kept as document 297. It appears in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on the 1944 Quebec Conference, published by the Department of State. The text shows the British prime minister briefing his own foreign secretary in the days right after the Quebec meetings ended.
frus-1944-quebec-d97:
Secretary of Agriculture Claude Wickard wrote to President Roosevelt on August 23, 1944. His letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. Wickard ran the department that oversaw American food production. Food was a weapon and a relief tool in wartime.

Cabinet voices beyond war and diplomacy also reached the President. Armies and allies alike needed American food shipments. Planners expected hungry civilians across liberated Europe that winter. A letter from Wickard brought those concerns into summit preparation. For readers, it widens the Quebec story beyond generals and diplomats. Feeding people formed part of winning the peace.
frus-1945-50-intel-d197: A text titled "Memorandum for the File" bears the date 17 July 1946. It survives in print as document 197 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. No CIA yet existed: a board called the National Intelligence Authority ran the work, with the Central Intelligence Group as its staff. The form is a note to the file: no request and no order.
frus-1945-50-intel-d297:
The memorandum of 6 August 1948 names the Record by the Chief of the Special Procedures Group (Cassady) as the man it was written for. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 297 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Reform of the CIA was in the air, with the Dulles survey under way and each agency guarding its own role.

A record memo speaks to the future reader more than to any chief: it exists so the file tells the truth later. Such notes anchor the rest of the paper trail around them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d397:
Robert Schow, the CIA's assistant director for special operations, wrote to planning chief J. Prichard Childs on 26 August 1949. The memo is document 397 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Special operations meant secret work abroad, the most guarded part of the young agency. Schow's office ran that work while Childs tried to fit it into one government wide plan. Their exchange shows the pull between secret action and central control that marked the CIA from its first years. Coordination papers like this one rarely name foes or lands, but they set the frame for all later work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d97:
Magruder wrote to McCloy again on 25 October 1945, keeping his near-monthly rhythm of reports to his patron. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By late October the SSU's position had a shape: tolerated in the War Department, eyed by State, and priced hard by the Budget Bureau. Magruder's letters steered between those forces. Readers should attend to what a chief in his spot could and could not say. He could plead usefulness; he could not command a future. The thread's interest lies in that narrow path, walked in careful prose through the whole autumn of decision.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d197:
Alarmed, Churchill answered on 19 November 1944. This excerpt from his message number 825 to Roosevelt is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It seizes on the President's promise to bring the American divisions home once Germany falls.

Put the two facts together, Churchill argues, and the sum is grim. If the Americans sail home at speed, the French lack an equipped postwar army. They have no time to raise one and no battle experience either. Who then holds down western Germany, up to the present Russian occupied line? Britain could not take the task on without American and French help. All would rapidly fall apart, as it did last time. He closes with a hope that his fears are groundless: “I put my faith in you.”
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d297:
Operations Grenade and Veritable puzzle the combined chiefs in these minutes of 31 January 1945. The Combined Chiefs of Staff record, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, catches a live argument about Eisenhower's coming offensive in the north. The sitting opened at half past two in Floriana.

Brooke questions a line in the record: he had not understood that Veritable was free of Grenade, but rather that it depended on it. General Smith explains the ground. Bradley is advancing on the Prüm-Bonn axis, and a quick reach to Euskirchen would help Veritable as well as Grenade would. Veritable hangs on neither, he says. Eisenhower, then at Bradley's headquarters, must decide by 1 February whether to halt Bradley and shift the troops north for Grenade instead.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d397: Harry Hopkins explained a delay to the President in this note passed at the February 8, 1945 plenary. The Joint Chiefs, he wrote, had told Sumner Welles something awkward. Defending the coasts of certain South American states against Japan would be hard for the United States. That, Hopkins added, was Welles's excuse. The note concerns why some Latin American states had not declared war. An editors' footnote adds a twist: the Defense Department later found no evidence in the Joint Chiefs' files to support Hopkins's statement.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d497:
Roosevelt put the same worry to Churchill in a letter of February 10, 1945. The United States, alone among the three great powers, would have a single vote in the Assembly of the world organization. That fact might endanger Senate ratification of the Dumbarton Oaks agreement. From their talk, he understood Churchill would not object to extra American votes if needed for parity.

He wrote, he said, because Churchill understood the American political situation so well. In reply, he hoped for agreement to the suggestion, should public opinion require some proposal. The letter shows the President counting Senate votes in the middle of the Crimea.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d97:
Colonies and mandates get a briefing book paper of their own under the heading “Dependent Territories.” Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It reports that the State Department has drafted three papers and shared them with no other government yet.

One draft lays out a plan for world trusteeship. A second sets up regional boards to advise on dependent areas. A third states how such areas should be run. The topic was dropped from the Dumbarton Oaks talks, but British, Soviet, and Chinese delegates showed strong informal interest. The drafts were under review by the Secretary's staff group and by the War and Navy Departments before going to other capitals.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d197:
The American chargé in Belgrade reported a Yugoslav plea in a telegram extract dated July 7, 1945. The extract is document 197 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full message appears later in the volume.

Foreign Minister Šubašić expressed a hope, the extract says. He hoped the Big Three meeting will make a public reference to the Tito-Šubašić agreement. He also hoped it will remind the Yugoslav government that it must be carried out. That agreement was meant to join Tito's movement with the exiled royal government and lead to free elections. Shantz adds that he and the British representative believe such action would be desirable. The fragment shows the junior partner in Belgrade's coalition government looking to the summit to hold Tito to his promises.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d297:
Melbourne's despatch from Bucharest, dated June 25, 1945, takes stock of the Rumanian armistice as Rumanians and Russians then saw it. It was the third in his series of broad reports, after pieces on the Rumanian attitude and the Russian attitude. The armistice deal, he notes, touched nearly every problem in the country.

With the war in Europe over, Rumanians asked what the armistice still required of them. Melbourne records how officials, the public, and the Soviet authorities each read its terms. Reports like this one gave Washington a ground level view of a country under Soviet control as the Potsdam talks drew near.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d397:
East Prussia's future is decided in one short recommendation in a briefing book extract dated June 30, 1945. East Prussia should be ceded to Poland, the paper advises. The exception is the Koenigsberg district, which presumably will go to the Soviet Union. The rest of the German province would pass to Polish rule.

The basic data explain the bargain. The Warsaw Polish government claimed the whole of East Prussia. The Soviet Union favored Polish acquisition of the province, or all of it except the northeastern sector. That sector, including the chief city and port of Koenigsberg, Moscow intended to annex itself. The extract shows the map of eastern Europe being redrawn.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d497:
President Truman presses Churchill for joint timing in a message dated July 2, 1945. Ambassador Harriman has informed him, Truman writes, and he concurs, that the new Polish Provisional Government of National Unity has been established in conformity with the Crimea decision. The new government has addressed parallel communications to both leaders, requesting recognition.

On the basis of the assurances the new government has given, and on Harriman's recommendations, Truman plans to accord recognition effective at 7 p.m., Eastern War Time, on July 3. Now the matter has moved this far forward, he argues, any further delay would serve no useful purpose and might even prove embarrassing to both of us.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d597:
Acting Secretary of State Joseph Grew wrote to Secretary Byrnes on July 13, 1945, enclosing a press statement. The letter is document 597 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Grew's statement, made on July 10, dealt with reports of Japanese peace feelers.

Grew gives two reasons for speaking out. First, talk in U.S. speeches and editorials about a Japanese peace offer was growing fast. He feared it would sap war morale at home. He also feared Japan would read it as proof that America would settle for a compromise peace. Second, his firm statement would clear the ground for the President. Whatever Truman later said about what unconditional surrender would and would not mean would then hit with full force in Japan.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d697:
Joseph E. Davies, head of the President's War Relief Control Board, wrote a history memo on Russia, Turkey, and the Straits. Undated and filed July 4, 1945, it is document 697 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It briefs the conference team on the deep roots of the dispute.

Davies starts with Peter the Great, who saw in 1697 that Russia needed ice-free ports. Russia has since sought control of the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles, the doors to the Black Sea. It has also sought Constantinople, holy to the Orthodox faith. Turkish rulers have maneuvered by war and alliance to block those aims since 1640. Their clash made the Eastern Question of the nineteenth century. Davies sums up its drives in a short list. Russia and Austria thirsted for the Mediterranean. Britain guarded the India route. Christian peoples wished for freedom from Turkish rule.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d97:
Ambassador Harriman renewed his requests to Vyshinsky in a letter dated June 25, 1945. The urgent letter is document 97 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Eisenhower had cabled again about scouting Zehlendorf, using the Halle-Berlin highway freely, and enlarging General Parks's party at Babelsberg.

The most pressing matter, Harriman writes, is a high-frequency radio telephone terminal and teletype system in Berlin, with a relay point near Luckenwalde. Major General Stoner and his Signal Corps group, sent from Washington for the job, wait at Frankfurt. The installations take time, and late starts risk missing the conference opening. Harriman also asks that the local Soviet commander in Berlin be allowed to decide such small matters on the spot.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1097:
British drafters wrote this extract of an Economic Sub-Committee report on July 21, 1945. It treats the liability of Italy and Austria to reparations, on economic grounds only. For Italy, the finding is blunt. She already owes America and Britain about 500 million dollars for relief supplies, and the debt is still growing.

Paying that debt alone, the committee holds, would exceed Italy's power to pay abroad for many years. Neither creditor will lend her money to pay reparations, and UNRRA will not ship free goods for that end. The draft suggests other amends instead: Italy might supply, free of charge, goods UNRRA needs for Allied countries such as Greece and Yugoslavia.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1197:
On 19 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum, the same day as a companion paper. Two staff notes in one day show the American military team working at full pace. Each took up a different side of the summit's military questions.

The chiefs' staff had to keep the envoys supplied with the services' view while talks moved fast. Papers were drafted, cleared, and sent within hours. This one is the second of its day's pair. Together the pair shows how much paper a single day of a summit could draw from one staff.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1297:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 18 July 1945. Like its American mates, it did the staff thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The British run of papers in the volume mirrors the American one, date by date.

London's chiefs wrote with their own burdens in view: a tired army, a vast navy bill, and duties from Europe to Asia. This note carries that view at the talks' start. It is preserved in an American volume because the allied staffs shared their paper. That sharing is itself a fact about how the Western war was run.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1397:
Jefferson Caffery, the American ambassador in France, wrote to Georges Bidault, the French foreign minister, on 1 August 1945. The volume prints six Caffery letters to Bidault from the turn of August 1945. The letters came as the Potsdam Conference reached its close in Germany.

France's absence from Potsdam rankled in Paris, and Bidault worked to win a place in the councils that would run Germany. Caffery's letters carried the American answers, welcome or not. This letter was written on the day the Potsdam Protocol was signed. It shows the settlement's second tier being built in parallel. A shut-out ally was being brought into the peace, on terms set here. The run of letters is the volume's fullest view of that process.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-97: Placed after document 710 without a number of its own, this brief note comes from the editors of the Potsdam volume. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series act as signposts in a dense archive. They link papers, explain odd gaps, and give dates the documents omit. Readers who work through the July 1945 files meet this one as a short pause for context.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d797:
Roy Melbourne, the acting American representative in Rumania, wrote to the Secretary of State on July 17, 1945. Document 797 opens Melbourne's thread in the volume. He held the Bucharest post while its chief was absent. Rumania's armistice regime made his desk a hard one. The letter joined the second Potsdam volume.

An acting head of mission writes with care. Melbourne had full duties and a borrowed title. Readers see him reporting Rumania's state as the summit opened. His facts fed the Balkan side of the talks. The document shows the alliance's eastern posts at work: small teams, large problems, and a direct line to the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d897:
The Acting Secretary of State cabled Assistant Secretary William Clayton at Babelsberg on July 17, 1945. The cable takes up a British note about Edwin Pauley's instructions on interim exports from Germany. A wording problem in those instructions had caused confusion in London and Washington.

The Department reads Pauley's approval duty narrowly. His consent is needed only for goods claimed as restitution, not for exports in general. General Eisenhower holds charge of supplies and allocations. The cable says Judge Rosenman backs this reading. It asks Clayton to confirm that Pauley agrees before Washington answers the British note.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d997:
George Kennan sent Washington the full text of his note to the Soviet Foreign Office in this airgram of July 27, 1945. The note, coded Safehaven, concerns control of German assets in Spain. Kennan recalls an American proposal of June 18 for a joint approach to Madrid on behalf of the powers occupying Germany.

Since Soviet officials had issued like warnings to Sweden and Turkey, Washington assumes Moscow has no objection. The note states the shared aim: to prevent German property from being hidden or drained away, and to allow return of looted goods. It says America and Britain will soon ask Madrid to let their missions take control and active management of German property in Spain.
frus-1964-68v03-d97: A 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note from the late 1965 Vietnam volume. The buildup. This note provides that context. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
gao-gaoreports-b-296197: Aerosol Monitoring & Analysis took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298197: Tarheel Specialties doubled its July 2006 protest — two case numbers, one specialty fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298297: Lakota Technical Solutions took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Tech firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-298697: HoveCo took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing. The process stays the same for all.
gao-gaoreports-b-310797: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by CETENAGROUP. Decided February 14, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-297: The Senate restaurants' 2004 and 2003 books got a GAO audit in 2005, and the report examines the revolving fund's statements. The review grades the cafeteria ledgers. The senators' lunches were audited. The statements had to hold up. The senators' lunches were audited.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-897: DOE lab contractors' support costs could be cut in 2005, and GAO's report says additional opportunities existed to reduce the overhead. The findings do the math. The report warns that the lab dollars deserved trimming. The opportunities had to be seized.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-97: SSA's disability claims bots needed guardrails in 2005, and GAO's report says the fast-track effort had to add controls. The findings demand the brakes. The report warns that the disabled applicants deserved a sound system. The safeguards had to be added.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-997: Election officials' views got a GAO review in 2005, and the report gathers local officials' takes on voter registration management. The findings collect the wisdom. The report warns that the voters deserved fair rolls. The views had to be heard. The voters deserved fair rolls.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-397: War trauma diagnoses needed steady rules in 2006, and GAO's report says the war department had to name what its doctors weighed in the mental checks. The findings demand the standards. The report warns that the unseen wounds deserved careful calls. The rules had to be named.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-97: Voluntary climate programs needed a push in 2006, and GAO's report says EPA and DOE should do more to encourage progress. The findings demand the effort. The report warns that the green pledges needed backing. The agencies had to do more.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-597: The UN's books needed disinfecting in 2007 — GAO's report says the world body's oversight could grow teeth with real internal controls in place. The findings press for audit muscle at Turtle Bay. The report's pitch to Congress: keep paying the dues, but start demanding receipts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-697: The terror-fighting playbook had a missing page in 2007 — GAO's report says U.S. law agencies lacked orders for helping foreign partners hunt terrorists. The findings expose the cooperation gap. The report demands the missing directives: teamwork needs a rulebook.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-97: States' Medicaid bills spiked in downturns in 2007, and GAO's report offers strategies to help them handle the rising costs. The findings share the playbook. The report warns that the safety net should not snap when the economy did. The states needed the strategies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-197: The Government Accountability Office dug into federal Real Property: Strategy Needed to Address Agencies' Long-standing Reliance on Costly Leasing in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
garland-wayside-courtships-1897:
Appleton published Wayside Courtships in New York in 1897, with rights reaching back to 1895. A verse up front muses that the meeting of true lovers' eyes seems wrought of chance. Yet the same grim law may rule there as at a grave, the poem warns.

Love stories from the country roads of the Middle West fill the book. Young farm folk find each other at husking bees, church socials, and long walks home. The romances stay sweet without turning soft or false. Garland keeps his realist's eye on the hard lives behind each tender moment, in a charming and humane gathering.
gooderige-witch-stapenhill-1597:
Alice Gooderidge of Stapenhill faced her neighbors' charges in 1597, and the full record of her case survives in print. The Most Wonderfull and True Storie sets out her examinations at length. Few Elizabethan trials left so much of the questioning itself on the page.

The claims are small and close to home: beasts sicken, children ail, and old grudges turn sour. Under hard questioning, the talk moves from harm done to pacts and spirits. Readers can watch a village quarrel grow, page by page, into a capital case. The pamphlet is a tight, clear window on a county trial.
gorky-creatures-that-once-were-men-1897:
J. K. M. Shirazi translated Creatures That Once Were Men into English in 1905, from Maxim Gorky's early stories of the 1890s. Chelkash opens the volume: a bold harbor thief takes a peasant lad on a night smuggling run. Their clash over the money shows two Russias meeting in one boat.

Twenty-six Men and a Girl sets its scene in a damp bakery, where bakers worship a shop girl from afar. Other tales fill doss-houses and roads with tramps, outcasts, and wanderers. Gorky wrote from his own years of wandering, and the tramps made him famous. His sympathy for the lowest became a signature of Russian writing. These early stories still carry raw force.
haines-cia-ufo-role-1997:
A historian inside the CIA told the agency's own UFO story in 1997. Gerald Haines, of the CIA History Staff, wrote CIA's Role in the Study of UFOs for Studies in Intelligence. His account runs from the first saucer summer of 1947 to the year 1990.

Haines tells of the Arnold wave, the secret Robertson Panel of 1953, and the long years of quiet watch. He shows how spy planes and spy craft bred many of the sightings the public laid to space ships. The piece is rare: an agency judging its own part in a myth it helped feed. It stands as the in-house word on the matter.
harsha-charita-cowell-thomas-1897:
E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas made the first English Harsha-Charita in 1897 for the Oriental Translation Fund. Banabhatta, court poet of the seventh century, wrote the life of his king, Harshavardhana, as historical romance. The work opens with Bana's own wandering youth before it reaches the throne it celebrates.

Ornate Sanskrit prose was Bana's glory, and the translation labors honorably to suggest it. Courts, armies, hermitages, and a kingdom on the move pass in gorgeous procession. The book stands as both royal biography and a summit of Sanskrit prose art, now open to English readers.
holderlin-hyperion-1797:
Friedrich Hölderlin published Hyperion, his only novel, in two parts in 1797 and 1799. The text here is the German original, from the second edition of 1822. No English translation of the book is in the public domain. Hyperion, a young Greek, tells his life in letters to a German friend.

He recalls his teacher Adamas, his friend Alabanda, and his love Diotima. He joins the Greek rising against Turkish rule and sees hope curdle into bloodshed. Grief turns him toward nature, poetry, and solitude in his own land. The letters read as hymns as much as narrative. German readers prize the novel as a pillar of their Romantic age.
james-vi-daemonologie-1597:
King James the Sixth sets out the lore of witches in Daemonologie, his book of 1597. James had sat through the North Berwick trials, where witches were charged with raising storms to sink his ship. In talk form, two men weigh magic, witch craft, and ghosts. The king's voice backs the hunts and gives their proof a crown's full weight in law and faith.

He went on to rule England as its first James. His book roamed both realms at once. It shaped the hunts and e'en the stage tales of his age. Few kings wrote such a text.
james-will-to-believe-1897:
William James published The Will to Believe in 1897, a set of essays on faith and inquiry. The title essay defends our right to believe before proof is complete. Some options in religion and life, James argues, are forced, living, and momentous. In such cases, waiting for proof is itself a choice with costs.

Other essays treat morality, life's worth, and the relation of mind and brain. James writes with candor and personal warmth. The book applies pragmatism to religion without reducing faith to utility. It became a classic defense of faith as a legitimate option. Philosophers still assign the title essay.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lutsk-lutzk-101:
Lutsk, a district city in Russian Volhynia, receives a long historical entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The city stands on the right bank of the Styr river. Between 1224 and 1227 about three hundred Karaite families moved there from Wilna. Rabbinite Jews arrived around the same time.

The article follows the community through charters, wealth, and expulsion. Lutsk Jews appear in Witold's 1388 charter of privileges for Lithuanian Jews. By the late fifteenth century the community was rich, with members farming the taxes. In 1495 the Jews were expelled from Lithuania and their estates were handed to nobles. They returned in 1503 and formed two communities, one Rabbinite and one Karaite, each with its own synagogue. The entry preserves a detailed record of a mixed Jewish town under Polish and Russian rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maier-joseph-vo:
Joseph von Maier, a German rabbi honored with nobility, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in 1797, he presided over the first rabbinical conference, held at Brunswick in 1844. He also sat on the Jewish Consistory of Wurttemberg. He died at Stuttgart on August 19, 1873.

The article is brief but points to a singular honor. The King of Wurttemberg ennobled Maier for his charity and his part in the religious movements of the day. That grant made him the first German rabbi to belong to the nobility. The entry cites the Allgemeine Zeitung des Judenthums of 1873 for the fact. For readers, the short notice marks a milestone in the standing of rabbis within German society. It also places Maier among the organizers of modern rabbinic conferences, where reform questions were first debated openly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marcus-lewi-lew:
Lewi Marcus, called Lewin, a German lawyer, receives a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Rhena, Mecklenburg, on October 15, 1809, he worked tirelessly for his fellow Jews. That labor earned him the nickname the Gabriel Riesser of Mecklenburg. He died at Manchester, England, in 1881.

The article lists the civic heights he reached. Marcus was the first Jewish deputy of the Mecklenburg Diet. He rose to become its vice-president. The city of Schwerin made him an honorary citizen. For seventeen years he served as acting president of its municipal council. He also presided over Schwerin's Jewish community. The brief notice preserves a lawyer whose public career marked how far Jewish emancipation had come in one small German state.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maurice-charles:
Charles Maurice, who built Hamburg's Thalia Theater into a famous house, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels. Born at Agen, in France, on May 29, 1805, he knew not a word of German until he followed his father to Hamburg at twenty-two. In 1831 he took charge of a minor Hamburg playhouse. When the great fire of 1842 destroyed it, help poured in, and he rebuilt it as the Thalia. He died at Hamburg on January 27, 1896.

Maurice managed the city theater as well for a time, then gave his whole strength to the Thalia until 1885. His son's death forced him back to work in 1893, in his late eighties. The entry praises his eye for acting talent: he developed Bogumil Dawison and Friederike Gossmann and encouraged several other stars before their fame was made.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mekize-nirdamim:
Mekize Nirdamim, the “Awakeners of Those Who Slumber,” was a society for publishing old Hebrew books and manuscripts. Richard Gottheil and A. S. Waldstein describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was founded at Lyck in 1864 under patrons including Nathan Adler, Sir Moses Montefiore, and S. D. Luzzatto. It was refounded at Berlin in 1885. Its committee spanned Rome, Paris, St. Petersburg, Philadelphia, and Budapest, a map of Jewish scholarship.

The entry is mostly the publication record of the society, a rescue list. On it stand the Diwan of Judah ha-Levi, 120 responsa of the Geonim, and the Mahzor Vitry. On it stand the Halakot Gedolot, the commentary of Maimonides on Tohorot, and the responsa of Meir of Rothenburg. And dozens more join them, works that existed only in manuscripts or rare printings. For anyone tracing how editions of medieval Hebrew literature came to be, the entry is a checklist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meridian-date-1:
Meridian, the date-line where the calendar day changes, poses a peculiar problem for Jewish law. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein work it through in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. On which side of the line is it Sabbath? Civil Jewry can follow the international line at 180 degrees. But religious law cannot rest on so recent a convention, the entry argues. The convention is unsettled too. The Talmud never mentions the matter.

The trail begins with Judah ha-Levi's "Cuzari" in the twelfth century. It sets Jerusalem as the world's navel and puts the Jewish date-line ninety degrees east of it. That reckoning leaves China in the far east, divides Korea, and gives Australia the American date. The article continues to the polar question raised in the "Sefer ha-Berit." Where day and night last six months, count twenty-four hours. Then let the sun go.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micrococcus-pro:
Micrococcus prodigiosus, the microbe of miracles, is a blood-red bacterium whose spots on food were once read as signs from heaven. Joseph Jacobs and L. Errera wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it in 1906. An Italian doctor, Vincenzo Sette, first described it in 1819, growing on polenta, and later scientists renamed it three more times.

The article describes a tiny, motile bacterium that spreads by simple division, forms no spores, and stains its colonies red, pink, or brown. It thrives on potatoes, bread, milk, meat, and even communion wafers, carried by germs in ordinary dust. Those accidental blood-spots, the writers explain, were long taken as Heaven's wrath and fed the old belief in bleeding miracles.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mnemonics-hebre:
Mnemonics, in Hebrew simanim, signs, are the catchwords and catch-sentences of rabbinic tradition. They helped memory hold long chains of law. Crawford Howell Toy and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach treat them in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The Talmud is full of them. They appear wherever a sequence of rulings might blur together and need a hook.

The first class the article describes is built from a Bible verse, a proverb, or a saying from daily life. It is introduced by the formula, and let thy sign be. The Babylonian teacher Naḥman bar Isaac invented them by the dozen. A verse like Thou hast set me behind and before could pin down the order of a discussion. It kept similar cases from being confused.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-jo:
Mordecai ben Joseph of Avignon was the most prominent Jew of thirteenth-century Provence. Solomon Schechter and A. Peiginsky profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 as the man who fought the badge. His adversary was the Dominican Pablo Christiani. Pablo persuaded the pope to order southern France's Jews to wear humiliating badges on their clothing. Until then they had been exempt.

Mordecai and a fellow Jew named Israel resisted. They were imprisoned by the inquisitors and bought their freedom for a large sum. Then Mordecai went over their heads. As delegate to the royal court with Solomon of Tarascon, he won a decree from Charles I against the inquisitors. The decree is dated March 26, 1276. It was unopposed, since Pablo was dead. Ibn Verga tells the story in Shebeṭ Yehudah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mudawwar-elias-:
Elias ibn al-Mudawwar was an Arabic poet and physician who lived at Ronda, probably in the early twelfth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and M. Seligsohn. The Arab historians knew him chiefly as a poet. The entry tells one sharp anecdote about him.

At Ronda, Elias quarreled with another Jewish physician, as rivals in one trade often do. One day he learned a secret that could ruin the man. Instead of spreading it, he sent his rival a two-line poem in Arabic. It said that no friendship can exist between two of one profession, as when sun and moon collide, no light comes of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-ben-simai:
Nahum ben Simai was a Palestinian amora of the third century, the son of the tanna Simai. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He is sometimes cited under the name Menahem. The sages called him the most holy man and the son of the saints.

The reason given is striking: all his life he never looked at the portrait stamped on a coin. At his funeral every statue was covered, so that even in death he would not see a human likeness. Only a few of his halakic sayings survive. He is also said to have preached at Tarsus on a verse from Exodus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nazir-isaac-113: Isaac Nazir stands near the start of the Cabala. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. One account calls him the real founder of cabalistic science. It says Elijah showed him its secrets in a vision. The entry warns that this account is not fully trustworthy. Isaac passed the secrets to Jacob Nazir. Jacob taught Abraham b. David in turn. Abraham entrusted them to his son, Isaac the Blind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-norzi-11597:
Norzi is an Italian family of scholars and rabbis. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The name likely comes from the town Norcia. Mantua held two distinct branches of it, Mortara says. Many of its members won note across centuries.

Benjamin wrote on the calendar in 1477. Eliezer glossed figures in Ibn Ezra's Sefer ha-Shem. Isaac of Ferrara ruled on a slaughter dispute in print. Raphael wrote ethics at Ferrara and Mantua. One name towers over the rest of the line. Jedidiah Solomon gave his life to the Bible's text. His Masoretic commentary collated manuscripts far and wide. He traveled abroad hunting one rare work for it. Finished in 1626, it became a standard aid. Print spread it later as Minḥat Shai.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-omar-i-ibn-al-k:
Omar the First was the second calif, or chief, of Islam. Joseph Jacobs and Mary W. Montgomery wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took the post after Abu Bakr in 634. He was killed by a foe in the year 644. Men call him the great shaper of Islam.

Under Omar, Syria, Persia, and Egypt fell to Arab rule. He set up the divan, a state office for funds. It kept lists of Arabs who shared the spoils of war. It kept strict counts of tax and tithe as well. He set the count of years from the Hegira flight. His name is tied to a harsh decree for Jews. It set Jews and Christians apart by dress and tax.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ostrogorski-moi:
Moisei Yakovlevich Ostrogorski was a Russian writer on rule and wealth. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in the year 1854. His father was a Jewish teacher at Grodno. He read law at the University of St. Petersburg.

For a time Moisei held a small post in the courts. His first books were time lines of the Russian past. One such book came out in the year 1872. It was oft reprinted and used in schools for years. In 1876 he began a yearly book on the law. His famed works came later in his life's work. One treats the rights of women in public law. One treats how parties are formed in the United States. That work grew into a three part study of parties.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappus-11897:
Pappus was a chief of a revolt under Emperor Hadrian. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Hadrian ruled the Roman realm from 117 to 138. Pappus is named at all times with Luliani by his side. Luliani was most likely the brother of Pappus in blood.

The two men came at first from Alexandria, in Egypt. They lived in Palestine in the days of the revolt. Men called them the pride of Judaism in that age. They were seized at Laodicea, for a cause not now known. Their judge died all at once, and they went free. The day of that escape is kept as a feast day. When the Temple was to be built, they set up funds. They set coin stands on the road from Acre to Antioch.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pelican-ka-at-1:
