The pelican is named in the Bible as an unclean bird. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It appears in the food laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy. The prophets picture it alone among ruins.

Two kinds of pelican live on the Syrian coast. The white pelican is the common one there. The bird stores food in the pouch under its bill. It presses the pouch to its breast to feed its young. That habit bred a famous false tale. People said the pelican fed its young with its own blood.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pizzighettone-d: David Pizzighettone was an Italian Talmudist and physician. The Executive Committee and A. Peiginsky wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the first half of the 1500s. He practiced medicine at Cremona, in Italy. At Venice he edited books for the Bomberg press. He wrote the introduction to its Maimonides edition. One old claim makes him rabbi of Ferrara. The entry flatly calls that claim wrong.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-portsmouth-1229:
Portsmouth is an English seaport on the coast of Hampshire. Joseph Jacobs and Isidore Harris wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its Jewish congregation dates from 1747. It is one of the oldest in the English provinces. It had a rabbi of its own from the start.

In the wars with France the town grew rich and busy. Many Jews came for trade in those years. For a time the town had two synagogues. Peace in 1815 shrank the Jewish group again. The newer building fell out of use at last. It was sold off to a dealer in dry goods. The older building serves the congregation to this day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-portugal-ancien:
Portugal is a kingdom in the southwest of Europe, called Lusitania in old times. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote its long article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there as long as they lived in Spain. Their lot was much like that of Spanish Jews. Church law pressed on them later here, and less hard.

Until the expulsion, Portugal saw no open attacks on its Jews. The first king, Affonso Henriques, found Jews settled in his land. They lived at Santarem, Lisbon, and Beja. The article traces their life under king after king. It shows a long calm that Spain did not match. That calm ended with the forced choice of exile or baptism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbiner-mordec:
Mordecai ben Abraham Rabbiner was a Russian rabbi of Courland. Herman Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Sloboda, a suburb of Bauske, in 1758. He died at Bauske in 1830. Through his mother he came from Mordecai Jaffe. That man made the famed law books called Lebushim.

Rabbiner held the rabbinate of Bauske for thirty years. He held it from 1800 until his death. He wrote a book of rulings called Gedullat Mordekai. He wrote a book of sermons as well. His grandson printed both books after his death. The grandson added rulings of his own house to the set.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rausuk-samson-1:
Samson Rausuk was a Hebrew poet born in Lithuania in 1793. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Wilkowiski and first worked as a merchant. He died in London on September 11, 1877.

The article says he helped welcome Sir Moses Montefiore to Russia in 1846. In 1848 he went to London for good. There he served as librarian of the bet ha-midrash. He held that post for nearly a quarter century. London Jews saw him as their poet laureate for years. His Hebrew poems often marked events of the day. The entry honors a learned poet far from his birthplace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-resurrection-12:
Resurrection is the belief that the dead will rise again. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board, George A. Barton, and Kaufmann Kohler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Early Hebrews pictured the dead in Sheol. Life there was colorless and dim, they believed.

The article traces how hope for rising grew slowly. Job first longs for resurrection in his suffering. Jeremiah and Ezekiel made the person the moral unit. That shift made individual hope possible, the writers argue. Some psalm writers instead sent righteous souls straight to God. Later, messianic hope brought resurrection back. Isaiah promises the dead will live again. Daniel expects many sleepers in dust to awake. The entry follows a doctrine across centuries of texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-of-escal:
A. Peiginsky wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel of Escaleta, also called Samuel Sulami. He was a French Talmudist, poet, and giver to charity in the fourteenth century. Jacob of Provence ranked him among the first poets of Provence. He lived first at Narbonne, then at Perpignan.

Samuel took a side in the religious disputes of 1303 to 1306. He backed the liberal party. He sheltered the hunted Levi of Villefranche in his own house. He held firm despite warnings from Ben Adret. Then his daughter died, and grief shook his resolve. He read his losses as punishment for sin. He withdrew his help from Levi and joined Ben Adret. In the end he backed the ban on young students studying the sciences.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarasohn-kasrie:
Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Kasriel H. Sarasohn. He was an American journalist. Sarasohn was born in Paiser, in Russian Poland, in 1835. He died in New York City on January 12, 1905. He trained for the rabbinate at home. In 1866 he gave up that plan and emigrated to America.

In New York, Sarasohn founded the Jewish Weekly and the Jewish Gazette in 1874. In 1886 he added the Jewish Daily News. No Hebrew Jewish paper then existed in the United States. He struggled even to obtain the needed type. In 1882 he founded the Hebrew Sheltering House. It later became a home for the aged. He also chaired the relief committee for the Kishinef sufferers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schomberg-meyer:
Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Meyer Löw Schomberg. He was an English physician. Schomberg was born at Fetzburg, in Germany, in 1690. He died in London on March 4, 1761. His family's original name was Löw, which he changed to Schomberg. He took his medical degree at Giessen in 1710.

Schomberg practiced at Schweinburg, Blankenstein, and Metz in turn. About 1720 he came to England. The Royal College of Physicians licensed him in 1722. He was then so poor that the college took his bond for the fees. Through London's Jewish merchants he built a glittering practice. His income reached 4,000 guineas a year. He joined the Royal Society in 1726. He backed his son Isaac in the son's long fight with the college.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shamir-13497:
Shamir names a substance harder than any stone in Bible and legend. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. In three Bible verses it means adamant, fit for a cutting point. Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah all use the word that way.

Later Jewish and Christian tales gave the shamir wondrous power. It could split the hardest material without effort. Tradition counts it among ten marvels made at twilight on creation's first Friday. It was no bigger than a grain of barley. Nothing hard enough to resist it could be found. The entry follows one small word from stone tool into legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shklovski-isaac:
Isaac Vladimirovich Shklovski was a Russian journalist born at Yelisavetgrad in 1865. Isidore Singer and Max Rosenthal wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was schooled at his home town's gymnasium. At sixteen he began placing poems and prose in South-Russian papers.

In 1886 officials charged Shklovski with revolutionary activity. He was banished to Sredne Kolymsk in Yakutsk province. He stayed in Siberian exile until 1892, studying Yakut life. He learned native languages and wrote sketches of the region. His book on northeastern Siberia appeared in 1895. A French version followed the next year. From 1896 he reported from London for a Moscow liberal daily. Exile had turned a young writer into an expert on Siberia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ben-jose:
Simeon ben Joseph of Lunel was a Talmudist of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Wilhelm Bacher and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His Provençal name was En Duran of Perpignan. He lived at Montpellier, Lunel, and, after 1306, Aix.

The expulsion of Jews in 1306 drove him to Aix. Simeon is known chiefly for the Abba Mari controversy. He backed Abba Mari as his active partisan and lieutenant. Almost no writings of his survive beyond three letters. One letter, Hoshen ha-Mishpat, answers Meiri of Perpignan sharply. Meiri had refused to sign a ban on philosophy students. Simeon set out the orthodox grievances against those students. Another letter asks Solomon ben Adret to uphold the ban. The entry recalls a fighter in the culture war over philosophy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-slander-13797:
Slander is false and harmful defamation of a person's good name. Wilhelm Bacher and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Spreading evil reports to injure a name brought a fine. It also brought an award of damages. The article sets slander apart from evil speech about true faults. True but harmful speech was banned, but not fined in the same way.

One case deals with a husband who questions his new wife. If his charge about her virginity proves baseless, he is whipped. He must also pay one hundred silver shekels to her father. He loses the right of divorce as well. Rabbinic rules against slander stayed very strict in later law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-vabian-:
Vabian L Solomon was premier of South Australia, born about 1849. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of Judah Moss Solomon. Early in life he went to the Northern Territory. There he engaged in business and became mayor of the chief town.

He also became linked with the Northern Territory Times newspaper. Returning to Adelaide, he entered the House of Assembly. He won recognition as an authority on finance in Parliament. In December 1899 he became premier for a short time. He also sat on the Federal Council for Australian federation. That council brought about the union of the colonies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steblicki-sebli:
Joseph Abraham Steblicki was a German convert to Judaism of note. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was the son of a Catholic butcher at Nikolai. He was born there about 1726 and died in 1807. He was well educated in Jesuit colleges in his youth.

He became a teacher, city treasurer, and council member at Nikolai. Retiring in 1780, he turned to religious studies in earnest. He began to observe the Sabbath and the dietary laws. On the Day of Atonement in 1785 he attended synagogue services. The law then in force prescribed death for his conversion. Frederick II suspended the case, and officials left him unmolested.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tagin-aramaic-h:
Tagin are the small crowns drawn atop certain Hebrew letters. Crawford Howell Toy and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Each crown holds three strokes shaped like tiny zayin letters. The New Testament calls such a mark a tittle. Only scrolls of the Law carry these ornaments.

Seven letters bear the crowns on their upper bars. Printed Pentateuchs leave the flourishes out entirely. The tagin belong to the Masorah tradition. A manual called Sefer ha-Tagin tracked their forms. Tradition traced it to stones Joshua set in the Jordan. The book passed from high priest Eli to Samuel. Later hands hid it under the Temple threshold. Ezekiel carried it to Babylon in exile, legend says. The entry mixes scribal fact with a chain of legend.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teller-leopold-:
Leopold Teller was a Hungarian actor born at Budapest in 1844. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He was born on April 3 of that year. He studied medicine briefly at Vienna's university. In 1862 he quit for a Laibach theater company.

For ten years Teller played small theaters across the region. Iglau, Klagenfurt, Troppau, and Leipsic fill that list. From 1874 he belonged to the famed Meininger troupe. His roles included Shylock, Iago, and Franz Moor. He also played Gessler and Marinelli on stage. Hamburg's city theater engaged him in 1890. He retired from acting in 1899 at Hamburg. There he taught elocution in his later years. His own play met with considerable success. The entry follows a doctor turned villain specialist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tiktiner-rebecc:
Rebecca bat Meir Tiktiner was an Austrian authoress who lived at Prague. Schulim Ochser wrote this article with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. She died there, apparently, in 1550. Few women of her century published in Hebrew. Her name survived through two printed works.

Her main book, Meneket Ribkah, appeared at Prague in 1609. Cracow reprinted it in 1618. Seven gates, or sections, treat a housewife's duties. Talmudic and Midrashic anecdotes fill its pages. She also wrote a poem for Simhat Torah. That festival marks the yearly end of Torah reading. The entry preserves one of the earliest known Hebrew women writers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trent-german-tr:
Trent, oldest city of the Tyrol, was a bishop's seat from 1027 to 1803. Joseph Jacobs and Aaron Tänzer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A few Jews, likely from Italy, settled there in the 1300s. Bishops favored them as useful businessmen. Jews owned houses, estates, and their own school.

Good relations ended with the Simon of Trent case. A priest's preaching stirred the ritual-murder charge of 1475. Rich Jews were killed and their property seized. Survivors were expelled, and the community dissolved. Pope Sixtus IV sanctioned the proceedings in 1478. For centuries no Jews dwelt in Trent again. Even in 1638 the old case barred Jewish settlement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ur-14597: Ur of the Chaldees, Abram's original home, is identified with a Babylonian ruin mound. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. The Bible mentions Ur four times in all. Genesis twice, and Nehemiah once, name the place. Modern scholars place it at Al-Mukair, south in Babylonia. The mound stands on the Euphrates' right bank. Ur was an ancient seat of moon worship. It ruled as a political center by 3000 B.C. Some scholars link its moon god Sin to Sinai.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolfler-bernard:
Bernard Wolfler (born 1816) was an Austrian doctor who ran the Jewish hospital of Vienna. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Bohemia, he read thought at Prague first. He then took up medicine at Vienna from 1836 to 1842.

He worked two years at the town hospital of Vienna. He then practiced on his own at Prague for four years. In 1849 he took charge of the Jewish hospital of Vienna. A rich gift from Baron Rothschild gave the hospital a new home. Wolfler ran the new house with great care and zeal. He toured the hospitals of the West to learn their ways. In 1872 he set up free care for the sick poor. His homes took in lung cases each summer at no cost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhak-ben-hako: Yizhak ben Hakola was a scholar of Palestine in the third century. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at the same time as Joshua ben Levi. He passed on rules in the names of four older men. One tale of his lives on in a midrash. It treats the clash of the herd men of two kings. Those kings were Abimelech and Abraham of the old tale. It tells how that clash was brought to a calm end.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zebulun-15197:
Zebulun was the sixth son of Leah in the Book of Genesis. Emil G. Hirsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From him came the tribe that bears his name. That tribe is named in the Books of Numbers and Psalms.

In the split of the land the tribe got a set tract. It lay north of Issachar in the hills of the north. It lay west and south of Naphtali at the same time. It lay east of the tribe of Asher in the west. Yet two old songs hint at land by the sea as well. Those songs stand in Genesis and in Deuteronomy. The bounds in Joshua are hard to make sense of now. The tribe's lands were rich and crossed by great roads. Those roads ran from the Jordan to the sea in the west.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zunser-eliakim-:
Eliakim Zunser was a Russian badhan, a wedding entertainer, and a poet in verse and song. Joseph Jacobs and G. Selikovitch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Wilna in 1845, he had a local name as a poet by sixteen. He set his rhymes to music and sang them at weddings and other feasts.

Zunser's method was more refined than the old wedding fooling, and hosts paid him well. After his Shirim Hadashim appeared in 1861, he composed over six hundred songs. Most sing of the Jewish nation; others praise railroads, light, Columbus, and the golden land of America. In 1889 he toured America and settled in New York as a printer and publisher.
kent-repertory-homoeopathic-materia-medi:
James Tyler Kent changed how homeopaths find remedies when his Repertory appeared in 1897. A repertory works backward from the usual books: start with the patient's symptom, then find which remedies match. Kent arranged symptoms under rubrics, headings for each kind of sign, and graded the drugs under each one.

Grades show at a glance which remedies fit a sign most strongly, a Kent hallmark. His school, the Kentian line, made this the finding tool of daily practice. Later repertories copied its plan, which is why the 1897 first edition counts as the most influential book of its kind in the field.
kingsley-travels-in-west-africa-1897:
Mary Henrietta Kingsley paddled, traded, and collected her way through West Africa in 1893 to 1895, and Travels in West Africa of 1897 made her famous. Her route ran through French Congo, Corisco, and the Cameroons, often where no European woman had gone. Religion, law, and daily life pass under her sharp, funny gaze.

Kingsley wrote with a trader's respect for African systems and a naturalist's eye for fish and forest. Her vivid first-hand observation corrected armchair ideas of the coast at a stroke. The book remains one of the great travel works of its century, bold and alive on every page.
lang-book-of-dreams-and-ghosts-1897:
Andrew Lang was a Scots scribe of tales, myths, and verse. His Book of Dreams and Ghosts came out in 1897. Lang had a foot in both camps: folk lore and the new mind hunt. The book gathers tales he found strong and strange.

Houses with ghosts, wraiths of kin at the point of death, and dreams that come true fill the text. Lang tells each tale well, then asks what it may mean. He will not force a creed on the reader at the close. The book is a chief text of the ghost hunt in its prime years.
lang-modern-mythology-1897:
Lang returned to the fight over myth in this 1897 book, answering Max Muller and the school that explained myths as a disease of language. Muller had read the gods as faded metaphors for sun and storm; Lang thought that reading ignored the evidence of living peoples.

Drawing on folklore and anthropology, Lang argued that myth grows from early beliefs and rites, not from wordplay. He defends the savage origin of tales that classical writers polished into literature. The argument is sharp, learned, and often funny. The book marks a turning point, when the study of myth passed from philology to anthropology.
libavius-alchemia-1597:
Andreas Libavius was a German schoolmaster and doctor whose Alchemia, published in 1597, is the first full textbook of chemistry. He gathered the scattered recipes of the art into one ordered course. He wrote to defend honest work at the furnace against quacks and scoffers alike.

The book treats workshops, furnaces, vessels, and the making of salts, metals, and medicines in clear order. Libavius insists that each claim be tested and written down so that another worker can repeat the trial. Students of the science see in his book the bridge from old recipe lore to chemistry as a taught and tested craft.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Volume Eleven carries Motley's story from 1619 to 1623. Chapter Twenty-One describes Barneveld's execution at The Hague. Motley details the Advocate's conduct on the scaffold. The printed sentence went out to all the provinces.

He judges the proceedings irregular and deeply inequitable. The scene centers on the Inner Court beside the old castle. Brown brick buildings and a beechen grove framed the execution ground. The volume closes the Barneveld tragedy with its author's verdict attached. The Inner Court's beechen grove overshadowed its eastern side, he notes. Three-storied brown brick ranges surrounded the spacious paved quadrangle.
loma-a-citizen-of-venus-1897:
William Windsor published this Venus novel in St. Paul in 1897. The Windsor and Lewis Publishing Company issued it. Windsor held law and philosophy degrees, his title page boasts. He had written on creation, phrenology, professions, and happiness before.

A portrait frontispiece presents his friend Loma, citizen of Venus. Duke University's Perkins Library preserved the rare copy scanned here. The Internet Archive digitized it in 2010 for modern readers. Its Venusian visitor belongs to early American science fiction's fringe. Great Secrets of Happiness numbered among Windsor's earlier titles. St. Paul's Windsor and Lewis company published his Venus tale.
mach-analysis-of-sensations-williams-189:
C M Williams published his translation of Ernst Mach's Contributions to the Analysis of the Sensations in 1897. Mach, an Austrian physicist and philosopher, first issued the work in German in 1886. He asked what the world is made of at the level of direct experience: colors, sounds, pressures, and spaces.

Mach argued that bodies and even the self are bundles of such sensations, held together by habit and use. That phenomenalist psychology cut away hidden substances behind experience. Einstein credited Mach's critique of absolute space and time as a spur to relativity. The Vienna Circle later took Mach as a forerunner. Williams's English brought that influence to British and American readers.
maitland-domesday-1897:
F. W. Maitland published Domesday Book and Beyond in 1897, his masterpiece of legal history. Maitland rebuilds English law and society from Domesday Book, the great survey of 1086. Three essays study the land, the township, and the growth of legal ideas. Manors, tenures, and courts are explained from the records themselves.

Maitland writes with wit and lucidity rare in legal scholarship. He shows how modern law grew from feudal soil, step by step. The book founded legal history as a modern field in England. Lawyers and historians alike rank it among the finest works of its century. It teaches readers to think historically about law itself.
malory-morte-darthur-strachey-1897:
Thomas Malory completed Le Morte d'Arthur in prison around 1470, and Caxton printed it in 1485. The 1897 edition, associated with Israel Gollancz and Strachey, presents the complete work. Malory braided French romances into one great English epic.

Arthur's birth, the Round Table, and the Grail quest unfold in sequence. Lancelot and Guinevere's love brings the fellowship toward its ruin. The last battle leaves Arthur wounded and borne away to Avalon. Malory's prose mixes chronicle plainness with sudden, moving eloquence. His book made Arthur England's own hero for all later ages. Tennyson, and nearly every Arthurian writer since, drank from Malory's well.
manilius-astronomica-creech-1697:
Marcus Manilius sang the stars in Latin verse in the first years of the Roman Empire. The Five Books of M. Manilius, in Thomas Creech's 1697 English rendering, gives his Astronomica in English verse. The poem maps the heavens and the sway men believed the stars held over life.

Manilius lays out the signs, the circles of the sky, and the fates each birth hour was said to bring. Creech, a fine English poet of his day, keeps the verse swift and clear. The work is at once star lore, fate lore, and high poetry. It shows what the early Empire thought when it looked up.
manouvrier-pithecanthropus-1897:
Leonce Manouvrier, a Paris sage of the study of man, gave this cool look at Dubois's Java ape man in 1897. Dubois had named his find Pithecanthropus erectus, the ape man who walks upright. The claim had split the learned world since its first show in 1894.

Manouvrier weighs the thigh bone, the skull cap, and the teeth with a dry, sharp eye. He finds the proof short of the bold claim, and says so in plain terms. The paper is the voice of the Paris school at its most wary, in a famed row.
matthews-navaho-legends-1897:
Washington Matthews was an army surgeon posted to the Southwest who learned the Navajo language and won the confidence of Navajo singers. His 1897 book collects the great legends he recorded from them, presented with care for their ceremony and meaning.

The legends include the creation and emergence of the people, and the stories behind the Night Chant and Mountain Chant, the long healing ceremonies Matthews also studied. He explains the songs, sandpaintings, and rites that carry the stories into practice. Matthews treated Navajo religion as a noble system when many dismissed it. His book remains a foundation for the study of Navajo tradition.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-st-cloud-being-s:
Volume six of the St. Cloud letters opens at letter ten. The writer dates it from Paris in September 1805. A tea party at a rich upstart's house starts this letter's tale.

There he meets Madame Chevalier, famed from the court of Paul the First. He draws her as short, fat, coarse, and artful in manner. Her past in Lyons, on stage and in clubs, fills the page. Revolution lifted such folk fast, and the writer spares no scorn. Her husband first met her in a house of ill fame there. Stage wages of twelve hundred livres a year were her peak in France.
mendeleev-principles-chemistry-kamensky-:
Dmitri Mendeleev, the Russian chemist who built the periodic table, explained his system in The Principles of Chemistry. George Kamensky translated the sixth Russian edition into English, and volume one came out in 1897. The periodic law, which orders elements by weight and likeness, guides the whole book. Mendeleev expounds that law himself, as its discoverer.

Volume one works through the elements in order, group by group. Facts about each element sit inside the pattern the law predicts. Gaps in the table, for Mendeleev, pointed to elements not yet found. Readers get the table from the hand that built it. Few textbooks carry such authority.

Kamensky's 1897 English version of Mendeleev's Principles of Chemistry closes with volume two. The first volume set out the periodic law and began the march through the elements. Volume two gives the systematic chemistry of the elements under that law. Each family of elements receives treatment in its place in the order.

Mendeleev stresses likeness within groups and change across periods. His tables and summaries let readers see the whole system at a glance. The pair of volumes completes the set in English. Chemists of the day learned the periodic system from these pages. The work shows a discoverer teaching his own science.
musaeus-hero-leander-1797:
Musaeus the Grammarian, a Greek poet of late antiquity, told the tale of Hero and Leander in a short epic of some three hundred lines. The English verse version here dates to 1797. Hero was a priestess of Aphrodite at Sestos, and Leander swam the Hellespont by night to reach her tower.

A lamp in the tower guided his swim, until a storm killed the light and the sea took him. Hero, finding his body at dawn, threw herself from the tower to join him. The sad tale fed Marlowe, Chapman, Keats, and Byron, who swam the strait in its honor. It is the last flower of Greek epic.
nansen-farthest-north-vol1-1897:
Fridtjof Nansen, a Norwegian scientist and skier, locked his ship Fram into the Arctic ice in 1893 to drift across the polar sea. Volume One of Farthest North, from 1897, tells the plan and the first half of the drift. No one had tried such a voyage before.

Nansen explains his bold idea: let the ice carry the ship, and learn the Arctic Ocean's currents on the way. The volume covers the Siberian coast, the freezing-in, and life aboard through the first polar night. Then Nansen leaves the ship for his dash toward the Pole. The drift proved his theory and changed polar science.
nansen-farthest-north-vol2-1897:
Volume Two of Nansen's Farthest North completes the Fram expedition of 1893 to 1896. Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen had left the ship on skis and sledges, aiming for the North Pole. They reached farther north than anyone before them.

The volume tells of their turn back, the winter in a stone hut on Franz Josef Land, and their rescue by a meeting with a British expedition. Meanwhile the Fram broke free of the ice with all hands safe. Nansen's narrative mixes science, hardship, and wonder. The two volumes made him a hero across Europe and America. Their meeting in the ice is one of travel writing's great scenes.
openalex-w2018743597:
Diego Laplagne, Maria Soledad Esposito, Veronica Piatti and colleagues compared new brain cells made at different life stages. Their paper appeared in PLoS Biology in 2006. Part of the hippocampus makes new neurons throughout life. The team asked if adult-made neurons work like those made early in life.

They labelled neuron parent cells in young and adult animals. The labels used glowing proteins of different colours. They then recorded signals from neighbouring neurons of different ages. Adult-born neurons received much the same inputs as early-born ones. They could also fire signals when stimulated. Their firing behaviour matched closely too. The authors propose that both groups form one functional population. The finding matters for understanding adult brain growth.
openalex-w2056327497:
Alfonso Zavaleta, Maria Salas, Armando Peruga and colleagues reported youth smoking rates in Peru. Their paper appeared in BMC Public Health in 2008. Peru had joined the world tobacco control treaty. A new national law aimed to cut tobacco use and exposure. Planners needed data on young people.

The team used the Global Youth Tobacco Survey. It was run in four Peruvian cities. Students reported their smoking and related behaviours. The survey also covered exposure to smoke and advertising. Such data show where prevention should focus. School-based surveys can be repeated to track change. The results support Peru's new tobacco control efforts. They also allow comparison with other countries.
openalex-w2107915297:
Jorge Alvar, Ivan Dario Velez, Caryn Bern and colleagues produced world estimates of leishmaniasis cases. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2012. The work formed part of a World Health Organization update. National experts supplied recent case data. Published studies were reviewed alongside.

The review covered nearly a hundred countries and territories. Two main disease forms were counted separately. Skin disease cases far outnumber visceral cases. Many cases are never officially reported, they stress. True totals likely exceed reported counts several-fold. Country profiles detail treatment and control in each place. The estimates guide funding for neglected disease programmes. They remain a standard global reference.
openalex-w2132343497:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this measurement in the European Physical Journal C in 2015. They pinned down the jet energy scale for the ATLAS detector, which sets how the energy of particle jets is read. They also measured how uncertain that scale is, since every jet-based result leans on it.

The team used proton collision data and balanced jets against well-measured reference objects like photons. Computer simulations gave the first calibration, and data checks corrected the rest. In the central detector, the scale uncertainty fell below one percent for mid-energy jets. It rose for softer jets and for jets far forward, reaching about six percent at the edges.
openalex-w2172927897:
Isabelle Dusfour, Pilar Zorrilla, and Amandine Guidez led this 2015 study in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. They probed how Aedes aegypti beats the spray deltamethrin in three French overseas lands. This pest spreads several viruses. Pyrethroid sprays are the main class used against it, yet they kill it less and less well worldwide.

Groups came from French Guiana in South America, Guadeloupe in the Caribbean, and New Caledonia in the Pacific. All three lands had already met this spray failure in the field. The study set out to pin down how the pest resists in each place. Its gene activity data were posted in a public archive for reuse.
openalex-w2173352997:
Andrés Rubiano, Nancy Carney, Randall Chesnut, and Juan Puyana published this review in 2015 on global neurotrauma research. Traumatic injury to the brain or spine is among the most serious public health problems worldwide. It robs people of potential, above all in low- and middle-income countries where care is thinnest.

The authors stress that research must fit each region's own needs and obstacles. In rich countries, patients skew older and crashes dominate, while poorer regions see young pedestrians and riders hurt most. They urge cheap, fresh tools like mobile health apps, better registries, and studies designed for local realities. Copying questions from rich settings, they warn, may miss what poorer places need most.
openalex-w2563105997:
Cristian Koepfli, Wang Nguitragool, and Natalie Hofmann, with colleagues, published this 2016 methods study in Scientific Reports. It tests droplet digital PCR, a technique for counting malaria parasites in blood. Knowing parasite density exactly matters for understanding how malaria behaves and harms people. Common methods need an external standard curve, which makes results hard to compare between studies.

Droplet digital PCR counts DNA directly, with no standard curve needed. The team used it on patients and on people carrying parasites without symptoms. For Plasmodium falciparum it proved more sensitive than standard quantitative PCR, and equally sensitive for Plasmodium vivax. Repeat measurements varied far less than with the older method. The authors conclude the technique gives sensitive, accurate counts. That helps studies where absolute parasite numbers, not rough estimates, are essential.
openalex-w2582944297:
Giovanna Micarelli reviewed Marisol de la Cadena's book Earth Beings for Universitas Humanística in 2016. The review, written in Spanish, presents the 2015 Duke University Press volume. De la Cadena is an anthropologist who worked closely with the Turpo family in the Peruvian Andes. Her book follows earth beings, mountain spirits called tirakuna, and the people who relate to them.

The book tells seven stories, Micarelli explains, framed by two interludes. They cover indigenous leadership, land struggle, Andean shamanism, and collaboration with a Washington museum. Ausangate, a being that is also a mountain, runs through the conversations. The stories resist neat conclusions and keep crossing between local and global scales. Micarelli presents the book as an important statement that culture alone cannot capture Andean worlds. In them, she notes, there are more than one but fewer than many ways of being.
openalex-w4200236397:
Peter Potapov, Svetlana Turubanova, Matthew Hansen, and colleagues mapped world cropland from satellites, in Nature Food in 2021. Consistent global data on farmland are needed to track progress toward sustainable food production. The team analysed two decades of satellite records to measure where cropland grows or shrinks. Their maps cover the first twenty years of this century.

Cropland expanded faster in the second decade than the first, above all in Africa and South America. About half of the new farmland replaced natural vegetation and tree cover. Because population grew faster still, cropland per person shrank over the period. Output per hectare rose through more intense farming. The maps expose a clash between feeding people and protecting ecosystems.
openalex-w4281836397:
Praveen Dhyani, Cristina Quispe, Eshita Sharma, and colleagues review the anticancer potential of plant alkaloids, in Cancer Cell International in 2022. Cancer kills about ten million people a year worldwide. Standard treatments work, but they are costly and tumours often grow resistant over time. Plant compounds offer a cheaper, proven source of cancer drugs. Alkaloids, a family of plant chemicals, are among the most successful.

The review focuses on six alkaloids, including colchicine and the vinca drugs vincristine and vinblastine. For each it covers medical uses, how it attacks tumours, and prospects for lab-scale production. Many of these drugs stop cell division by targeting the cell's internal scaffolding. The authors aim to support affordable cancer care built on these molecules.
openalex-w7204224797: Brazil once reserved schooling for the elite; the republic promised it to all. This article traces the right to education from empire to republic through the country's constitutions. The authors show how each charter redrew who counts as a student. A legal-history study of citizenship learned in the classroom.
openalex-w7204531397: Brazil's prisons hold far more people than they were built for, and the Federal District is no exception. This article studies overcrowding and the shortage of places through the lens of human rights. The authors review norms, court rulings, and international standards. A sobering legal study of what happens when punishment outruns capacity.
openalex-w7204882697: Sadness and worry during and after pregnancy affect both mother and baby, yet they often go unnoticed. This review pulled together fifteen studies from 2006 to 2024 to measure how mood disorders in this period shape outcomes. The authors sum up what the research shows about harm to mother and child alike. A careful summary of why a new mother's mental health deserves the same care as her physical healing.
openalex-w7204993797: Modern schooling often treats students as future workers first and people second. This philosophy-of-education article argues that market-style thinking has gone deeper than business methods in schools: it has reshaped what education is for. The author traces the shift from instrumental reason to a market logic that redefines learning's purpose. A challenging critique for readers asking what school is really selling.
openalex-w7211996497:
Ana Patricia Pereira Ribeiro, Lorrana de Souza Freitas, and Robson Costa Pessoa write about the nurse's role in catching sepsis early in emergency care. Sepsis is the body's runaway response to infection; it can race toward organ failure and death, and its first signs are often faint and nonspecific. In crowded emergency rooms, the authors argue, the nurse stands in the decisive position: reading the patient at triage, watching vital signs, and mobilizing the wider team fast.

Their review gathers national and international guidance on screening tools, warning signs, and first interventions. Structured clinical protocols, they conclude, must be joined with the sensitivity of nursing care itself. That pairing shortens the time until treatment begins, changes outcomes for patients, and builds care that is both safe and humane. The article makes a professional case: early sepsis recognition is nursing work at its most consequential.
openalex-w7212112697:
Adriana Martins Reis and Debora Leite Silvano set out good practice for libraries that serve autistic students. A library is a public door to knowledge. For students on the autism spectrum, that door can stick. Blocks can sit in how staff speak, how facts are laid out, and in plain bias. The pair read past studies and Brazil's laws on access to build their guide.

Good practice, they find, sorts into six strands. Welcome and clear speech come first. Then come the layout of the space and access to facts in more than one form. Staff training and a voice for the student round out the list. One strand gives each student a guide of their own. The gains, the authors note, reach past one group. A calm, clear library serves all who walk in.
openalex-w7213438997:
Emanuel Lucas Vasconcelos and co-authors compare men's and women's results in a basic inorganic chemistry course. Their 2026 document study uses records from a state university covering twenty semesters, from 2015 to 2025. In total, 411 student records were analysed, grouped by sex as inferred from first names.

Women's final averages were slightly higher than men's across several assessments. Their pass rate was also a few points higher. The authors stress that the gaps were small and described only, with no claim of a deep cause. Results must be read against the many factors behind academic performance. The name-based grouping is noted as a clear limit of the study.
openalex-w7220659897:
Karen Esteves Ezezinos led a 2026 study of land use change around the many springs of the Ribeirão Achado basin in Santana do Paraíso, Brazil. The team registered the basin's springs, nearly two hundred, and built land use maps for 2008, 2014, and 2020 to see what was happening on the ground that feeds them. Pasture and shrubs, the predominant cover, shrank somewhat over the period, while dense vegetation held almost steady.

Degraded areas and planted forestry both grew, including on land occupied by springs, where more springs sat in degraded or forestry areas in 2020 than in 2008. The advance of degradation and forestry over spring areas, the authors conclude, demands conservation and recovery actions in the permanent preservation zones that should shield these water sources. The study turns satellite categories into a local warning: the basin's water begins exactly where its cover is thinning.
openalex-w7221197697:
Aline Silva de Jesus led a seven-author study, published in 2026, on oral health in the workplace and its effect on employee well-being and productivity. Untreated mouth disease reaches beyond the mouth, the authors argue, striking at self-esteem, general health, and how well a worker can do the job.

Set in the corporate environment, their work treats the mouth as part of occupational health rather than a private concern left to each employee. Pain, infection, and lost teeth can quietly tax concentration, attendance, and performance. The study makes the case that companies and workers share an interest in prevention and timely dental care. It speaks to occupational health readers looking for whole-person arguments inside workplace wellness.
plaw-105-1-1997: This 1997 joint resolution making technical corrections to the Omnibus Consolidated Appropriations Act, 1997 (Public Law 104-208), and for other purposes. Joint resolutions carry the force of law when passed by both chambers and signed. It stands as Public Law 105-1 of the 105th Congress.
plaw-105-10-1997: Passed in 1997, this federal law designates the J. Phil Campbell, Senior, Natural Resource Conservation Center. Designations put names on the official map and into federal records. The library keeps it in the public record of how federal laws get made.
plaw-105-100-1997: This 1997 law appropriates federal funds for the government of the district of columbia and other activities chargeable in whole or in part against the revenues. plos-pbio-0020097:
Mark Jung-Beeman, Edward M. Bowden, Jason Haberman, and co-workers scanned brains during sudden insight for PLOS Biology in 2004. People solved word problems either by steady work or by a flash of insight, the classic aha moment. Brain imaging let the team compare the two routes.

The insight route lit up a distinct pattern, including an area tied to loose word links, just before the answer came. A burst of activity marked the moment the solution broke through. The study gives hard data on a mental event that feels instant and mysterious. It suggests insight is not magic but a real brain process that can be measured, timed, and perhaps trained.
plos-pbio-0020197:
Marcel Cardillo, Andy Purvis, Wes Sechrest, and a broad team assessed risk in the world's carnivores in PLOS Biology in 2004. They asked whether crowded human areas raise the extinction risk of meat-eating mammals like lions, wolves, and bears. Data covered species across the globe.

The team found that where people live densely, carnivores face higher risk, even after accounting for other traits like body size and range. Big predators need space, and dense human settlement eats that space. The result gives conservation a clear, testable driver to watch. It suggests that saving carnivores will depend as much on managing human spread as on guarding the animals themselves.
plos-pone-0000097:
Reijo Laaksonen, Mikko Katajamaa, Hannu Päivä, and a large team used systems biology to hunt drug side-effect markers in PLOS ONE in 2006. Some widely used drugs harm a small share of patients, and doctors cannot yet tell in advance who is at risk. The team studied a statin known to cause muscle problems in rare cases.

By reading genes, proteins, and blood chemistry together, they found pathways tied to the toxic response and candidate markers in plasma. A blood test that flags risk before harm starts would change how such drugs are prescribed. The strategy, reading the whole system at once, is the paper's lasting point, beyond the one drug studied.
plos-pone-0000197:
Jonas Binladen, M. Thomas P. Gilbert, Jonathan P. Bollback, and colleagues published this sequencing methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The team used coded PCR primers, molecular barcodes attached during copying, so many samples could be sequenced at once by 454 parallel sequencing. That let them run high-throughput sequencing of multiple related gene copies in one batch.

Barcoding samples cut the cost of sequencing many specimens at once, a bottleneck in genetics at the time. The authors show the coded primer approach works on real amplification products. The trick became standard practice in the sequencing era that followed, from ancient DNA to microbiome studies.
plos-pone-0000297:
Barry Nicholls and Paul A. Racey published this bat study in PLOS ONE in 2007, posing a practical question in the title. Bats avoid radar installations, the authors report. That raises the idea that electromagnetic fields could deter bats from colliding with wind turbines, a growing cause of bat deaths.

Wind farms kill many bats, and a cheap deterrent would help both wildlife and operators. The authors document bats steering clear of radar and ask whether the effect can be borrowed. The paper links an odd behavioral observation to a real conservation technology problem.
plos-pone-0000397:
Naotaka Fujii, Sayaka Hihara, and Atsushi Iriki watched the monkey brain adapt during social interaction, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Neurons in the parietal cortex respond to movement, both one's own and others'. The team asked whether those motion-related neurons change their behavior as social situations unfold, a process they call dynamic social adaptation.

Reading others' movements is basic to social life: it underlies imitation, joint tasks, and judging intent. If single neurons adjust on the fly during interaction, the brain's social machinery is more flexible than a fixed wiring diagram suggests. The work helps connect brain cell activity to the give-and-take of real social behavior.
plos-pone-0000497:
Claudia Rodríguez-Almazán and colleagues found that unrelated proteins can help a folding protein succeed, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Proteins must fold from loose chains into exact shapes, and many fail and clump. The team showed that interactions with unrelated proteins increase the stability and formation of native proteins from unfolded monomers.

The result is counterintuitive: bystanders are usually expected to interfere, not assist. It suggests the crowded cell interior may actively support folding through weak, nonspecific contacts. That idea reframes how chemists think about making proteins in test tubes, where adding inert partner proteins might rescue yields of hard-to-fold products.
plos-pone-0000597:
Patric Hagmann and colleagues mapped the human brain's wiring as a network, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. They used diffusion MRI, which tracks water movement along nerve fibers. With it, they mapped human whole-brain structural networks. Those networks are the web of connections between brain regions in living people.

A structural network map is the scaffolding on which all brain activity runs. Network analysis reveals hubs and communities in that scaffolding, giving neuroscience a common map for comparing healthy and diseased brains. This paper was an early statement of the connectome idea, that the brain's connection pattern is itself a key to how it works.
plos-pone-0000697:
Heng Tao, Anthony J. Berno, David R. Cox and co-authors linked skin cell movement in a dish to gene variants, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Wound healing after injury to the epidermis remains hard to promote, partly because its factors are poorly understood. One essential step is re-epithelialization, where keratinocytes, the skin's main cells, migrate to cover the wound.

The title reports that migration rates in vitro are associated with SNPs in the KRT1 interval, a genome region named for a keratin gene. If inherited variants predict how fast skin cells crawl, healing speed may be partly written in DNA. That link could guide treatments for slow-healing wounds.
plos-pone-0000797:
Dev Churamani, Michael J. Boulware, Timothy J. Geach and colleagues characterized a new enzyme that makes calcium-releasing messengers, in PLOS ONE in 2007. ADP-ribosyl cyclases are remarkable enzymes able to catalyze several reactions. Among their products are cyclic ADP-ribose and NAADP, potent messengers that mobilize calcium inside cells. Not all cyclases, however, had been characterized at the molecular level.

Their subject is a novel intracellular cyclase, working inside the cell rather than on its surface. Characterizing it at molecular level means its sequence, its products, and how it is regulated. Calcium signals control everything from fertilization to secretion, so a new source enzyme redraws parts of that map.
plos-pone-0000897:
Thomas Webb and Robert Freckleton tested a classic size rule in animals where females are the larger sex, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In most species the sexes differ in size, and females are often bigger. Rensch's rule describes how that gap tends to change as species get larger overall.

Webb and Freckleton asked whether the rule holds when females lead in size. Their answer, flagged in the title, is that such species break the rule about half the time. A half kept rule is still useful, but it needs a better explanation. The study pushes biologists to ask what drives size gaps, not just describe them.
plos-pone-0000997:
Cheng Ding, Yan Liu, Yin Wang and colleagues found a brake on a special class of B cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. B1 B cells follow their own development path and do jobs distinct from standard B cells. What sets the size of that lineage was largely obscure.

Using mice that lack the Siglecg gene, marked with a glowing protein, the team show Siglecg limits the B1a branch. It does so by down regulating NFkappaB activation, a master switch for immune cell growth. A defined brake explains why this lineage stays a minority. It also gives immunology a handle for raising or lowering that population on purpose.
plos-pone-0001097:
Jason Slot and David Hibbett traced a nitrate eating gene cluster that jumped between fungi, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Some fungi carry a cluster of high affinity nitrate assimilation genes that switch on together. The cluster holds a transporter, a reductase and a related enzyme, a full kit for feeding on nitrate.

Using phylogenetic analysis, the pair present evidence the cluster moved by horizontal transfer between fungal lineages. A whole feeding kit moving at once can shift a species' ecology in one step. Their study ties that transfer to ecological transitions in fungi, changes in where and how species live. Gene clusters make such leaps visible.
plos-pone-0001197:
Age-related macular degeneration is the leading cause of blindness in the Western world, mainly affecting people over fifty. Peter Francis and colleagues studied variation in the complement factor H gene in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. That gene had repeatedly been shown to be a major factor in susceptibility to the advanced disease.

The authors examined haplotypes, the inherited blocks of variants in the gene. They checked their associations with drusen, the deposits that mark early disease, and with advanced macular degeneration. Sorting out which variant patterns raise risk sharpens genetic counseling and points at the complement system as a treatment target.
plos-pone-0001297:
DNA helicases are enzymes that unwind the double helix, a step required for repair, recombination, and replication. Sudha Sharma and Robert Brosh studied one human helicase, RECQ1, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Humans have five helicases of this family, several tied to diseases of premature aging and cancer risk.

The authors report that human RECQ1 responds to DNA damage. It is also required for resistance to genotoxic stress and for suppression of sister chromatid exchanges, a sign of faulty repair. Their work assigns concrete duties to the least-studied member of the family. It matters for understanding how cells guard their genomes.
plos-pone-0001397:
Yunfeng Li and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two proteins that uncouple energy use in cells. One protein, when raised, had been tied to weak insulin release. The other tends to drop in the muscle of people with type 2 diabetes. The team asked whether sugar drives these two proteins in unlike ways.

Working with insulin making cells of the pancreas, they tested how sugar levels shift each protein. The two did not move in step, which fit their hunch of opposed effects. The result helps clarify how fuel use is tuned in these cells. It may bear on why insulin release fails as diabetes takes hold.
plos-pone-0001497:
Jan Brascamp and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how past views shape what we see now. When an image can be read two ways, sight flips between the reads. Shown at gaps, the image tends to return in the same read as before. The team asked how long that memory of a past read lasts.

They found the pull of past views works on more than one time scale at once. Both brief and longer spans shape the next read. That layered memory helps the brain settle vague input fast. It also shows past sight aids, rather than biases, clear seeing in many cases.
plos-pone-0001597:
Kristine Briedis, Ayelet Starr, and Philip Bourne published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the human kinome, the full set of kinase enzymes. Kinases are prime drug targets, but some stay hidden when gene codes stray too far from known ones. Shape based searches can catch what code searches miss. The team ran such a search across the human set.

Their search found two kinases that code based hunts had missed. New kinases widen the list of druggable targets. They also show the known kinome was not yet closed. Each such find can seed a new drug line for cancer and other ills.
plos-pone-0001697:
Robert G. Wallace and Walter M. Fitch studied how bird flu crosses borders in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The strain is highly pathogenic influenza A H5N1. Its geographic spread is a necessary step toward the virus evolving human-to-human spread. As it travels, it diversifies in response to local farming and social conditions.

The authors report that H5N1 immigration is filtered out at some international borders, meaning the virus fails to establish in certain countries it reaches. The full text gives the family-tree analysis of virus samples and the border patterns they found. Knowing which borders hold, and why, could help target surveillance where the virus is most likely to break through.
plos-pone-0001797:
Blerina Kola and co-authors studied how the hunger hormone ghrelin acts in the brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Ghrelin and cannabinoids both stimulate appetite, possibly through the hypothalamic enzyme AMPK, a key regulator of appetite and metabolism. Rimonabant, a blocker of the cannabinoid CB1 receptor, can block ghrelin's hunger effect.

The team reports that ghrelin's hunger effect is mediated through central activation of the endogenous cannabinoid system. The full text gives the feeding experiments and the blocker tests. Two appetite systems acting as one pathway helps explain why CB1 blockers cut hunger so strongly, and why their side effects were so broad.
plos-pone-0001897:
Antoine Lutz and colleagues scanned the brains of meditators in a 2008 PLOS ONE study on compassion. Past scans had shown that two brain areas, the insula and the front cingulate, react when a person feels another's pain. What no one knew was whether training the mind to feel compassion on purpose would change that response.

The team used brain scans while skilled and new meditators heard sounds of people in distress. They compared how each group reacted as they held a kind, caring state of mind. The study tests whether long practice reshapes the brain's response to suffering. That bears on how mental training might aid care work and health.
plos-pone-0001997:
Alfredo Rodriguez and co-authors built a program that finds and sorts tiny knobs on nerve cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The knobs, dendritic spines, are where most excitatory synapses sit, and their shape is tied to learning and memory. Gauging their three-dimensional forms by hand was slow and imprecise, which blocked firm statistics.

Their software detects spines in fluorescence microscope images in three dimensions and classifies their shapes on its own. Fast, precise counts let labs compare spine types across health and disease. Such tools turn a craft task into data that large studies can trust.
plos-pone-0002097:
Karthik Jayapal and co-authors compared gene messages to proteins over time in a soil bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Streptomyces coelicolor is a model for the bacteria that make most of our antibiotics. Many biological processes are dynamic, with deep shifts at both the molecular and body level. Systems analyses profile either gene messages or proteins to watch them.

The team looked for genes where the two do not move together, divergent mRNA-protein dynamics. Where message and protein part ways, control must sit after the message is made. Such genes warn against reading gene activity as protein truth.
plos-pone-0002197:
Sophie Colomb and co-authors traced how two genes guide nerve growth in the fruit fly embryo, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A hard problem in brain science is finding the cues that tell growing nerve fibers where to go. Those cues build the neat, repeated wiring of a nervous system.

In the fly, the genes Engrailed and Gooseberry-Neuro work together in a nerve cell called neuroblast 6-4. The team shows their joint action triggers the growth of the rear commissure bundles, bridges of fibers that cross the embryo. Small switches like these lay down the roads that whole brains are built from.
plos-pone-0002297:
Tomonori Takeuchi and co-authors studied a protein found only at one kind of synapse in the cerebellum, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The cerebellum tunes movement. In its Purkinje cells, a protein called delphilin sits exactly at parallel fiber synapses. There it binds a glutamate receptor, GluR delta2, essential for long-term depression and motor learning.

Mice lacking delphilin let the team test its role head-on. They found both long-term depression, a lasting weakening of synapses, and the optokinetic response, a learned eye movement, were enhanced. An unusual result like this refines the model of how this region learns.
plos-pone-0002397:
Agudelo-Romero, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Patricia Agudelo-Romero, Pablo Carbonell, Miguel A. Perez-Amador, among others. Its subject is virus Adaptation by Manipulation of Host's Gene Expression. Viruses adapt to their hosts by evading defense mechanisms and taking over cellular metabolism for their own benefit.

Alterations in cell metabolism as well as side-effects of antiviral responses contribute to symptoms development and virulence. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002497:
Dettenhofer and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Markus Dettenhofer, Fen Zhou, Philip Leder, among others. Its subject is formin 1-Isoform IV Deficient Cells Exhibit Defects in Cell Spreading and Focal Adhesion Formation. Regulation of the cytoskeleton is a central feature of cell migration.

The formin family of proteins controls the rate of actin nucleation at its barbed end. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002597:
Krach and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Sören Krach, Frank Hegel, Britta Wrede, among others. Its subject is can Machines Think? Interaction and Perspective Taking with Robots Investigated via fMRI. When our PC goes on strike again we tend to curse it as if it were a human being.

Why and under which circumstances do we attribute human-like properties to machines? The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002697:
In 2008, Miao Hao and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was Structure-Activity relationship and Substrate-Dependent phenomena in effects of ginsenosides on activities of Drug-Metabolizing P450 enzymes. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Miao Hao, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Ginseng, a traditional herbal medicine, may interact with several co-administered drugs in clinical settings, and ginsenosides, the major active components of ginseng. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002797:
In 2008, Jianqiao Ge and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about distinct neurocognitive strategies for comprehensions of human and artificial intelligence. The catalog record names Jianqiao Ge first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Although humans have inevitably interacted with both human and artificial intelligence in real life situations. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002897:
Darby Harris and Seth DeBolt measured how orderly plant cell walls are in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The wall is the main load-bearing frame of a plant and shapes growth, form, and defense against stress. Yet how its parts are built and adjusted was still not well understood at the level of mechanism.

Their topic was relative crystallinity, meaning how much of the wall material sits in neat crystal form. They studied how that trait is assembled and how plants adapt or adjust it. Growers and materials scientists both care, since wall structure affects crop strength and plant-based materials.
plos-pone-0002997:
Xiaomin Yu, Qing Zhou, Sung-Chou Li and co-authors catalogued silkworm microRNAs across development in 2008. MicroRNAs are tiny regulators that tune gene activity after genes are read, affecting development and metabolism. The silkworm Bombyx mori is both an industry animal and a model insect, and its genome had been sequenced.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the team describes the silkworm's microRNAs and how their expression changes across multiple developmental stages. Stage patterns hint at which growth steps each microRNA governs. The catalog supports silk biology and wider insect development research. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003097:
Qian-Jin Zhang, Xiao-Lin Li, David Wang and co-authors studied dendritic cells taking up tumor material by trogocytosis in 2008. Two parts of the antigen presentation pathway, TAP and MHC class I, are often deficient in tumor cells. Restoring them was shown to restore presentation, but tumors find other escapes.

Trogocytosis is nibbling membrane from another cell. The team reports it moves MHC-I peptide complexes from tumors and infected cells to dendritic cells, enhancing cross-priming and adaptive T cell responses. Published in PLOS ONE, that transfer could help vaccines work around tumor hiding. The article appeared in PLOS ONE, an open access journal anyone can read free online.
plos-pone-0003197:
Jonathan Livny, Hidayat Teonadi, Miron Livny and colleagues present a large-scale method to find bacterial small RNAs in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Diverse bacterial genomes encode many small non-coding RNAs, called sRNAs, that regulate a wide range of biological processes. Computer algorithms had proven effective at finding sRNA-encoding sites, but tools and infrastructure to run those computations at scale were lacking.

The team offer high-throughput, kingdom-wide prediction and annotation of bacterial non-coding RNAs. Readers get a pipeline meant to work across many species, not just one model bacterium. Broad coverage can reveal regulators that single-genome studies would never see.
plos-pone-0003297:
Yaron Ideses, Yifat Brill-Karniely, Lior Haviv and colleagues rebuild actin structures in the lab in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. During cellular migration, regulated actin assembly takes place at the cell leading edge, with steady breakup deeper in the cell interior. Actin polymerization at the plasma membrane pushes out cell protrusions such as lamellipodia and filopodia.

The title reports that the Arp2/3 branched actin network drives filopodia-like bundle formation in vitro. Readers see one network produce structures usually credited to another system. Rebuilding cell edges from parts helps settle how protrusions really form.
plos-pone-0003397:
Jennifer M. Tsuruda, Gro V. Amdam, and Robert E. Page studied honey bee behavior in this 2008 paper. Some bee colonies store far more pollen than others. That hoarding habit comes with a set of linked body and behavior traits. The authors tested whether the habit shares roots with female traits linked to reproduction.

They compared bee strains bred for high and low pollen storage. The bees' senses responded to sugar and other cues in line with their strain. Those responses tied social behavior to the reproductive side of the colony. The link hints that one gene network shapes both sets of traits.
plos-pone-0003497:
Yasuhiro Watanabe, Eri Morita, and Yasuyo Fukada studied a faulty enzyme in ALS for this 2008 paper. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis kills the nerve cells that move muscles. Some inherited cases trace to mutations in an enzyme called SOD1. How that mutation causes such wide cell damage stayed elusive.

The team focused on single misfolded units of mutant SOD1. Those units stuck to cell surfaces in an adherent form. Such sticky misfolded protein may seed damage in motor neurons. The work offers a concrete form to target in therapy design. ALS moves fast once it starts, and no cure exists for it yet.
plos-pone-0003597:
Liliana D. Kojic and co-authors eyed a tumor entry route in this 2008 paper. A protein called AMF/PGI acts outside cells as a motility signal. Its receptor, gp78/AMFR, is overexpressed in many human cancers. Earlier work showed raft-based uptake of the signal is high in metastatic cells.

That uptake did not rise the same way in non-metastatic cells. Raft-dependent endocytosis thus marks aggressive tumor behavior. Hijacking the route could smuggle drugs straight into tumor cells. The study maps a doorway worth targeting. Few such routes are known, which makes each mapped one worth study.
plos-pone-0003697:
Uri Yerushalmi and Mina Teicher published this modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Synaptic plasticity, the change in strength between neurons, is a leading candidate for how brains learn and remember. How such plasticity itself arose is a separate question. The authors built a model of evolving cellular development.

Within their model, networks grew whose synapses could change with experience. Watching plasticity evolve in the simulation offers clues to how real brains came to rewire themselves. The work links two fields that rarely meet: the evolution of development and the study of learning.
plos-pone-0003797:
Stefan Kulick, Claudia Moccia, Xavier Didelot, and colleagues published this bacteria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Helicobacter pylori lives in the stomachs of half of humanity and can cause gastritis, ulcers, and cancer. It naturally takes up DNA from its surroundings, and mixed infections let strains swap genes.

The team examined what that imported DNA looks like after transformation. They found mosaic imports, with pieces of the recipient's own sequence sprinkled inside the new DNA. The interspersed pattern reveals in fine detail how this ulcer bacterium shuffles its genes with neighbors.
plos-pone-0003897:
Camille Macé, Damien Seyer, Chanez Chemani, and co-authors hunted for biofilm genes in a hospital germ in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article concerns Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that often infects patients in hospitals. It forms biofilms, slimy layers that protect it from drugs and defenses. An earlier protein study had flagged one unknown protein made more in biofilms.

The authors traced that protein to a gene cluster they named bac. They report the cluster helps the germ build biofilms and cause disease. Naming such a cluster gives drug hunters a fresh target. Weakening biofilms could make stubborn infections easier to treat.
plos-pone-0003997:
Sergey Kuznetsov and Andrei V. Khokhlatchev reported a new way tumor suppressors get destroyed in 2008. NORE1A and RASSF1A are proteins that restrain cell growth. Both are switched off in many kinds of cancer. Silencing of their promoters was the best-known route to losing them.

Their PLOS ONE article describes cutting of both proteins by calpain enzymes. That cutting, called proteolysis, offers another route to losing their restraint. Cancer cells may exploit more than one route at once. Blocking the cutting could help keep tumor suppressors in place. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004097:
Hua Shen, Bethany M. Tesar, Wei Du, and co-authors studied aging and transplant responses in 2009. More older people now wait for solid organ transplants. How aging changes immune responses to a graft was not well understood. Both donor cells and recipient immunity prime the response.

Their PLOS ONE article tested whether aging impairs those priming steps. They found aging weakens recipient T cell factors, both intrinsic and extrinsic. Weaker priming could mean older recipients reject grafts differently. The results may guide gentler drug regimens for older patients. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004197:
Edith Roussel and colleagues published this insect study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Social insects owe part of their success to a division of labour. The standard explanation is a response threshold model. Workers differ in how strong a task signal must be before they respond. So different workers pick up different jobs.

Roussel's team reappraised that picture using aversive responsiveness and learning, asking how bees respond to unpleasant stimuli and what they learn from them. Their angle tests whether the same thresholds that assign work also shift with experience. The study refines a core idea about how insect societies organise themselves.
plos-pone-0004297:
Terence Murphy and colleagues published this plant genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Arabidopsis thaliana, the standard lab plant, has three genes resembling the abasic endonuclease genes of bacteria, yeast, and animals. In those organisms, such enzymes perform base excision repair, fixing DNA bases damaged by oxidation and other insults.

The team tested whether the plant versions are required for seed development. Their analysis of mutants shows the roles these repair genes play as seeds form. Seeds must guard their DNA through dormancy, since a seed's genome is the whole future plant.
plos-pone-0004397:
The earliest dinosaurs come from Late Triassic rocks in South America. Ricardo Martinez and Oscar Alcober described one from the Ischigualasto Formation in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper names it a basal sauropodomorph. That group later gave rise to the giant long-necked sauropods. The fossil dates to the Carnian age, near the group's dawn.

By the Carnian, the main dinosaur branches were already split. A very early sauropodomorph called Saturnalia was already known. A second basal form helps show how the line began. The authors use it to trace early sauropodomorph evolution. Finds like this anchor the family tree of the largest land animals ever.
plos-pone-0004497:
Breathing, not just wings, may have made giant flying reptiles possible, argue Leon Claessens, Patrick O'Connor, and David Unwin in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pterosaurs were extinct reptiles of the Mesozoic era and the first backboned animals to fly by flapping. Evidence shows their wings were efficient and their flight control strong.

Far less was known about the lungs that powered that flight. The authors reconstruct how the pterosaur breathing system evolved. They argue that advances in respiration came first and made true flight, and later aerial gigantism, possible. Some pterosaurs grew to the size of small planes. Tying their size to their breathing gives a fuller account of how the largest flying animals ever lived actually worked.
plos-pone-0004597:
A faulty PINK1 gene tangles several cell systems at once in Parkinson's models, report Wencheng Liu, Cristofol Vives-Bauza, Rebeca Acin-Perez, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. PINK1 is a mitochondrial kinase, an enzyme inside the cell's power plants. Mutations in it cause an autosomal recessive, early form of Parkinson's disease, known as PARK6.

The team reports that PINK1 normally exists as a dimer, a paired unit, in mitochondrial protein complexes that travel with the respiratory chain. When PINK1 is defective, mitochondria malfunction. The proteasome, the cell's protein shredder, also falls short, and alpha-synuclein, the protein that clumps in Parkinson's brains, aggregates. One broken gene linking energy, cleanup, and clumping explains much of the disease picture.
plos-pone-0004697:
William Stork and colleagues studied how plants handle a defense hormone after bug attack, for PLOS ONE in 2009. When insects chew a leaf, the plant makes a fast burst of jasmonic acid. That burst turns on many defenses that slow further feeding and help heal the wound.

Far less was known about how the burst fades or spreads. The team tracked how the hormone is changed after repeat attacks and how it moves through the leaf. Their work frames the burst as a kind of plant memory. It may help crops resist pests with less spray. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
plos-pone-0004797:
Anne Farina and colleagues studied post transcriptional regulation of cadherin-11 in prostate and breast cancer cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cadherin-11 is a cell adhesion molecule important in embryo growth, bone formation, cancer invasion, and homing of cancer cells to bone. It also plays roles in rheumatoid arthritis, yet very little was known about how its expression is regulated.

The team found control after transcription by GSK-3 and beta catenin pathways. That layer of control affects how much protein cells make. It may influence spread to bone, a major clinical problem. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0004897:
Jennifer Shen and colleagues deciphered von Hippel Lindau linked pancreatic manifestations by inactivating Vhl in pancreatic cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The syndrome is a pleomorphic familial disease marked by highly vascularized tumors including hemangioblastomas, pheochromocytomas, renal carcinomas, cysts, and neuroendocrine tumors of pancreas. Cell specific inactivation in mice separates which pancreatic lineages generate which lesion types during growth and adult life.

Different cells of origin produce cysts versus tumors. Mouse models mirror human pancreatic spectrum. Lineage knowledge guides surveillance imaging. Rare disease steps illuminate angiogenesis. Later work can build on these findings and test them in broader settings. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004997:
In southern Africa, HIV hits the general population hard. Men who have sex with men were largely excluded from surveys. Epidemiologic data for them were among the sparsest anywhere. Stefan Baral and colleagues filled part of that gap in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied Malawi, Namibia and Botswana. They measured HIV prevalence, risk and human rights.

The data reveal a hidden, high-risk group. Its members face stigma and legal threats alongside the virus. Excluding them leaves a blind spot in epidemic control. The findings argue for including them in surveillance and care. They also document rights abuses that shape risk. Public health cannot succeed while ignoring this population.
plos-pone-0005097:
Muscle cells prune themselves as they mature. That pruning is apoptosis, controlled cell death. Runaway pruning destroys muscle in disease. Michelle Smith, Yolanda Huang and Mohanish Deshmukh studied how pruning is restrained. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They focused on myotubes, the young fibers of skeletal muscle.

As muscle cells differentiate, they switch on a brake called XIAP. XIAP restricts the apoptotic pathway. The cells evoke their own protector at the right moment. That self-brake keeps pruning in check. The finding points to a built-in defense for muscle. Boosting it might fight muscle loss in neuromuscular disease. The study shows development builds in its own safeguards.
plos-pone-0005197:
