A family of proteins called SREBPs acts as a master switch for fat and cholesterol in mammals. These switches control genes for taking up and making cholesterol, fatty acids, and triglycerides. Chatterjee and colleagues hunted for new controls on that switch in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The team identified novel genes and pathways that regulate how strongly SREBPs work. Each new regulator is a possible handle for drugs aimed at high cholesterol or fatty liver. The work widens the map of fat control beyond the few switches that were already well known.
plos-pone-0005297:
Chloroplast genomes in grasses evolve faster than those of most other flowering plants. Why that speedup happened, and when, stayed obscure for years. Zhong and colleagues traced the pattern in ancestral grasses in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study estimated how the pace of chloroplast evolution changed over time. Change came in episodes, with bursts of adaptation rather than a steady fast rate. Episodic evolution helps explain the grass family's success and gives plant scientists a timeline for genome change in a vital crop family. Grasses feed much of the world, from wheat to corn to rice. So the pace of change in their green cells is a clue to how these crops may cope with a hot, dry world.
plos-pone-0005397:
TRAIL is a protein that can order infected or abnormal cells to die, and it takes part in HIV disease by depleting CD4 T cells. Huang and colleagues studied what controls TRAIL in HIV-infected macrophages in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Type I interferons, the early antiviral signals, regulate TRAIL in those macrophages. Interferon regulatory factors carry out part of that control. The pathway links the innate alarm system to a death ligand that harms the very cells HIV patients can least afford to lose. Drugs that curb this virus must save CD4 cells, not just block the germ. So a path that links the alarm to the loss of those cells is a fresh place to aim a cure or a shield.
plos-pone-0005497:
Oren Parnas and colleagues studied a yeast gene tied to genome stability in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When the gene ELG1 is faulty, yeast suffer extra DNA swaps, lost chromosomes, and gross breaks in their genome. The gene's protein resembles part of the tool that loads clamps onto DNA during copying.

The team found that the Elg1 complex also helps hold sister copies of DNA together after copying. That holding step, called cohesion, keeps chromosomes paired until the cell divides. A fault there can scramble the genome, which links this small yeast gene to big questions about cancer.
plos-pone-0005597:
Gal Markel and co-authors tested a way to boost natural killer cells against tumours in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Natural killer cells are immune cells that can kill cancer cells without prior training. They are used in cell therapies, above all around stem cell transplants.

The team matched a receptor on the killer cells with its partner on target cells to pick stronger pairings. Choosing donors whose cells match in the right way could make the therapy hit tumours harder. That would be welcome in cancers that resist other treatments. Stronger killer cells could also help patients whose own immune systems are weakened by transplant drugs.
plos-pone-0005697:
Alana Conti and colleagues studied in 2009 how alcohol changes a key learning site in the mouse brain. Mice lacking two enzymes, AC1 and AC8, react to alcohol in unusual ways. Those enzymes help nerve cells adjust the strength of their links, a base of memory.

The team found that the two enzymes start a self-correcting response at the synapse when alcohol arrives. This presynaptic response acts like a brake, steadying the circuit. Knowing which molecules set that brake helps explain why alcohol's effects differ between people. It also marks paths for drugs aimed at problem drinking.
plos-pone-0005797:
Iain Anderson and co-authors read the genomes of a little-studied order of methane-making microbes in 2009. Methanomicrobiales make methane in swamps, guts, and sediments. By ribosomal genes they sit near one class of methanogens, yet their metabolism looks like another's.

Full genomes let the team sort them into three classes with distinct toolkits. That order sharpens how scientists model methane output from nature, a greenhouse concern. It also shows how genome reads can settle mismatches between a family tree and a lifestyle. These microbes punch far above their size in climate terms.
plos-pone-0005897:
Mareike Selcho and co-authors tested in 2009 what role dopamine plays when fly larvae learn to link a smell with a taste reward or punishment. Even fly larvae form and recall such odor associations. Their simple brains make them a clean model for the basics of learning.

The team probed dopamine signaling during classical conditioning in the larvae. Dopamine is a universal teaching signal in animal brains, but its exact classroom duties vary. Pinning them down in a minimal brain informs models of learning everywhere. The study adds larval data to a story mostly built on adult flies and bees.
plos-pone-0005997:
African horse sickness can kill more than nine in ten horses it strikes. Rachael Chiam, Emma Sharp, Sushila Maan and colleagues worked on a safer vaccine in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper gives ponies a vaccine built on MVA, a weakened virus used as a carrier, loaded with parts of the horse sickness virus.

Current vaccines carry worries of their own, so a carrier-based shot is an appealing swap. The team measured the antibody response the ponies raised after the shot. Antibodies are the first sign a vaccine has taught the body its lesson. The study supports the carrier route as a path to guard horses against a dreaded disease.
plos-pone-0006097:
A family of fertility genes runs through the animal kingdom, from flies to people. Hongyan Xu, Zhendong Li, Mingyou Li and colleagues added fish to that family's map in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper reports the gene boule in fish, and shows it is expressed in germ cells of both sexes in medaka, a small lab fish, in adults and in embryos.

Relatives of boule differ in their habits: one is male-only before meiosis, another serves both sexes. Finding boule active in both sexes in fish reshapes the family's story. Since these genes are essential for fertility across species, each new map point helps explain human fertility problems written in the same ancient code.
plos-pone-0006197:
Brain inflammation and Alzheimer's disease are closely linked, but which immune signals drive the damage is less clear. Tomomi Kiyota and colleagues focused on CCL2, a signal that calls immune cells in, in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Earlier work with mice making extra CCL2 had shown stronger microglial responses, the brain's own immune reaction.

The team reports that extra CCL2 speeds the forming of amyloid clumps and worsens thinking problems. Those clumps are a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. The work names one pathway by which inflammation may push the disease forward. It suggests that calming that signal could be worth testing as a treatment idea.
plos-pone-0006297:
Watching tuberculosis bacteria inside a living animal usually requires invasive sampling. Stephanie Davis and colleagues turned a bacterial enzyme into an imaging beacon in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A tracer molecule, FIAU, is switched on by bacterial thymidine kinase and can then be detected by scanners.

Their goal was to use that reporter for Mycobacterium tuberculosis in live animals without surgery. Non-invasive tracking shows where infection sits and how treatment shrinks it. Animal studies of new TB drugs gain a direct readout. The approach builds on imaging methods proven in other bacteria.
plos-pone-0006397:
A virus that helps a parasitic wasp turns out to sit where three virus families meet. Yves Bigot and colleagues studied the symbiotic ascovirus DpAV4a in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The virus markedly increases its wasp vector's fitness by raising survival of wasp eggs and larvae inside moth hosts.

The authors place the virus at the evolutionary intersection of iridoviruses, ascoviruses, and ichnoviruses. Shared ancestry among large DNA viruses is written in its genome. A wasp's partner virus thus informs the whole family tree. Symbiosis and evolution meet in one genome.
plos-pone-0006497:
Myriam Ermonval and co-authors studied two membrane proteins that meet in PLOS ONE in 2009. The cellular prion protein is attached to cell membranes and is abundant in lipid rafts, ordered patches of membrane. This protein is absolutely required for the neurodegeneration seen in prion diseases. The team examined its interaction with tissue non-specific alkaline phosphatase in membrane microdomains.

Partners of the prion protein may explain what it does in healthy cells. They may also show how it turns harmful. Membrane microdomains are where many signals are organized. Finding a partner there adds a piece to the prion puzzle, which still lacks a full picture of normal function.
plos-pone-0006597:
Saeid Taheri and co-authors correlated two imaging measures after stroke in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. Variations in apparent diffusion coefficient of water and blood-brain barrier permeability after ischemia have both been suggested as injury markers. The correlation between them was their question. Ischemia is the loss of blood flow that causes stroke damage.

They mapped spatiotemporal correlations: how the two measures relate across space and time. If they track together, one scan may stand in for both. If they diverge, each tells a different part of the injury story. Such mapping helps interpret brain scans after stroke.
plos-pone-0006697:
Wiâm Ramadan, Oxana Eschenko, and Susan J. Sara studied sleep and memory in the hippocampus for PLOS ONE in 2009. Sleep clearly helps memory, as many human studies show. The brain mechanisms behind that benefit remain debated. The authors focused on fast brain waves called ripples. Ripples appear in a hippocampal area known as CA1 during sleep.

They tested whether sharp wave and ripple events help lock in associative memory. Associative memory links one thing to another, such as a place and a reward. If ripples do the locking, disturbing them should weaken later recall. The work connects a specific sleep rhythm to a specific memory job. It helps explain why sleep after learning protects new associations.
plos-pone-0006797:
Gerard Honig and his team gave mice a much-used mood drug for a long stretch in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug is citalopram. It is an SSRI, a drug that blocks the reuptake of serotonin. Serotonin is a brain signal that shapes mood and acts. These drugs lift serotonin flow by blocking its cleanup. Vast numbers of people take them for low mood and fear.

Long use led the mouse forebrain to make less serotonin, and the drop lasted. So the brain made less of the signal while its cleanup stayed blocked. That shift may explain why such drugs act slowly or fade with time. It muddies the simple tale of how SSRIs help. The find counts for how long-term use of these drugs is judged.
plos-pone-0006897:
David Metzgar and his team read bacterial traits off DNA type codes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Group A Streptococcus sows ills from sore throats to grave deep strikes. Strains split wide in drug proof, in how sick they make man, and in how fast they spread. The stock code is emm typing, a read of one surface gene. A wider code reads more gene spots at once.

Joined, the codes let the team guess drug proof and strength of a strain. Guesses from code can speed the reply to an outbreak. Labs can flag grave strains long before slow tests end. The work shows how much sick-care sense hides in type codes. It firms up the watch on a germ with many guises.
plos-pone-0006997:
Sara Lindström, Malin Eriksson, Tandis Vazin, and colleagues built a stem cell screening chip in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interest in reprogramming factors had made stem cell screens a hot tool. Researchers wanted fast ways to study cells gaining or losing their stem identity. The team answered with a miniaturized microwell chip.

Their device cultures stem cells in many tiny wells at once. Thousands of small experiments can then be read in parallel. The chip is designed to be easy for ordinary labs to use. Cheaper, faster screening speeds the search for conditions that steer stem cells safely.
plos-pone-0007097:
Agnieszka Rzadzinska, Elisa Nevalainen, Haydn Prosser, and colleagues studied hearing structures in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hearing rests on stereocilia, tiny bristles on inner ear cells. They stand in a staircase pattern of graded lengths. That pattern is kept by constant actin turnover at different rates. Two unusual myosin motors were already tied to the system.

The team showed myosin VIIa interacts with twinfilin-2 at stereocilia tips. The partnership sits exactly where length is controlled. Defects in these proteins cause deafness. Each new tip interaction helps explain how the ear builds its precise sound ladder.
plos-pone-0007197:
Jessica Bauer, Gerhard Liebisch, Claudia Hofmann, and colleagues studied fat-like molecules in bowel inflammation in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their models were mice with experimental colitis, a condition resembling inflammatory bowel disease. Diet and drugs that change lipid metabolism are candidate treatments for such disease.

The authors measure changes in bioactive lipids during colitis. They focus on ceramide and the drug imipramine, and how each affects an enzyme called matrix metalloproteinase-1. Their work connects lipid changes to tissue damage pathways in the gut, which may guide new treatment ideas for bowel inflammation.
plos-pone-0007297:
Philippe Lehours, Zongli Zheng, Anna Skoglund, and colleagues studied stomach bacteria linked to a rare lymphoma in 2009. Helicobacter pylori infects the stomach and usually causes chronic gastritis. Some strains are associated with gastric MALT lymphoma, a cancer of immune tissue in the stomach lining.

The authors ask whether the bacterial surface sugar, called lipopolysaccharide, differs in lymphoma strains. They compare Lewis antigen expression in dozens of MALT strains and gastritis-only strains. They also track a bacterial gene island linked to virulence. Their comparison tests a direct link between bacterial surface and lymphoma development.
plos-pone-0007397:
Renaud Becquet, Ruth Bland, Valériane Leroy, and colleagues pooled data on breastfeeding and HIV transmission in 2009. Both breastfeeding pattern and duration are associated with postnatal HIV acquisition by infants. Their relative contributions had not been reliably quantified, leaving feeding advice for mothers with HIV uncertain in many low-resource settings.

The authors pool individual data from West and South African cohorts. In urban West Africa, stopping breastfeeding early was recommended, but exclusive breastfeeding was common. They separate effects of pattern from effects of duration. Their PLOS ONE analysis informs safer infant feeding guidance where formula is risky.
plos-pone-0007497:
Jyrki Selinummi and colleagues published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on automated analysis of cell images. Fluorescence microscopy is the standard tool for such work. It has real drawbacks: few usable color channels, overlapping dye signals, and added cost. The team asked whether ordinary bright field images could serve instead. Their test case was macrophages, immune cells often screened in large numbers.

Plain light images carried enough detail for the automated analysis. That means many screens may not need fluorescent dyes at all. Dropping the dyes makes large-scale cell work simpler and cheaper. It also avoids artifacts that staining can add. The study gives labs a leaner way to run image-based screens. A standard microscope method turns out to hold more information than its routine use suggests.
plos-pone-0007597:
Rohit Mehra and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the bacterium that causes relapsing fever. Borrelia hermsii is a spirochete, a spiral-shaped bacterium, spread by ticks. It is famous for antigenic variation: it swaps its outer coat proteins to evade the immune system. Those coat proteins, called Vsps, come in many serotypes. The team examined the relation between each variant's structure and its function.

Different Vsp serotypes seem to do more than disguise the bacterium. Evidence suggests they also influence where in the body the bacteria settle. A coat that both hides the germ and steers it is a double tool. Mapping which structures go with which behaviors helps explain the waves of fever. Each relapse follows a coat change, so the coat catalog is central to the disease. The study connects protein shape to the bacterium's strategy.
plos-pone-0007697:
Andre Sousa and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It concerns a gene variant tied to diabetes and heart disease. The gene is called TCF7L2, and one variant, named rs7903146, has been linked again and again to type 2 diabetes. Diabetes in turn raises the risk of coronary artery disease.

The team asked whether that variant also tracks how severe heart disease becomes and whether patients survive. They report that it does. A variant known for diabetes may therefore also help flag which heart patients face the greatest danger.
plos-pone-0007797:
Mariangela Chisari and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It watches how G proteins behave when a cell's receptors are stimulated. G proteins relay signals from receptors to the cell's machinery. The team measured an effector enzyme, phospholipase C-beta, as it responded.

Sensors tracked the making of two messenger molecules in living cells. The results show that G protein subunits split apart after stimulation. They also move to new places inside the cell. Both the split and the move shape the cell's answer. Signaling is thus a matter of travel as well as chemistry.
plos-pone-0007897:
Santina Bruzzone and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It tests a metabolic drug in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The model, EAE, mimics the immune attack that strips nerve insulation. Activated T lymphocytes drive that attack.

The drug blocks Nampt, an enzyme cells need to make NAD, a core energy molecule. Blocking it in activated T cells caused catastrophic NAD depletion. Treated mice showed less demyelination and less disability. The approach turns an energy dependency into a weakness. It suggests a new angle for treating autoimmune disease.
plos-pone-0007997:
Alfredo Castello and colleagues showed how the AIDS virus quiets a host cell in PLOS ONE in 2009. HIV carries a cutting enzyme, a protease, that snips viral proteins into shape. The team found it also snips two host proteins the cell needs to start making its own proteins.

With those start factors cut, the cell's normal protein making stalls, while the virus can still push its own agenda. The sabotage helps the virus take over the cell's workshop. Blocking the cut is hard without harming the drug targets already in use, but the step is now clearly mapped.
plos-pone-0008097:
Hui Zhu and Andrew Bendall studied a gene that tells cartilage cells when to swell and harden in PLOS ONE in 2009. Bones grow by first laying down cartilage, then swapping it for bone. The gene, Dlx5, works inside the cartilage cells themselves.

In mice, Dlx5 drove that swelling step, and it could also cover the job of its sibling gene Dlx6 when that gene was missing. A backup that truly works is a gift to the growing skeleton. The finding helps explain why some gene faults spare the bones they were expected to harm.
plos-pone-0008197:
Jennifer MacKellar, Samuel W. Cushman, and Vipul Periwal described waves of fat growth in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. When mammals eat more calories than they burn, the surplus is stored mainly as fat. Steady excess requires fat tissue to enlarge over time. Faulty fat growth may be a key factor in insulin resistance.

The team studied the genetically obese Zucker fatty rat. They tracked how its fat tissue expands in waves rather than smoothly. Knowing the timing of growth helps explain when tissue takes in new cells. It also frames how obesity develops in this widely used model.
plos-pone-0008297:
Zoltan Beck and colleagues studied red blood cells and HIV in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. CD4 cells are the major target of HIV infection in blood. Claims that HIV-1 also binds red blood cells had generated controversy. The Duffy blood group antigen was proposed as the binding site. Binding without complement proteins was part of the dispute.

The team examined the question directly with infectious virus. Human erythrocytes selectively bound and enriched infectious HIV-1 virions. If red cells carry virus, they could shape how HIV spreads in the body. The finding reopens a debated part of HIV biology.
plos-pone-0008397:
Fa-Xing Yu and Yan Luo studied gene regulation by glucose in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Thioredoxin interacting protein, or Txnip, is a multifunctional protein. It helps regulate the cell cycle and cellular metabolism. Its expression is induced by glucose, adenosine-containing molecules, and other cues. The underlying regulatory mechanism was not fully known.

The team found tandem ChoRE and CCAAT motifs control Txnip expression. These DNA motifs and their associated factors respond to glucose or adenosine signals. Pinpointing the switches explains how diet-related cues tune this gene. That bears on diabetes and metabolism research.
plos-pone-0008497:
Alyssa Barry and co-authors analyze malaria vaccine targets in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Plasmodium falciparum causes the most deadly form of human malaria. Its antigens vary greatly, which blocks a broadly effective vaccine. Yet population genetics has rarely guided vaccine design. The team study genes for ten leading vaccine-candidate antigens. They gather data across parasite populations in a meta-analysis.

They find the population structures of those genes contrast sharply. Some antigens vary by place, others are more uniform. Vaccine design should account for those patterns. A vaccine built on a variable antigen may fail where strains differ most.
plos-pone-0008597:
Oliver Niehuis and co-authors study DNA swapping in a parasitoid wasp in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The swapping, called recombination, occurs in most species that reproduce sexually. Yet its gains for evolution remain elusive. Past work in the honeybee found a very high rate of swapping genome-wide. The wasp Nasonia is a relative with a distinct breeding system. Males hatch from unfertilized eggs in that system.

The team measure the swapping rate across the wasp genome. They assess how it shapes genome structure over time. A contrast with the honeybee tests if high rates are shared in this insect group. The work adds a key case to a long debate.
plos-pone-0008697:
Lukas Vrba, Taylor Jensen, James Garbe, and colleagues asked how two small RNAs get switched off. Their cancer study ran in PLOS ONE in 2010. The RNAs, miR-200c and miR-141, help cells keep a tidy, sheet-like form. When cells lose them, they can loosen and spread, a step toward worse cancer. Something must silence them in tumor cells.

The team checked DNA methylation, a chemical tag that often mutes genes. Healthy and cancer cells showed matching tag patterns near these RNAs. Heavy tagging lined up with low RNA levels. Finding the off switch suggests drugs that strip such tags might restore control.
plos-pone-0008797:
Minli Xu and Zhengchang Su built a faster way to compare gene switch patterns. Their methods paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Transcription factors bind DNA at sites described by frequency tables. Scientists often search databases for similar binding patterns. They also group patterns into families. Old comparison methods first align the patterns, which can distort short ones.

Their new method compares patterns without any alignment step. Tests showed it matches similar motifs and separates different ones well. Skipping alignment speeds large database searches. Gene regulation studies can now cluster thousands of motifs more cleanly.
plos-pone-0008897:
Asako Shindo, Yusuke Hara, Takamasa Yamamoto, and colleagues showed frog embryo cells need a calcium surge to line up correctly. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. During gastrulation, frog tissues fold and stream in coordinated ways. Each cell needs a clear internal direction, called polarity. Neighboring tissues interacting can trigger signals inside cells. Calcium spikes were the suspected trigger here.

When tissues touched, calcium rose inside the responding cells. Blocking that rise prevented proper polarization. Direction is thus set by a neighbor-triggered calcium signal. The mechanism helps explain how embryos organize their first great movements.
plos-pone-0008997:
Guillermo Solovey and Silvina Ponce Dawson modelled how calcium signals spread inside cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Calcium is a messenger cells use for a huge range of tasks. Its messages vary in space and time, from small blips to waves. Much of the calcium enters through channels called IP3 receptors, grouped in clusters.

The model follows calcium release spreading from channel to channel within a cluster. That percolation-style spread explains why signals can stay tiny or ignite fully. Small changes in the cluster tip the balance between the two outcomes. The maths helps make sense of calcium signals seen under the microscope.
plos-pone-0009097:
Matthias Mueller and co-authors profiled the surface spikes of many bird flu types in the lab, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hemagglutinin, the HA spike, is how flu viruses grab cells. Research had concentrated on the dangerous H5 and H7 subtypes. But bird flu mutates and reshuffles so fast that other subtypes matter too.

The team made HA proteins from several avian influenza subtypes. They characterised how antibodies recognise each version. A broader library helps test kits spot whichever subtype appears. Preparedness improves when diagnostics are not built for two subtypes only.
plos-pone-0009197:
Dana Gwinn, John Asara, and Reuben Shaw published this cell division study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells must enter and exit division in the right order, or copies go wrong. A web of signals times each step, backed by checkpoints that halt mistakes. The study focuses on raptor, a protein that helps control cell growth.

The authors report that raptor gains a phosphate tag during mitosis, the stage when chromosomes split. The tag is added by cdc2, a master enzyme that drives cells into division. That link ties the growth-control machinery directly to the division clock. It helps explain how cells coordinate growing in size with splitting in two.
plos-pone-0009297:
Hai Yu and co-authors published this hepatitis B study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hepatitis B virus comes in several genotypes, labeled by letters. A strain called W29, taken from patients in northwestern China, did not fit the known set. Related odd strains had also turned up in Vietnam and Laos.

Using family tree and distance analyses, the team grouped these strains together. They propose the cluster forms an additional genotype, named I. Adding a genotype is not bookkeeping for its own sake. Genotypes differ in how disease progresses and how treatment works, so a missed one can mislead doctors in the regions where it circulates.
plos-pone-0009397:
Xiaojuan Chen and co-authors published this diabetes imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Tissues outside the pancreas, like the liver, might be coaxed into making insulin. That would open a new route to treat diabetes. Watching insulin gene activity in those tissues, inside a living animal, was the challenge.

The team used mice carrying a glowing reporter tied to the insulin gene switch. Bioluminescence imaging let them detect insulin gene expression outside the pancreas in diabetic mice. A live readout like this can follow attempts to grow new insulin sources over time. It turns an invisible gene switch into a measurable signal.
plos-pone-0009497:
Gitit Shahaf, Michael Cancro, and Ramit Mehr used math models of B cell life in PLOS ONE in 2010. B cells make antibodies. Those that react too strongly without proper support signals are removed. This culling happens as B cells mature in the marrow and later in the body. The team modeled how long cells live and where losses occur.

Their model points to a shared death niche for new and mature B cells. In other words, both stages face removal in a like setting. That finding maps the immune system's quality control in a new way. It helps explain how the body prunes risky cells at more than one stage.
plos-pone-0009597:
Michael Moore and colleagues reported a whale rescue method in PLOS ONE in 2010. North Atlantic right whales are among the rarest large whales. Many die tangled in fishing gear. Rescue boats often cannot get close, because the whales evade them. The team tried sedating two free swimming whales at sea. Careful doses were given by injection to calm them.

Once sedated, the whales let boats approach for disentanglement work. The approach raised the chance of removing gear that would otherwise kill them. Sedation at sea carries risks, so dosing had to be exact. The study shows it can be done, giving rescuers a new option for a species near extinction.
plos-pone-0009697:
Genetic studies often fill in missing DNA data by informed guessing, a step called imputation. Peng Lin and colleagues asked how scientists can tell whether those guesses are trustworthy. They proposed a new statistic for the job in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Bad guesses can quietly distort the results of a genome-wide study. The new measure gives researchers a yardstick for the reliability of each filled-in variant. With it, teams can drop shaky values before they skew conclusions. It adds a quality check to a step many studies depend on. The paper speaks to anyone who builds or uses large genetic datasets.
plos-pone-0009897:
Proteins often work in teams, joining into complexes with shared surfaces. Giovanni Feverati and Claire Lesieur put those joining surfaces under a new lens. Their tool, called Gemini, appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Oligomers are small clusters of protein subunits.

An oligomeric interface is where protein subunits touch and bind. Studying those contacts explains how complexes hold together and fall apart. Gemini examines interfaces in a systematic way across many proteins. The view helps researchers predict assembly and design drugs that block it. Subunits that fit poorly cannot build a working complex.
plos-pone-0009997:
Fat cells grow larger in obesity, but not all fat depots carry the same health risk. Jean O'Connell and colleagues compared fat cell sizes in people with severe obesity. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The two depots are omental fat, deep in the belly, and subcutaneous fat, under the skin. Adipocyte size from each depot was set against metabolic disease markers. Severe obesity means a body mass far above the healthy range. Belly fat is long suspected of driving diabetes and heart risk. The comparison tests whether cell size itself tracks that danger.
plos-pone-0010197:
The authors were Sujatha Srinivasan, Congzhou Liu, Caroline Mitchell, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study sampled vaginal bacteria in women over short periods. Little was known about how quickly those bacterial communities change day to day. The team used PCR tests to track key bacteria in healthy women, and in women treated with antibiotics for bacterial vaginosis.

Bacterial vaginosis is an imbalance of the normal vaginal community, not a single germ. Tracking short-term swings shows how stable healthy communities are and how fast treatment shifts them. That timing knowledge can improve diagnosis and follow-up care for a very common condition.
plos-pone-0010397:
Katarina Järlestedt and co-workers asked whether calming a brain scar response changes injury size in newborn mice, for PLOS ONE in 2010. After brain injury, star-shaped support cells react and build up two structural proteins. This reaction is called gliosis. In adult mice missing those proteins, the reaction is blunted. The team tested baby mice with oxygen shortage plus reduced blood flow, a model of newborn brain injury.

Even with gliosis weakened, the injured area stayed the same size. So the support-cell reaction may not drive early damage, at least in newborns. That matters because some treatments aim at gliosis itself. If it does not set injury size, efforts should target other steps. Negative results like this save a field wasted effort.
plos-pone-0010497:
Hania Köver and Shaowen Bao proposed that brain flexibility stores our prior expectations in PLOS ONE in 2010. Perception blends fresh sensory input with what past experience predicts. Ambiguous signals get pulled toward the expected reading. How neurons physically keep those priors was unknown. Other theorists had suggested changing response patterns that shift over time. The authors advanced cortical plasticity, lasting change in cortex connections, as the storage mechanism.

If priors live in plastic connections, learning literally rewires perception. That would explain why expectations are stable yet updatable. The idea connects a math theory of perception, Bayesian inference, to brain hardware. It suggests experiments that track connection change as priors form. Theory papers like this steer the next round of experiments.
plos-pone-0010597:
Emmanuel Boucrot and colleagues questioned a textbook claim about how cells take in cargo, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cells swallow material by building small coated pits on their surface. A helper complex called AP-2 was long thought to be required for every pit.

The team lowered AP-2 levels in cells far below normal. Some cargo still entered cells at a healthy rate. Other cargo did depend on AP-2, as expected. So the helper is vital for certain loads but not for all. The result forces a more careful account of how coated pits form and work.
plos-pone-0010697:
Erich Loza Telleria and colleagues studied gut enzymes in the sand fly that spreads leishmaniasis, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lutzomyia longipalpis carries Leishmania parasites from person to person. Before a parasite can thrive in the fly, it must survive the fly's gut, where digestive enzymes called trypsins break down the blood meal.

The team measured when and how strongly the fly makes these trypsins. They also tested whether the parasite changes that pattern. Parasites that blunt digestion gain a safer start in the gut. Knowing the timing of the enzyme wave suggests when the parasite is weakest, a useful fact for blocking spread inside the fly.
plos-pone-0010797:
Julia Nowack and colleagues recorded body temperature in a small African primate, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The lesser bushbaby, Galago moholi, lives in dry savanna where food and water swing with the seasons. Torpor, a controlled drop in body temperature, saves energy. Among primates, true torpor was thought to be a lemur specialty.

Bushbabies in the wild dropped into torpor when conditions turned harsh. Their temperature fell for hours, then rose again on better days. Torpor on demand in a non-lemur primate widens the trait's known range in our own order. It also hints that early primates may have had more flexible body control than living species suggest.
plos-pone-0010897:
Maria Martin, Shaguna Seth, Dimitrios Koutsonanos and co-authors published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Flu shots given by muscle injection raise good blood antibodies, but protection might improve if the airways, where flu enters, were defended too. The team explored vaccination through the skin, a needle-free route, paired with natural compounds that rouse the immune system.

In their experiments, inactivated flu virus delivered across the skin, together with retinoic acid or oleic acid, drew immune scout cells toward nearby lymph nodes. The responses were strong, lasted a long time, and protected animals against a lethal flu challenge. Martin and colleagues show that route and additives together can upgrade a standard vaccine. Skin delivery could also ease mass vaccination, since it avoids needles and trained injectors.
plos-pone-0010997:
Viviane Hénaux, Michael Samuel and Christine Bunck published this bird flu modeling study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Predicting how bird flu moves through wild birds is key to protecting farms and people. Yet the most dangerous strains are so rarely found in wild birds that their behavior there is guesswork. The authors used modeling to fuse what laboratory and field studies do know.

They built a standard epidemic model with susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered classes, and fed it parameters from published challenge experiments, split by bird age and virus virulence. Infection led to shedding within a day or two, followed by a relatively short infectious period. Hénaux and colleagues also flag where ignorance is greatest. Their synthesis tells surveillance programs which measurements would most improve risk forecasts for wild waterfowl.
plos-pone-0011097:
Bull, Jessop and Whiteley examined Komodo dragons in PLOS ONE in 2010. These giant lizards bite large prey, which often escape at first but die later. A long held idea said germs in dragon saliva infect the wound and help finish the prey.

The authors weighed the evidence for that septic bite idea, looking at both its history and its ecology. Testing a famous claim matters because newer work pointed to venom instead. Their review helps settle what really makes a dragon bite so deadly. It is also a case study in how striking animal stories should be checked.
plos-pone-0011197:
Hsieh reported a land walking fish in PLOS ONE in 2010. One marine fish can move onto land, a rare feat for a fully water based species. The author studied the new movement pattern, involving fins and body, that makes that water to land shift possible.

A single locomotor innovation opened a whole new habitat to this fish. That mirrors, in miniature, the great move of early vertebrates onto land. Watching a living fish manage the shift shows what mechanical problems had to be solved. The case gives evolution research a present day test bed for an ancient transition.
plos-pone-0011297:
Marozeau, Innes-Brown, Grayden and colleagues tested sight and sound together in PLOS ONE in 2010. Listeners must separate one melody from another, a task called stream segregation. The team asked whether visual cues help that separation, and whether musicians and non musicians benefit differently.

Watching did assist the ears in sorting sound streams in their tests. Cross sensory help like this reflects how the brain normally works in a multisensory world. Musicianship shaped the size of the effect, adding a training angle. The findings inform hearing science and may comfort music lovers with hearing loss who lean on sight.
plos-pone-0011397:
Dan Yan and colleagues reported in 2010 a way to make radiation kill tumors more effectively. Radiation breaks tumor DNA, but cancer cells survive by repairing the breaks quickly. Two repair proteins do much of that work, and the team used a small RNA molecule to lower both at once inside tumor cells.

With the repair proteins reduced, tumors became far more sensitive to radiation in their tests. The strategy turns the cancer's own defense into a liability, so lower radiation doses might do the work of higher ones. That matters because radiation harms healthy tissue too. If the approach holds up in further testing, patients could gain stronger tumor control with fewer side effects. The paper offers a clear, testable route toward kinder and stronger radiotherapy.
plos-pone-0011497:
Xinwen Liang and co-authors traced in 2010 how one repair gene produces many different protein forms in mammals. The gene makes MsrB1, an enzyme that repairs proteins damaged by oxidation. Its diversity comes from two tricks: intronization, in which new introns are born inside the gene, and later processing that trims the protein into varied final forms.

Together those tricks let a single gene supply a whole toolkit of related repair enzymes with different traits. Such variety shows how mammals expand their defenses without adding new genes. For protein science, the case is a lesson in economy: evolution edits the script and the staging, not just the cast. Understanding how the forms differ may matter for aging research, since repair of oxidized protein is one of the maintenance jobs that falter with age.
plos-pone-0011597:
Benedetta Leuner, Erica Glasper and Elizabeth Gould studied sex, stress and brain growth in rats for PLOS ONE in 2010. Stress usually harms the hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory and mood. Stress hormones rise, new neuron growth slows, and cell branches shrink, changes linked to anxiety and low mood.

Sexual experience also raises stress hormones at first, so the team expected harm. Instead, repeated mating boosted new neuron growth in the hippocampus once the early hormone spike passed. The result shows that not all stress-like states damage the brain, and that rewarding experience can leave the brain better supplied with fresh cells.
plos-pone-0011697:
Anita Palepu and co-authors followed injection drug users in Vancouver, Canada, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Unstable housing and homelessness are widespread in this group, and the two problems feed each other. The team asked whether entering addiction treatment was linked to gaining stable housing over time.

Using prospective cohort data, they examined the treatment-housing link while tracking participants forward. Their findings bear on whether recovery programmes should treat housing as a core outcome rather than a side issue. For services, the evidence supports joining addiction care with housing support instead of tackling either alone.
plos-pone-0011797:
Roopa Nalam, Claudia Andreu-Vieyra and Martin Matzuk studied support cells of sperm production in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sertoli cells nurse developing sperm and are governed by several nuclear factors, including the retinoblastoma tumour suppressor protein. The authors hypothesised this protein mediates tumour formation in mice lacking inhibin alpha, a known Sertoli regulator.

Removing both inhibin alpha and the retinoblastoma protein led to early Sertoli cell dysfunction. The double loss reveals a partnership behind healthy sperm care. It also helps explain how Sertoli tumours arise when these guardians fail together.
plos-pone-0011897:
Luis López and co-workers tested in 2010 how best to treat skin cells that cannot make enough coenzyme Q10. This compound carries electrons in the cell's energy system and also acts as an antioxidant. Cells lacking it, taken from patients, offer a test bed for supplements such as ubiquinone, related CoQ compounds, and vitamin C.

The treatments did not all act alike: effects depended on which compound was used and how long the cells were exposed. Some analogs helped energy production while others diverged, a caution against treating all CoQ products as interchangeable. For patients whose illness rests on CoQ10 shortage, those time and compound details shape what a sensible supplement plan looks like.
plos-pone-0011997:
Ellouise Leadbeater and co-workers studied in 2010 paper wasps in which many helpers raise young that are not their relatives. In the wasp Polistes dominulus, nearly a third of co-foundresses are unrelated to the dominant female whose offspring they help rear. Helpers usually gain through family ties, so unrelated help is a puzzle.

The study asks whether helping is tailored toward direct fitness: gains the helper itself can bank, such as inheriting the nest. If unrelated helpers profit directly, their behavior is less altruistic than it looks. The wasps thus test a general rule of social evolution, that apparent selflessness usually hides a payoff somewhere.
plos-pone-0012097:
Yousef Jamali, Mohammad Azimi, and Mohammad Mofrad built a computer model of living cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. Real cells are soft, springy, and full of inner parts, and how they respond to push and pull helps them form tissues with the right shapes. Testing those responses in the lab is hard, so a good model lets researchers ask questions they cannot easily test on real cells.

Their model treats the cell as a soft material with inner structure, then watches how a whole group of cells behaves under force. It can show how single-cell stiffness adds up to the strength of a tissue sheet. Such models help explain how tissues hold their form, and how that form can fail in disease.
plos-pone-0012197:
Sara Alvarez, Javier Suela, Ana Valencia, and co-authors profiled chemical silencing marks in adult leukemia for PLOS ONE in 2010. In acute myeloid leukemia, cancer cells often shut genes off by coating them with methyl groups, a change that leaves the DNA letters untouched. Some patients also carry large chromosome rearrangements, and how the two kinds of change relate was not settled.

The team compared methylation patterns with each patient's chromosome status and outlook. If certain silencing patterns line up with certain rearrangements, they may refine prognosis beyond either test alone. They may also predict who benefits from drugs that strip methylation away, a therapy that helps only some patients today.
plos-pone-0012297:
Jinnuo Han, Perminder Sachdev, and Kuldip Sidhu combined two strategies to reprogram human body cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Turning an ordinary cell back toward a flexible, stem-like state had been achieved several ways, but usually by inserting foreign material, and usually in very few cells. Chemical and small-molecule treatments were already known to help the process along.

Their combined approach pairs an epigenetic treatment, one that loosens the chemical locks on genes, with a non-genetic method. Higher reprogramming rates without inserted genes would make patient-specific cells safer for therapy and easier to produce for research. Each gain in efficiency brings lab-grown replacement tissues a step closer to practical use.
plos-pone-0012397:
Peter Chen, Kristin Willner, Amy Butani and colleagues showed that rapid genome reading can spot engineered changes in the anthrax bacterium, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The 2001 anthrax letter attacks proved the need to identify biothreat germs fast and to tell apart strains that look nearly identical. Slow lab methods leave investigators guessing during an outbreak.

Using 454 pyrosequencing, the team drafted whole genomes quickly and picked out genetic modifications. Fast drafts let analysts spot insertions and swaps that mark a lab-made strain. The approach strengthens biodefense and outbreak tracing, where hours matter and a missed change can mislead the whole response.
plos-pone-0012497:
Vishal Patel, Gurkan Bebek, John Mariadason and colleagues predicted and tested gene networks behind intestinal cancer, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Colorectal cancer grows through stacked mutations, and a few driver genes give cells their growth edge. Most drivers are known, but the networks they disturb are not, and those networks decide how a tumor behaves.

The team used computation to predict which network links the drivers rewire, then tested the predictions in cells. Confirmed links become candidate drug targets that single-gene thinking misses. The predict-then-test loop is a practical template for turning cancer genome lists into treatment ideas.
plos-pone-0012597:
Lee and colleagues used computer models to study a bacterial protein called Obg, found in Bacillus subtilis. Obg belongs to a family of proteins that bind GTP, a small energy-carrying molecule. The protein has two parts that stay much the same across species, one that grips GTP and one rich in the amino acid glycine.

Their 2010 modelling study maps how Obg meets the nucleotides it binds, atom by atom in a virtual model. Knowing the shape of that grip helps explain what Obg does inside the cell. It also gives other researchers a base for tests on this whole protein family.
plos-pone-0012697:
Larsen, Lelic, Parsons and co-authors used a computer method to predict which virus pieces killer T cells can see. West Nile virus is a growing public health threat, and vaccines need targets the immune system recognises. Their 2010 study applied reverse immunology, scanning the virus's full protein with the NetCTL prediction tool.

The scan listed likely CD8 T cell epitopes, the short pieces shown to killer cells. Shortlists like this cut years of lab testing down to the best candidates. The same approach speeds vaccine work on many viruses.  Predicted pieces were ranked for follow-up laboratory testing.
plos-pone-0328697:
Neha Kardam and Denise Wilson compared computer methods that sort short student comments into themes. Universities collect thousands of brief feedback answers, and reading them all by hand is impractical. Their 2026 study used engineering students' expectations about support from teachers, assistants, and peers, gathered over several years.

Five topic models, from classic statistical methods to a modern language-model approach, were run on the same cleaned comments. The team judged them by theme coherence and by checks beyond machine scores, addressing a gap in earlier comparisons. Their aim is practical guidance: which method to use, when, and with what caution. Done well, such sorting can steer teaching support toward what students actually ask for.
plos-pone-0329197:
Judging diabetes care quality from the patient's seat requires a questionnaire that makes sense in local language and culture. Yohannes Mulu Ferede and colleagues translated a widely used chronic care survey into Ethiopian use and checked it carefully, in this 2026 PLOS One study at referral hospitals in the Amhara region.

Patients with type 2 diabetes answered the twenty-six questions, which cover five habits of good chronic care, in face-to-face interviews during spring 2025. Experts rated each question's relevance, and statistical checks tested whether answers grouped as expected and stayed consistent. The adapted tool gives Ethiopian clinics a validated way to hear how coordinated and supportive their diabetes care feels.
plos-pone-0341397:
Taoqing Liu and Yaqin Ren survey more than eight hundred physical education undergraduates in Guangdong, China, about how satisfied they are with the courses meant to make them teachers. Their framework ties six features of course design to three basic student needs drawn from a well-known motivation theory. The survey compared two related majors and probed which course gains best predict overall satisfaction.

Overall satisfaction sat at a moderate level. Teaching-focused majors rated course goals, knowledge gains, and skill building higher than sports-training majors, who were also far less keen to teach after graduating. Knowledge and skill gains correlated most strongly with satisfaction. Liu and Ren argue that programs should rebuild courses around what students feel they truly gain, especially for majors drifting away from teaching.
plos-pone-0341997:
Gambin and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 to validate a driving-based sleepiness test. Daytime sleepiness causes many road crashes, yet the standard lab test watches people lie still, which poorly matches driving. Their simulator version judges wakefulness during a driving task instead.

Fifty-four people will take both tests in random order: patients with sleep apnea after stopping or continuing their night therapy for a week, plus healthy controls. Stopping therapy briefly brings back sleepiness in a controlled way. If the simulator test matches the standard while feeling more like real driving, licensing decisions could rest on fairer evidence.
plos-pone-0344697:
Kabiru Ahmed and colleagues propose a fresh maths method for solving sets of linked equations that must stay inside a set of allowed values. Such problems show up in engineering and science models. Their method updates a good guess step by step, restarts when stuck, and tunes two dials by a rule that keeps the update well behaved.

Proofs show the method reaches a solution from any start, and do so without a strict smoothness demand that older proofs needed. That weaker demand widens the problems the proof covers. Tests against known methods on sample problems ran well. For users, the gain is a solver that is steadier on hard, constrained equation sets.
plos-pone-0346097:
Sabrina Hepner and co-workers compare the scattered side genomes, called plasmids, of the bacteria that cause Lyme disease. These bacteria carry many loose DNA circles and lines besides their main chromosome, and the mix varies wildly. Their 2026 study assembles eighty-six genomes across most known species in the group, thirty of them newly read, and counts and sorts every plasmid.

Each strain carried anywhere from a handful to more than twenty plasmids. Only two plasmids appeared in every strain. Species tied to rodents carried more plasmids than those tied to birds. Swapping and reshuffling looked constant, including for the system the bacteria use to dodge immunity. The loose genome may help these bacteria adapt to many hosts.
plos-pone-0346497:
Ethan Shaw, Suraj Chandramouli, and Michael Dzakovich present a kit of hydroponics parts that anyone can make on a home 3D printer, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Hydroponics grows plants in water instead of soil and gives tight control over growing conditions, but ready-made systems can be costly and hard to adapt.

The printed pieces snap together into a vertical tower with one or two columns and adjustable height, so the setup fits a classroom, greenhouse, or growth chamber. As a check, the team grew spinach under different salt levels and got results matching a standard deep-water system. They pitch the kit as a cheap, flexible option for research and teaching.
plos-pone-0347697:
Anna Khoperia and colleagues review seven years of liver cancer in Georgia, the Caucasus country that launched a national hepatitis C elimination program in 2015, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis C is a leading cause of hepatocellular carcinoma, so the team linked cancer, death, and treatment registries for cases diagnosed through 2022.

More than seventeen hundred cases appeared, mostly men around their early sixties, and two-thirds arrived at late stages; most patients had died by the end of follow-up. Screening of cancer patients for hepatitis C rose from rare to nearly universal, and over half of those tested carried the virus. The data show both the program's reach and how much cancer burden remains.
plos-pone-0347997:
Naomi Assame, Susan Greenhalgh, John Tingle, and Gillian Yeowell reviewed the laws and policies meant to help England's National Health Service respond when patients are harmed by their treatment. Searching medical and legal databases and grey sources from 2000 to 2025, the 2026 scoping review charted one hundred twenty-one records and synthesised them thematically, the first exercise of its kind.

The review found statute, policy, and stated NHS values pulling in different directions yet depending on each other. Most strikingly, workplace culture seemed to outweigh written rules in deciding how providers actually respond to harm. The authors call for research on how law and policy might shape that culture for the better.
plos-pone-0348097:
Béatrice Parguel, Marine Agogué, and Julie Gauneau ran two laboratory experiments on a double-edged question: what happens when women researchers appear more often in science media? Women remain undercovered relative to men. Their 2026 experiments showed members of the public and graduate students a simulated science newsletter with varied gender balance, then measured beliefs about ability, expertise, and academic careers.

Seeing more women researchers narrowed the gap between men's and women's confidence in their own ability in both groups. The public also rated women researchers as more expert, though graduate students did not shift on that point. Unexpectedly, male graduate students found academic careers less attractive when visibility rose. The authors draw lessons for universities and media about handling representation with care.
plos-pone-0348197:
Changning Ren and co-authors surveyed social media users in 2026 about when health posts by bloggers get adopted as guidance. Bloggers now shape health behaviour strongly, and the trust mechanics behind that influence needed a model.

More than twelve hundred people answered a structured survey. Perceived blogger competence changed how information quality and credibility flowed through usefulness into adoption. In short, competent seeming bloggers make good information land harder, and weak seeming ones waste it. The model helps health agencies choose partners for campaigns: expertise must be visible, not merely real, to move public behaviour.
plos-pone-0348497:
Antonio Pérez-Torres and co-authors present a method for spotting gearbox damage early, before a failing gear stops an industrial line. Their system listens to vibration signals, chops them into short windows, and sums up each window with measures from both the raw signal and its frequency pattern. A statistical method then compresses those measures and watches for drift away from healthy behaviour.

Tested on recorded data spanning different loads, speeds, and levels of wear, the method proved sensitive to slow, progressive damage and flagged faults while they were still in early stages. Two control statistics did the judging, separating normal running from failure conditions cleanly. The authors offer the approach as a practical tool for planned maintenance in plants where a breakdown is especially costly.
plos-pone-0348597:
Jong-Hyun Kim presents a fast way to simulate balloons on a computer, complete with inflation, deflation, and the spin a real balloon gives when air rushes in or out. Full fluid simulation is far too heavy for games or virtual reality. His method instead pushes the balloon's surface points around under simple constraints, adds reaction forces borrowed from airflow physics, and weights those forces by distance travelled along the surface.

Rotation is handled in one whole-body step rather than vertex by vertex, keeping the maths cheap. Tests on meshes of many shapes and weight distributions ran in real time even at high detail, while still showing recognisable balloon behaviours such as bulging and twisting recoil. Kim targets interactive uses, from games to virtual product demos, where plausible motion matters more than laboratory accuracy.
plos-pone-0348697:
Nima Kianfar and co-authors reviewed sixty-one studies on how ordinary people help track and control diseases spread by mosquitoes. Official surveillance is costly and patchy, while phone apps and backyard reporting can widen coverage cheaply. The team searched five major databases across a quarter century and catalogued how each project recruited helpers, checked their data, and used the results.

Most studies appeared after twenty seventeen and clustered in Europe and the Americas, with very few in Asia. Malaria drew the most attention, then dengue, and most projects ran in cities. The authors find citizen science a genuine complement to official systems, while warning that bias in who reports, and uneven data checking, still limit how far the results can be trusted.
plos-pone-0348797:
Satoru Iwata, Yumi Miura, and Takashi Iwamoto show a virus-free way to rearrange chromosomes inside a living mouse tissue. Big DNA swaps help scientists study how the genome is built and repaired, but virus delivery is slow and needs special labs. Their 2026 study uses electric pulses to push gene-editing tools into the lining of the mouse uterus.

The pulses produced the intended swaps between chromosomes at several sites. A very large flipped segment was also repaired with the help of a small donor template. Deep sequencing confirmed the new joins letter by letter, though changed cells were few, as expected. The shortcut gives labs a quicker, cleaner stage for studying DNA repair in the body.
plos-pone-0349097:
Isabel T Held and colleagues piloted a tiny implanted port that lets researchers drip medicine into a mouse's middle ear again and again without repeated surgery. The device answers a practical problem in hearing research: drugs meant to rescue faulty proteins in genetic deafness must reach the inner ear regularly. The human route under study runs through the middle ear. They adapted a button implant already used for blood vessel access.

Mice carrying a mutation that mimics a human deafness syndrome, and normal littermates, received the implant on one side only. Over four weeks the animals behaved and balanced normally, saline injections through the port ran smoothly for two weeks, and hearing was not significantly harmed. The authors call the approach feasible and offer it as a stand-in for testing ear tube delivery in people.
plos-pone-0349197:
Lewis D Taylor and colleagues fed Atlantic salmon extra vitamin D for six months and then read which genes switched on or off in the fish's skin. Skin is a salmon's first shield against the germs that plague fish farms, and vitamin D is known to shape immunity in other animals. So the team asked whether diet could tune that shield.

About one hundred and fifty genes changed with the diet, and a good share of them govern inflammation and the ways skin cells flag invaders to the immune system. The pattern pointed to calmer inflammation alongside stronger early defences. The authors suggest that getting vitamin D levels right in feed could help farmed salmon resist skin disease, a costly problem for the industry and for fish welfare.
plos-pone-0349297:
Yinghong Li and colleagues charted head and neck cancers across five East Asian countries from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-three, using the latest global burden estimates. They covered China, Japan, both Koreas, and Mongolia, tracking new cases, deaths, and lost healthy years, then projected trends forward to twenty thirty-eight. Smoking was examined as the leading suspected driver.

The five countries split sharply. China and Mongolia improved on both new cases and deaths, South Korea held cases steady while deaths dropped, but Japan and North Korea worsened on both measures. Patients everywhere skewed older over time, and smoking stayed the dominant risk factor. Forecasts see Japan and North Korea still rising. The authors argue that tobacco control remains the region's biggest lever against these cancers.
plos-pone-0349397:
Yi Wang and colleagues reviewed scans from two hundred and forty-five men whose prostate cancer blood marker rose again after surgery, a sign the cancer may be back. All received a modern tracer scan that lights up prostate cancer cells wherever they hide. The team recorded how often the scan found disease at each blood marker level and where the spots appeared.

The scan found at least one lesion in three quarters of the men. Detection climbed from just over half at the lowest marker levels to about nine in ten at the highest. Verified cases showed a pelvis-first pattern, with most disease in the surgical bed or nearby lymph nodes. Blood marker level, tumour grade, and how fast the marker doubled predicted a positive scan. The authors offer benchmarks to guide targeted salvage treatment.
plos-pone-0349597:
Huiping Lai and colleagues tested an added breathing routine for older adults with stable long term lung disease. Fifty one patients were split by chance. Both groups did whole body breathing exercise daily for three months. Half also added a cycle technique that loosens mucus through controlled breaths, huffs, and coughs, for thirty minutes a day.

Added training lifted one key lung flow measure, stretched six minute walk distance by about twenty metres beyond controls, and lowered breathlessness and overall symptom scores. Life quality marks also favoured the added routine. A cheap, drug free breathing cycle, practised daily, can give older lung patients a real functional gain.
plos-pone-0349697:
Hassan A Aljaberi, Saeed Rahmani, and Humam H Alrikabi reviewed records of more than two thousand Iraqi children to map how eyesight errors align with crossed or wandering eyes. Their 2026 study covered three specialist children's eye centers, comparing just over a thousand children with horizontal eye misalignment against a larger group without it, all measured with drops that relax focusing.

Inward-turning eyes came with strong farsightedness in most cases and appeared at younger ages. Outward-turning eyes leaned the other way, toward nearsightedness and astigmatism. Statistical modeling confirmed moderate to high farsightedness as a powerful predictor of the inward type, and nearsightedness with astigmatism of the outward type. The authors support early focusing checks for any child suspected of misalignment, since glasses alone can change the course.
plos-pone-0349797:
Chunyan Wang and colleagues ran large laboratory tests on strengthening sand with bacteria that deposit calcium carbonate, a natural cement. The open question was how the shape of the grouting pipe changes the treatment. They compared a standard straight pipe with a new spiral design across several injection setups in big sand columns.

Pipe design strongly shaped how far the cement spread and how even it was. A single injection pipe with one extraction point strengthened only a narrow zone around it. Setups with three injection points, and the spiral pipe, treated a much wider radius. For engineers, the message is that delivery hardware matters as much as the bacteria themselves.
plos-pone-0350097:
Xudong Gao, Jiying Shang, and Yu Song test a way of strengthening ageing concrete frames with tensioned cables, in this 2026 PLOS ONE engineering study. Buildings lose load-bearing strength over decades, creating safety risks. External cables can push back against sagging, but most research strengthens only the beams. This team reinforced beams and columns together and loaded a single frame until it yielded.

As the cables' sag increased, the frame's weakest zone moved away from the beam ends toward the joints, and peak strain fell sharply — by roughly seventy percent in their best case. Carrying capacity and yield load both rose with cable sag and more stirrup steel. Fuller reinforcement, they argue, buys old frames a safer second life.
plos-pone-0350197:
Adam Sundh and colleagues checked whether a one-leg hamstring strength test gives the same numbers when athletes repeat it on different days. Thirty college male athletes performed maximal pushes in a long-lever bridge position, heels on force plates, across three sessions. The team measured peak force and how fast force rose in the first fractions of a second.

Peak force proved steady between sessions, and early force measures were moderately to well consistent, though noisier. Small differences between sessions were mostly trivial. Coaches use such tests to track hamstring recovery and injury risk, so knowing the measurement error matters. A change bigger than that error band is likely real progress, not test wobble.
plos-pone-0350297:
Setor K Sorkpor and colleagues surveyed one hundred and seventy adults living with HIV in Ghanas Volta Region about shame, mood, food access, and views on daily HIV drugs. Strong drugs work only when taken steadily, yet inner shame can sour beliefs about treatment. Models tested whether low mood carries that effect, and whether hunger changes its strength.

Inner shame linked with more negative beliefs and attitudes toward the drugs. Low mood carried a clear share of that link. Hunger sharpened the path from shame to low mood, so indirect harm ran stronger where food was scarce. Care that treats mood and food need together, the authors argue, may protect drug adherence better than pills alone.
plos-pone-0350397:
Tessone and colleagues piloted a new tear-film camera at a specialist eye center in a 2026 study. Dry eye is common, yet its signs and symptoms often disagree. The camera measures the oily top layer and the watery layer beneath it at extremely fine detail, in adults with and without dry eye signs.

Eyes with clinical signs of dry eye had a clearly thinner oily layer than eyes without signs. Symptom scores from a standard questionnaire were gathered for comparison as well. A thin oily layer lets tears evaporate faster, so measuring it directly could sharpen diagnosis. The small pilot supports larger studies of camera-guided dry eye care.
plos-pone-0350497:
Stephanie Colwell, Prabhakar Chalise, Byron Gajewski, Isuru Ratnayake, and Dinesh Mudaranthakam published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It models count time series data that depend on place, such as case counts recorded across regions over time. The models used are COM-Poisson INGARCH models, statistical tools built for counts that bunch or spread unusually.

Spatially dependent counts appear in disease surveillance and crime statistics, where one area's numbers sway its neighbors'. A model that respects that dependence gives truer forecasts and alarms. Biostatisticians and public health analysts tracking outbreaks across counties are the readers for this modeling work.
plos-pone-0350697:
Joseph Shearer and colleagues checked whether heart failure risk scores built from blood proteins travel well between different kinds of studies. Three published scores, each built in a different setting, one community cohort, one trial, and one registry, were all tested in the same community group. Each score sums many proteins measured on the same platform into one number meant to forecast death.

All three scores predicted death over five years, and each held up after accounting for standard clinical measures. The scores overlapped only moderately, yet they agreed on a small set of proteins, with renin in all three. Calibration, whether predicted risk matched real outcomes, was strong. The practical message is reassuring: a protein score built in one population is not trapped there, and protein panels add information doctors can use beyond the usual chart.
plos-pone-0350897:
Rafaela de Almeida and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One clinical trial comparing a laser treatment against daily eye drops for glaucoma and high eye pressure. Thirty patients took part, and in each person one eye received the Pascal-pattern laser treatment while the other eye used travoprost drops, after a washout period. Pressure in both eyes was tracked for a year, including peak pressure during a water-drinking test.

For most of the year the two approaches lowered pressure by similar amounts, and by twelve months the laser-treated eyes averaged slightly lower pressure than the drop-treated eyes. Vision tests showed no meaningful difference or progression in either group. The authors say the laser matched a standard daily drop, which matters for patients who struggle with lifelong medication routines.
plos-pone-0351497:
Paula Hage Boutros and colleagues followed more than six hundred pregnant women across Lebanon to learn what shapes a babys birth weight. A Mediterranean style diet has been tied to healthier births, yet its role for babies born small or large for their stage was unclear. Diet, weight gain, blood pressure, mood, and background factors were tracked across pregnancy.

Babies of mothers who followed the local Mediterranean pattern most often landed in the healthy middle weight band. Single foods mattered in finer cuts: dairy linked with lower middle weights, dried fruit with higher ones. Steady weight gain guarded against small babies, while higher blood pressure raised small baby risk. Large babies tied to prior large births, more past births, and poor late sleep.
plos-pone-0351697:
Ahmed Tarfy leads a team of eight publishing the protocol for a first in human trial of a personalized cell therapy in advanced colorectal cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The treatment harvests T cells from the lymph nodes that drain a patient's tumor. Those nodes have already met the cancer. Their cells can be trained in the laboratory against the patient's own tumor mutations. Sequencing and prediction software select the targets. The trained cells return as a living drug.

The trial unfolds in three parts: collecting nodes and manufacturing the cells, a single infusion after immune conditioning chemotherapy, and follow up stretching to five years. Up to sixteen patients with stage four disease can join. Being a protocol, the paper promises no results; its value is transparency about how a bespoke therapy is built and judged. Safety at this stage outranks cure, and the staged design reflects that caution.
plos-pone-0352197:
Nathan Yu and colleagues tested twelve machine learning tools on a question about young drinkers. How early can a drinking pattern forecast the drinker someone becomes? The subjects were adolescent mice, and the drinking records were simulated from published mouse work. Long real records are scarce, so simulation filled the gap. The team fed each tool the record cut at growing lengths. That mimics a researcher deciding when a forecast can be trusted.

Six tools classified the final drinking paths with outstanding accuracy. They were near perfect by the end of the record and already strong at its midpoint. Four more tools did acceptably, and two lagged behind. The ranking gives addiction researchers a practical shortlist. It also shows how much observation an early, reliable signal costs.
plos-pone-0352397:
Al-Tameemi and colleagues set out a trial plan in 2026 on a fruit fiber supplement for fatty liver disease. The disease, tied to body metabolism, is now the leading cause of long-term liver trouble worldwide. Thirty adults in Nottingham will take either the fiber, called pectin, or a dummy supplement for six weeks, with neither side knowing which.

Blood, stool, and body measures will be taken before and after to track inflammation, gut microbes, and metabolic health. Gut changes are a prime suspect in how fiber might calm the liver. A small careful trial like this tests both benefit and practicality before a larger study is funded.
plos-pone-0352897:
Johanna Stähler and five colleagues test a hopeful idea — that training makes effort itself feel more valuable — and find it wanting, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Sixty-two young adults were assigned to eight weeks of high-intensity jump training or a control condition. Before and after, they pedalled a laboratory bike, sometimes at set intensities and sometimes choosing their own, while rating how effort felt and wearing brain scanners.

Nothing moved: not self-reported effort value, not willingness to work harder, not the brain signals. Statistical analysis favoured the null result rather than merely failing to find an effect. The value of effort, the authors suggest, may be a stubborn trait that a single training block cannot rewrite.
plos-pone-0352997:
Lin Ruan and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One laboratory study of a new weapon against drug-resistant urinary tract infections. The bacteria behind most such infections increasingly shrug off first-line antibiotics. The team tested a membrane-attacking compound called COE-D8 against ninety-three clinical samples of uropathogenic E. coli, most of which resisted standard drugs at high doses.

Nearly all the samples stayed sensitive to the new compound, which killed bacteria several times faster than standard antibiotics by tearing their membranes. Because the compound alone can harm host cells, the team paired it with the antibiotic fosfomycin, which lowered the needed dose and doubled survival in a mouse safety model. Bacteria also struggled to evolve resistance, supporting the pair as a candidate for stubborn infections.
plos-pone-0353197:
Goldschmidt and colleagues, in a 2026 study, grow three cell lines from a benign but stubborn jaw tumor of dogs, called canine acanthomatous ameloblastoma. Living cell lines let researchers test treatments in dishes before animals. The lines were grown from naturally occurring tumors, confirmed as dog and as surface-type cells, and read at DNA and RNA level.

The lines kept their parent tumors' mutations, including a change in a growth gene found in every sample, and shared a set of other mutations in most lines. Their gene activity matched the known fingerprint of this tumor from earlier studies and clustered far from healthy gum tissue. Growth programs linked to invasion and several signaling pathways stayed switched on in the dish. The authors say careful profiling, including where lines drift from their tumors, is what makes them trustworthy stand-ins for pre-clinical testing.
plos-pone-0353397:
Wohnrade and colleagues tested sound-wave scanning as a marker of nerve disease in mice in a 2026 study. The disease studied slowly kills the nerve cells that move muscles, and trials lack easy ways to track its course. Mice bred to develop a similar illness had their leg nerves and muscles scanned over time.

Scans picked up nerve shrinkage and muscle wasting at the same time as, or earlier than, standard nerve tests and movement checks. Scan changes also matched tissue damage seen under the microscope. A painless scan that tracks disease this closely could help test new drugs in animals first, and it may later guide similar tracking in people.
plos-pone-0353697:
Daniel Sanin-Villa and four colleagues write the day-ahead timetable for a small local power grid, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Their microgrid mixes wind turbines with batteries, and the challenge is deciding each hour what to generate, store, or draw, while wasting as little energy and emitting as little carbon as possible. Batteries do the balancing: soaking up surplus wind, covering calm spells, and steadying voltage.

Their genetic-algorithm scheduler was tested against two established optimisation methods under identical conditions, on two standard test networks of different sizes, in both connected and islanded modes. Careful scheduling matters because every wasted kilowatt in a microgrid is a larger share of the whole than in a national system.
plos-pone-0353797:
David Bellini and co-authors report a 2026 study of how men feel about heat therapy before and after trying it. Heat therapy here means sitting in hot water, a habit linked in past research to lower heart disease risk. Twenty young, active men took a one-hour soak in warm water and answered custom surveys just before and just after the session.

Most men expected the soak to feel easy and calming, and many still found it pleasant, yet half said it was harder and less fun than they had guessed. Given a free choice, they would have stayed in for about half the set time. Heat and time demands, the authors argue, may keep people from using a therapy that could help them.
plos-pone-0353997:
Yuanyuan Dai and colleagues built a faster way to measure how pear flesh bends and flows under pressure. Such measurements matter for sorting, packing, and shipping fruit without bruising it. Their 2026 study combined squash tests on Huangguan pears with computer models of the tissue and a machine learning system.

The learning system acted as a stand-in for slow physics simulations, reading spatial patterns and sequences in the test data. A tuned genetic search then picked the tissue values that best matched real squash tests. Errors stayed very small compared with the lab measurements. Dai and colleagues say the approach cuts the need for destructive testing and can guide gentler fruit handling equipment.
