plos-pone-0354097:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 review and data study, search blood gene data for markers tied to how proteins are tagged and edited after they are built. Such edits, called posttranslational modifications, help control protein behavior, and their failure is suspected in Parkinson's disease. The team hoped to find a few genes that flag the disease or suggest treatment targets.

Starting from hundreds of genes that differed between patients and healthy people, the team kept only those tied to protein editing, then let machine learning rank them. Three genes passed checks for diagnostic value and were all turned down in patients. Further analysis linked the gene set to immune signaling, and patients showed fewer of several active immune cell types. The team also mapped the genes and screened compounds that might act on them. They present the three genes as candidate blood markers, pending wet-lab proof.
plos-pone-0354297:
Kazi Afaq Ahmed and three colleagues published this 2026 study of investment risk in Pakistan, built around the Altman Z-score, a long-used formula that flags firms heading toward distress. They combined company traits, economic conditions, and political stability into an investment risk index and tested what drives it.

Firm traits, the wider economy, and politics all moved risk significantly, and larger firms surprisingly carried more of it. Fixed asset buildup and tax expenses also mattered. Ahmed offers the index as a structured diagnostic for investors, with lessons that may travel to other developing economies.
plos-pone-0354497:
Tope Olubodun and co-authors reviewed published cases of stomach paralysis linked to a popular class of diabetes and weight-loss drugs. These medicines, called GLP-1 receptor agonists, commonly slow the gut, but full gastroparesis is less recognised. Their 2026 systematic review searched four databases for real-world reports through late 2025.

Only twelve reports covering thirteen patients met the review's rules. Most patients were women with type 2 diabetes, though some had no diabetes. Semaglutide appeared most often, and symptoms began anywhere from hours to months after starting, often after a dose rise or careless restart. The authors urge clinicians to watch for the condition and to record cases carefully, since evidence remains thin.
plos-pone-0354597:
Kanoksing and colleagues, in a 2026 study, look for gene variants that shape the pattern of asthma in adults. One form of asthma is driven by a set of immune signals that raise certain white blood cells and narrow the airways over time. The team genotyped one hundred twenty-five patients and measured their lung function, blood cells, and immune signals.

Two variants stood out. One in the IL5 gene tracked strongly with high levels of eosinophils, a white cell type tied to allergic inflammation, and with weaker lung function. Each extra copy of the risk letter added to the effect. A variant in the IL13 gene tracked with more of the helper cells that drive this inflammation and with a higher risk of fixed airflow blockage. Other variants showed smaller links. The authors suggest gene tests could one day help sort asthma patients for targeted treatments.
plos-pone-0354797:
Michael Meece and four colleagues test light therapy on injured fruit fly eyes in this 2026 study, carefully varying the dose. Shining near-infrared light on tissue, called photobiomodulation, is proposed to aid healing, but studies use such different settings that results rarely compare. The team damaged fly retinas with light, then treated the flies twice daily for ten days at two wavelengths and four total doses.

One wavelength clearly helped: at 850 nanometers, photoreceptor function recovered better, and stronger doses worked better still. The other wavelength, 950 nanometers, produced no real recovery at any dose, apart from a hint of benefit at one middle dose. Energy molecule levels rose under some treatments but did not line up neatly with recovery, suggesting several processes are at play. The authors say wavelength choice matters as much as dose.
plos-pone-0354897:
Karar Zunaid Ahsan and four colleagues published this 2026 study of fairness in mothers' health care in Bangladesh. They linked national surveys of mothers and health facilities across 2001, 2010, and 2016. They asked whether gaps between poor and non-poor women in pregnancy care, facility births, and complication treatment closed faster where clinics were better prepared.

Overall use rose, yet poor and non-poor gaps persisted and sometimes widened, especially for giving birth in facilities. Ahsan concludes that upgrading clinics alone does not deliver fairness, and policy must target the women still left behind.
plos-pone-0354997:
Subina Bajracharya, Sadikshya Neupane, and Parita Shrestha published this 2026 community study of a simpler way to spot overweight children in Bharatpur, Nepal. Body mass index needs proper scales, height boards, and trained staff, which large school screenings often lack. The team measured three hundred children aged six to eleven, comparing neck size with standard body measures.

Neck circumference tracked the established measures closely and identified overweight children with useful accuracy, and the authors derived cutoff values for local use. Bajracharya presents the tape-around-the-neck check as cheap, quick screening for schools with few resources.
plos-pone-0355197:
Satoshi Kondo and colleagues surveyed 630 Japanese citizens about a proposed answer to doctor shortages: letting hospital paramedics take on more medical tasks. Their 2026 study measured the public's general trust in hospital paramedics and their acceptance of specific procedures, then repeated the questions after a short educational briefing about the paramedics' role.

Trust and acceptance started high and stayed high. The briefing nudged acceptance of paramedic procedures up slightly but did not move general trust, which the authors suspect already rests on confidence in ordinary ambulance paramedics. For policymakers, the results suggest the public is not the obstacle to task shifting; building credible certification and training systems is the work that remains.
plos-pone-0355297:
Pingping Xie, Jinfa Gu, and Jie Huang pool in 2026 trials of neuromuscular training for young male tennis players, covering power, speed, and skill drills. Earlier reviews mixed groups and lumped outcomes together, blurring what helps. Their search kept controlled trials of healthy male players and split outcomes such as stroke speed, serve accuracy, sprint, jump, and agility.

Training favoured stroke speed, short sprint, jump height, agility, and serve accuracy in pooled results, but not placement accuracy. Certainty was low or very low for every outcome. No single drill type is proven, the authors warn, and better trials with longer follow up are needed.
plos-pone-0355397:
Isaac Faustino and co-authors checked whether children in state protective custody face more forceful interventions in emergency departments. They studied thousands of behavioural health visits by children between 2021 and 2023. Their 2026 analysis compared children in protective custody, children with a new report filed, and children with no involvement.

Children in custody received sedating injections and physical restraints more often than the other groups. By three days into the visit window, about one in six had received an injection, well above the other groups. Adjusted models confirmed a higher risk rate for custody children. Faustino and colleagues argue the gap demands scrutiny of how departments care for the most vulnerable children in crisis.
plos-pone-0355497:
Mirinae Kim and Young-Hoon Park ask in 2026 whether bleeding inside the eye in advanced diabetic eye disease follows the seasons. They reviewed several thousand affected eyes seen at a Seoul hospital over three years and compared monthly bleeding rates with weather records. Pressure inside the eye before and at bleeding was also checked.

Bleeding peaked in late spring and early summer. Temperature, humidity, and rain did not explain the pattern in their models. Eye pressure at bleeding differed from pressure at the prior cold season visit, hinting that pressure shifts or seasonal blood sugar changes may play a part. More study is needed, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355597:
Baoguo Luo and co-authors built a machine learning shortcut for judging whether bridges can safely carry permitted overweight vehicles amid normal traffic. Such vehicles need official authorisation, and full engineering simulation of every crossing is far too slow. Their 2026 framework learns from a detailed grillage model of bridge behaviour under mixed traffic.

The model predicts how much the heavy vehicle amplifies load effects compared with ordinary traffic alone. Training data came from systematic runs of the high-fidelity simulation, which captures how loads spread across the deck. The learned surrogate then answers in a fraction of the time. Luo and colleagues aim the tool at permit offices facing rising volumes of exceptional loads.
plos-pone-0355697:
Tomoki Sakaguchi and three colleagues compare the spores of four fission yeast species under the microscope, in this 2026 study. Fission yeasts are workhorse organisms for cell biology, and the best-known species makes spores with a distinctive bumpy coat tied to toughness. Whether its relatives share that design was unknown. The team imaged spores from all four species with light and electron microscopy, then stress-tested them.

Surface structures differed sharply between species. The fibrous coat and the dense outer layer seen in the famous species were largely missing from the other three. Its spores also survived heat and alcohol best. The authors conclude that each fission yeast evolved its own spore architecture, possibly tuned to its habitat, a reminder that even close relatives solve the survival problem differently.
plos-pone-0355997:
Shinhyun Kim and colleagues ran a computer-based hunt for new drug candidates that mimic risperidone, a medicine that blocks dopamine D2 receptors, but stay out of the brain. Their 2026 study starts from a quirk of such drugs: raising the hormone prolactin outside the brain may protect nerve cells, while brain exposure causes sedation and movement side effects.

Starting from four hundred look-alike molecules, the team filtered for ones predicted not to cross into the brain, then docked the survivors against the receptor in simulation. Eight beat risperidone's docking score, four kept the key contacts inside the receptor, and one stayed most stable in motion simulations. The shortlist now awaits real lab testing, which the authors stress has not yet happened.
plos-pone-0356197:
Yan Zhao and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE grading how well hospitals across China's thirty-one provinces turned resources into care between 2019 and 2023. They combined a three-stage efficiency model that strips out outside influences, a dynamic index tracking change over time, and a spatial statistic that tests whether efficient provinces cluster together.

Average efficiency sat below the ideal frontier, leaving real room for improvement, though the trend rose over the five years. Stripping out those advantages lowered scores, showing that good conditions had propped some provinces up, and the regional ranking reshuffled: the center briefly passed the east, while the west trailed throughout. Technical progress, not better management alone, was the main brake on output growth. Efficient provinces clustered stably below the Yangtze River, while low-efficiency clusters mostly dissolved by 2023, suggesting catch-up. The map is offered as guidance for national hospital reform.
plos-pone-0356497:
Kinza Shahid and colleagues produced the largest protein catalogue yet for Fasciola gigantica, a liver fluke of buffalo and cattle that also infects people. They worked from adult worms taken from naturally infected buffaloes in Punjab, Pakistan. Their 2026 proteomics study separated the fluke's proteins. It verified them by antibody blotting and identified them by mass spectrometry. The focus was the proteins the parasite secretes into its host.

Nearly five thousand proteins were catalogued, including a large set of predicted secreted ones. The functional profile leaned heavily on enzymes that cut, dissolve, and oxidize. That is the toolkit of a parasite that burrows through tissue and feeds on its host. A further slice tied to immune manipulation. Each such protein is a candidate target for drugs or vaccines against a costly livestock disease.
plos-pone-0356597:
Eric Pelzl and four colleagues study a well-known Mandarin sound change inside real conversation, in this 2026 experiment. When two low tones follow each other, the first traditionally rises, becoming indistinguishable from a genuine rising tone, a puzzle called third tone sandhi. Ten pairs of native speakers played a phrase-matching game. One read a phrase aloud and the other picked it from a screen, under conditions that did or did not trigger the change.

The setup produced real confusion exactly where the sound change predicted it. Pairs coped mainly by keeping the first low tone lower toward its end, effectively avoiding the full change and preserving the contrast. The authors say even a tightly structured game can reveal how speakers steer around ambiguity, a first step toward understanding how this rule behaves in everyday talk.
plos-pone-0356697:
Xingyue Pu and Zhigang Zhong track whether China's cancer hospital beds are shared fairly, using fifteen years of national statistics in this 2026 study. Oncology beds grew steadily from 2008 to 2022, though growth slowed. The authors measured fairness two ways, against population and against land area, using standard inequality tools that also separate disparities within regions from those between them.

Judged by population, bed allocation was quite equal and improved over the period. Judged by geography, it was severely unequal throughout, with no improvement, meaning patients in sparse regions face long journeys regardless of headcounts. Most inequality in both views came from within regions rather than between them. The authors argue policy should now chase geographic accessibility and local balance, to ease the notorious difficulty cancer patients face getting admitted.
plos-pone-0356797:
Chaoqun He and Racidon P Bernarte surveyed six hundred Chinese livestream shoppers. Half were young digital natives, and half were older adults. The survey asked what makes them buy again from a live commerce host. Their 2026 study modeled three facets of service quality. They were the host's professionalism, the interactive experience, and after-sales support. Trust served as the middleman. Generation was the dial that turns each effect.

All three facets built trust, and trust fed intentions to return. But the generations weighted them differently. Older shoppers leaned hardest on professionalism and after-sales care. The young prized interactivity. The authors advise platforms to segment their playbook. They suggest certifying hosts for older audiences. For the young, they suggest investing in interactive features, even augmented reality try-ons.
plos-pone-0356997:
Kathleen O'Connor and coauthors published a 2026 genomics study in PLOS ONE on a quiet kind of variation in Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium behind many skin and hospital infections. Genes can spell the same protein with different codons, and bacteria prefer some spellings, affecting how much protein gets made. The team measured codon bias across thousands of genes in a reference strain and compared it with all public complete genomes of the species, sorted by disease, institution, and site.

Bias varied gene by gene and isolate by isolate. Ribosome machinery genes showed the strongest, most consistent bias everywhere, suggesting heavy pressure to keep them highly expressed. One hospital's genomes, from Nairobi, stood out as most different. In a well-known strain, higher bias scores did tend to mean more protein in culture. Silent spelling choices, they say, are a real layer of this pathogen's diversity that evolution studies have largely skipped.
plos-pone-0357497:
M. Arunadevi and colleagues published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on a common manufacturing defect: layers splitting apart when glass-fiber composite panels are drilled. Delamination weakens the finished part, and it depends in tangled ways on drill shape, size, speed, and feed. The team ran a full grid of drilling trials on glass-fiber laminates, photographed the damage, and trained a neural network that also had the physics of cracking built into its learning rules.

The physics-informed network predicted the damage measure very accurately on held-out trials. Feed rate mattered most, followed by laminate thickness and drill diameter, while faster spindle speeds actually reduced damage by cutting more cleanly and pushing less. Interactions mattered too, especially between feed and speed. Adding the physics constraints made predictions sturdier and better at generalizing. The authors offer the model as a planning aid for shops that drill composite parts.
plos-pone-0357597:
Shuang An, Dan-ni Gu, He-jun Huang, Jun-qiang Luo, and Rong-rong Liu wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about tourism in Tianshui, China. It models tourist loyalty, the choice to return or recommend a place. Three forces are built into the model: how crowded the place feels, what social value visitors think the trip gives them, and how good they judge the service to be.

The method is structural equation modeling, which tests how several influences act on each other at once. Crowding can sour a trip even when service is good, and the model weighs that tension. Destination managers in Tianshui and other growing Chinese tourist cities can use the results to balance visitor numbers against experience.
plos-pone-0357797:
Veronika Frybortova and coauthors published a 2026 mouse study in PLOS ONE on whether a ketogenic diet changes how the body handles ozanimod, a drug used in multiple sclerosis. High-fat, very-low-carbohydrate diets are being explored alongside MS therapy, but diets can retune the liver enzymes clearing drugs. Female mice ate a normal or ketogenic diet for four weeks; the team then measured metabolism, gut microbes, liver enzymes, and the drug's path through the body.

The diet produced the expected ketosis, raised blood cholesterol, and reshaped gut microbial communities, while most other measures moved only modestly. Liver enzyme activity shifted both ways: one family sped up, another slowed, and a third trended down. Drug exposure in ketogenic mice ran somewhat higher, though the difference was not statistically firm. The signal is small, they say, but real enough that diet-drug interactions deserve attention as the therapy spreads.
plos-pone-0358597:
Yueyi Tan leads a team of six using machine learning to map how two kinds of shops compete for space in Shenzhen, China, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Convenience stores run light, cheap, and everywhere; supermarkets and malls are capital heavy and choosy. The team fed geospatial data and measures of how people perceive streets into a stack of interpretive models that can reveal bends and interactions, not just straight line effects.

The two formats followed distinct locational logics. Convenience stores spread widely and reacted strongly to nearby competition, to the proximity of everyday services, and to how a place feels to pedestrians. The big formats clustered where returns justify their cost. Untangling which urban features pull each format helps planners zone commercial districts deliberately, and helps chains pick sites with their eyes open about which game they are playing.
plos-pone-0358797:
Sarah Alexandra Marshall leads a team of six asking what a health program for low income Black men with chronic illness would need to succeed, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The group studied is underserved in the southern United States, and one proposal on the table uses a universal basic income to open access to care. Before any launch, the researchers interviewed thirty-one interest holders, including men from the target population, about conditions such an intervention must respect.

Five themes emerged. The men typically delay seeking care. Relationships are strained by incarceration and poverty. Prison health services and ordinary healthcare are not built to help them. Community level barriers pile up. Racism and poverty are intertwined and entrenched. The authors argue any fair intervention, income based or not, must work at individual, family, community, and institutional levels at once, or it will fail the very people it names.
plos-pone-0359197:
Kateřina Abrhámová, Alexandra Gredová, Karolína Navrátilová, Mohamed Boumaiza, and Petr Folk wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on yeast genetics. It studies the intronic RNA of RPL22 paralogs, copies of a ribosomal protein gene, and reports that this RNA acts as an allosteric switch, a molecule whose binding changes a protein's behavior.

Introns were long treated as waste cut out of genes, so finding a working switch among them changes how yeast gene control is pictured. Paralogs are near-duplicate genes, and cross-talk between them can fine-tune protein production. Molecular biologists studying gene regulation are the readers for this small RNA with an outsized job.
pmc-13226597:
Wu and colleagues present a Chinese expert consensus on the first step in lowering cholesterol. Lowering LDL cholesterol, the panel stresses, is the most effective known way to cut heart and vessel disease caused by clogged arteries. Past studies show that active early treatment lifts the share of patients who reach their LDL goal and improves outcomes.

The consensus weighs which starting strategy fits which patient, rather than leaving the first move to habit. Choices at the start matter because delay lets risk build while doses stay too low. For Chinese clinicians, the document sets a shared, evidence-based opening play for a very common and deadly risk factor.
pmc-13237797:
Buist and colleagues assess custom-made implants for rebuilding long bones with a segment missing. Gaps in the thigh or shin bone, left by tumour removal or severe injury, are hard to bridge while sparing the nearby joint. Implants designed for one patient, built from three-dimensional scans by additive manufacturing, promise an exact fit where stock parts fail.

The study reviews how such implants performed in joint-sparing reconstructions. Fit alone is not success; the implant must bear weight for years and knit to living bone at its ends. Their experience helps surgeons judge when a bespoke implant is worth its cost and planning time.
pmc-13238797:
Yuan and colleagues report lung nodules that turned out to be rheumatoid disease, not cancer. Rheumatoid arthritis mainly attacks joints, yet the lungs are its commonest target outside them. Their patient, a man of seventy-four with a smoking history, was being treated for rheumatoid arthritis when scans found many nodules in both lungs, around their edges and linings.

In a smoker of his age, that picture screams cancer until proven otherwise. The nodules were rheumatoid ones, a rare form of the disease in the lung. Documenting the case helps chest doctors keep this possibility alive before ordering drastic treatment, and shows why a biopsy can change everything.
pmc-13241397:
van Wissen and colleagues at Leiden priced long-term exercise therapy for severely limited axial spondyloarthritis patients. Their randomized trial tracked two hundred fourteen Dutch participants for one year. Half got personalized exercise therapy; half got usual care. Costs and quality-adjusted life years were weighed from a societal angle.

Therapy patients averaged forty-one sessions, and uptake reached ninety-three percent. Extra physiotherapy costs were largely offset by savings elsewhere in care. Quality-of-life gains were tiny and statistically uncertain, as was the cost difference. The verdict: no clear economic winner, so cost alone should not block access.
pmc-13241497:
Maetzler's team at Kiel asked where on the body motion sensors best capture activity in early Parkinson's. 25 newly diagnosed, still untreated patients wore motion sensors for two weeks. Devices sat on the ankle, wrist, and lower back at once. Diaries turned daily doings into energy units for comparison.

Wrist and lower back sensors tracked diary motion about as well across effort levels. The ankle sensor lagged clearly behind both. Tremor hurt readings across the board, with the lower back coping slightly best. Maetzler's rare drug-free group gives trial planners concrete sensor placement guidance. None had started Parkinson's drugs.
pmc-13241697:
Amo-Tachie at Ghana describes a ninety-year-old whose standard heart failure dose turned toxic. The man had taken a small daily carvedilol dose as told for six months. Twice in one week he reached emergency care with dangerous low blood sugar. The first episode triggered a seizure; the second dulled his mind.

Pill counts proved he never overdosed, and scoring rated carvedilol the likely culprit. Stopping the drug and giving glucagon by vein restored him fast. He left care on day three with better kidney function. Amo-Tachie warns that aging livers and kidneys let standard doses build up without warning.
pmc-13243197:
Hassan Ahangar and co-authors describe a woman whose breathlessness led to a rare form of high blood pressure in the lungs that surgery can cure. Their case report appeared in Clinical Case Reports in 2026. The thirty-seven-year-old patient arrived with worsening breathlessness, back pain, and cough. Scans showed an enlarged right side of the heart, very high lung pressures, and wide gaps between air flow and blood flow in the lungs.

Surgeons cleared the blocked lung arteries in a major operation, and her pressures soon improved a great deal. Only later did an unnoticed early pregnancy come to light, ending in miscarriage at fourteen weeks. The strain pregnancy puts on blood flow may have unmasked her illness, the authors suggest. The case warns doctors to think of this diagnosis in women of childbearing age with unexplained breathlessness.
pmc-13245797:
Zaizen, Koga, and Tsutsumi studied skin biopsies from patients with dermatomyositis, an autoimmune disease that attacks muscle and skin, in this 2026 PLOS One paper. They stained samples from twenty-two patients and thirteen controls to map where complement proteins, antibodies, and a viral-sensor protein called MDA5 sit in the skin layers.

Patient skin carried clearly more complement C3c and two antibody types, IgM and IgA, in the upper dermis where the inflammation occurs, a pattern pointing to immune-complex injury. MDA5 appeared in the outer skin of everyone, but in patients it also showed up strongly in inflammatory cells and tiny blood vessels deeper in the skin. The map helps explain how the skin damage develops.
pmc-13247297:
Huang and co-authors measured how canal building unmasks crabs in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Two fiddler crab species living side by side in estuaries rely on matching the mudflat's color to hide from predators. The team photographed crabs in engineered canal habitats and in natural mudflats nearby, scoring body-to-background color matching with a vision-based metric.

Both species matched their background significantly worse inside canals, where construction had changed the substrate's color and light properties, while brightness and pattern measures shifted less. The authors warn that this sensory disruption could raise predation on the crabs and ripple through estuary food webs. Habitat engineering, they argue, should be judged on visual ecology too, not structure alone.
pmc-13247797:
Samson, Maximo, and Nelson combined brain chemistry and brain-network imaging in people experiencing psychosis for the first time, in this 2026 Psychological Medicine study. Sixty-seven patients who had never taken antipsychotics and one hundred ten healthy controls underwent spectroscopy measuring GABA, the brain's main inhibitory messenger, in the anterior cingulate cortex. They also had resting-state scans of connectivity in four major networks.

Patients had significantly lower cingulate GABA. Connectivity differed between groups in several networks. The key result was an interaction: in healthy brains, more GABA tracked with stronger connectivity in parts of the executive control and salience networks. In patients the relationship flipped negative. The authors argue that disturbed inhibition is woven into the network dysfunction of early psychosis, not a side note, and that the mechanism deserves direct study.
pmc-13248897:
Bounyarith, Braun, and Kucyi tested a brain scanner that asks questions at the right moment, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study. People resting in a scanner have spontaneous thoughts, but random prompts catch brain activity only roughly. Their method watched two brain regions live and triggered a thought probe whenever either region flared.

Sixty volunteers took part, and after strict exclusions about forty to fifty remained per test. Probes fired by the posteromedial cortex, a daydreaming hub, indeed caught moments of low attention to the outside world. The insula hypothesis did not hold up. The authors say the method works and can sharpen studies of wandering minds.
pmc-13249197:
Walter and co-authors screened newly arrived asylum seekers for diphtheria in Heidelberg, Germany, in a 2026 study. Europe had seen a rise in diphtheria among displaced people during 2022 and 2023. Between August and October 2024 the team swabbed throats and wounds from a random sample of one thousand seventy-three arrivals and checked blood samples for immunity.

No toxin-producing diphtheria bacteria turned up at all. Wounds told a different story: nearly half of the inflamed wounds carried MRSA, a drug-resistant staph. About thirty-eight percent of participants lacked protective diphtheria antibodies, though almost everyone accepted vaccination when offered. The authors urge early testing, wound care, and vaccination at arrival.
pmc-13249697:
Ntais and Greek colleagues measured how well brain blood vessels flex in multiple sclerosis, in a 2026 study. Ninety patients with the relapsing-remitting form and forty-five matched healthy volunteers held their breath while ultrasound tracked blood flow speed in the brain, a stand-in for carbon dioxide response. Thinking tests and a standard disability scale completed the picture.

Patients' vessels reacted notably less than controls'. Weaker reactivity tracked with greater disability and with slower mental processing speed, and both links survived adjustment for other factors. The authors propose vessel reactivity as a measurable contributor to MS disability that routine scans miss, worth tracking alongside the usual immune markers.
pmc-13249797:
Papayanis and co-authors use a blood type clue to trace where a leukemia began, in a 2026 case report. A man with primary myelofibrosis, a bone marrow scarring disease, received a stem cell transplant from his brother, whose blood type differed from his own. Afterward his blood type switched to his brother's, a sign the donor marrow had taken over blood production.

Ten months later he relapsed with acute myeloid leukemia, yet his blood type stayed his brother's. That persistence argues the leukemia grew from relatively mature donor-lineage precursor cells, not from the deepest stem cells. The authors present the case as rare evidence about which cell stage drives this feared transformation.
pmc-13249897:
Huang and colleagues found that a mitochondrial cleaning machine needs an iron-sulfur cluster to work, in a 2026 Nature Communications study. Cancer cells must clear misfolded proteins from their mitochondria. If they fail, the proteins pile up and poison the cell. The team studied CLPX, one part of the cell's mitochondrial shredder.

CLPX carries a cluster of iron and sulfur atoms. It can only join its partner protein and cut up waste when that cluster is in place. Starving cells of iron broke the shredder. So did starving them of cysteine, a building block for the clusters. The cell then switched to digesting whole mitochondria instead. The authors map this weak point as a possible target in cancer cells that lean on the system.
pmc-13249997:
Ran Wang and co-authors present a spider-web-inspired battery material in this 2026 paper. Flexible zinc-ion batteries are safer than lithium ones, but their zinc electrodes fail early as spiky deposits grow and side reactions eat away at the surface.

The team built a layered gel that fills the battery, copying a web's mix of sticky spots and open paths for ions. Zinc ions moved through it quickly and evenly. In tests, zinc electrodes lasted 4,600 hours, over six months, and full flexible cells ran more than 10,000 charge cycles. The design could suit wearable devices that need long-lived, bendable power.
pmc-13250397:
Vasef and colleagues describe a teenager whose missing periods led doctors to a hidden chromosome condition and advanced ovarian cancer. Their 2026 Clinical Case Reports paper concerns a sixteen-year-old girl with Swyer syndrome, where a person with XY chromosomes develops as female with non-working gonads. Such gonads carry a high risk of cancer.

Hormone tests showed that her ovaries were not functioning, and chromosome testing confirmed the XY pattern. Scans found several pelvic masses, and surgery confirmed dysgerminoma in both ovaries with spread to nearby lymph nodes, staged as IIIC. She was referred for chemotherapy after the surgery. The authors stress that absent periods with this hormone pattern demand chromosome testing, so that cancer is not found late.
pmc-13250597:
Santoro, Waghmare, and Panaretos prove a striking result about telling probability distributions apart with kernel methods. Their 2026 Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences paper works with kernel covariance embeddings, which map a whole distribution into a point in a large mathematical space. The setting covers continuous distributions on very general spaces.

The authors show that two different distributions always map to Gaussian measures that sit on essentially separate supports, making them perfectly distinguishable in principle. A classical result on Gaussian measures, the Feldman-Hájek dichotomy, drives the proof. Even a tiny change to a distribution becomes maximally visible after this embedding. They call this the separation of measure phenomenon and suggest it explains why kernel methods work so well in practice.
pmc-13250697:
Neyon Loku Gamage and Koshila Ranasinghe review silent gene regulators in this 2026 article on parasitic diseases. These illnesses hit hardest in poor tropical regions, where late diagnosis and weak treatments keep death rates high.

The review covers small RNA strands that never become proteins yet steer how host and parasite interact. Some patterns of these strands in blood mark which disease is present and how severe it is. Others can be used to switch off genes a parasite needs to live, tested so far in worms, scabies mites, and other infections. The authors warn that delivery, stability, and safety hurdles keep clinical use experimental.
pmc-13251197:
Matthew Yang and colleagues mine gene lists for the roots of male infertility in this 2026 study. About one in ten men worldwide faces infertility, yet most cases never get a clear genetic answer, even as gene sequencing keeps finding single-gene causes.

The team gathered 596 candidate genes and focused on 178 with strong evidence. Group analysis showed these genes cluster in a few jobs: powering the tiny tails that move sperm, hormone making and sensing, and DNA repair. Many also switch on in organs beyond the testes, including hormone glands and the brain. The authors tie this to wider health links seen in infertile men and back whole-person care.
pmc-13253997:
Mamo Gobe and co-authors study udder infection in dairy cows in a 2026 survey near Gimbichu Town, Ethiopia. Milk from 384 cows was tested from December 2023 to May 2024 for mastitis and for Staphylococcus aureus, a key germ behind it. Drug response tests were also run on the germs found.

Mastitis prevalence was 39.06 percent, mostly the hidden subclinical form at 33.06 percent. The germ was found in 42 percent of mastitis milk. Many isolates resisted penicillin G, amoxicillin, and tetracycline, and 22.22 percent resisted drugs across two classes, prompting calls for routine drug testing and prevention.
pmc-13254097:
M Ferrandis-Vila and a large team test whether gut bacteria are host specialists in a 2026 pig study. They classified 1,198 E. coli isolates from cattle, chickens, humans, and pigs in four countries by family tree, labeling some as host-linked and others as generalists. Then 17 drug-resistant isolates were fed to weaner pigs.

Bacteria settled in the gut within 24 hours, with shedding peaking early and then falling. Only 12 of 17 isolates were found again, and four stayed long term, one each from pig, cattle, chicken, and generalist groups. The authors say pigs may show low host selectivity.
pmc-13254997: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2019 paper by Møller on parallel declines in insects and insect-eating birds in Denmark over 22 years, published in Ecology and Evolution. The journal editors and publisher agreed to retract it after third parties raised concerns. They found many inconsistencies in the data, including duplications affecting large parts of the data set, and judged the results and conclusions invalid. The author did not respond to requests for comment.
pmc-13255197:
Bao-Ngoc Mach and co-authors sequence a medicinal vine's chloroplast genome in a 2026 study. Cyclea hypoglauca is a wild climber in the Menispermaceae family, used in traditional medicine for centuries in southern China and Vietnam. The team mapped its chloroplast genome, the DNA inside leaf energy organelles.

The genome runs 159,596 base pairs in the typical four-part layout. It holds 129 genes in total, with 84 that code for proteins, 37 transfer RNAs, and eight ribosomal RNAs. The authors call it the first full chloroplast genome for this species, aiding family tree work in the family.
pmc-13259297:
Qingqing Yang and Lili Wu dress silicon carbide in tannic acid to steer heat through plastic. Tiny electronics need materials that shed heat along chosen paths without heavy filler loads. Their 2026 composite lays the treated particles onto woven cellulose acetate fibers, then locks everything in polyurethane.

The tannic layer, sticky and self-polymerizing, coats the fibers in a dense fish-scale pattern. Along the weave, heat moved about five times better than through plain polyurethane. The composite also withstood notably higher heat before breaking down. Across the weave, conduction stayed low, proving true directional control at modest filler levels.
pmc-13261297:
Yuji Nojima and co-authors report a 2026 case of a rare benign bone lesion arising from the second rib. The lesion, bizarre parosteal osteochondromatous proliferation, was first described by Nora and colleagues in 1983. It usually affects the small bones of the hands and feet. Rib cases are rare.

Their patient was a 41-year-old man whose chest X-ray at a routine checkup suggested a lung mass. CT imaging showed a lesion measuring 4.1 × 2.2 cm in the left second rib. Surgeons removed it for both diagnosis and treatment. Tissue examination confirmed the diagnosis of BPOP, also called Nora's lesion. The authors advise including it in the differential diagnosis of rib lesions that look benign. Because the lesion can recur, they recommend long-term follow-up.
pmc-13262097:
Xinyu Miao and Lizhi Zhou report the first complete mitochondrial genome, the small set of genes passed down through the mother, for the vesper bat Myotis chinensis, in a 2026 article. The bat lives in China and parts of Southeast Asia, and only parts of its mitochondrial DNA had been read before. Their specimen came from Henan Province, China.

Sequencing showed a circular genome 16,812 bases long, holding 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNA genes, and 2 ribosomal RNA genes. Its bases were 64.7 percent A and T, showing a clear bias. Comparing 40 Myotis species placed this bat closest to Myotis nattereri and Myotis bombinus. The authors offer the sequence as a reference for bat classification and evolution studies.
pmc-13262597:
Turgut Seber and colleagues measure the pituitary gland in fibromyalgia, hunting a structural clue to the syndrome's hormone quirks. Thirty women with fibromyalgia and twenty-six matched controls underwent precision brain MRI scanning. Their 2026 study traces gland volume by hand-drawn segmentation.

The fibromyalgia group's glands were significantly larger in volume than controls', by a clear margin. Gland height, by contrast, matched between groups. Empty sella, a flattening sometimes linked to pressure problems, appeared just once in each group. What a bigger pituitary means biologically is unresolved, the authors say, urging larger studies that pair imaging with hormone levels.
pmc-13263397:
Ahmad Hosiian and co-authors present a 2026 case report of liver-related jaundice in an 11-year-old Syrian girl. She had two weeks of severe itching, then yellowing of the skin and dark urine. Tests showed cholestasis, meaning bile flow was blocked or slowed, yet one key enzyme, GGT, stayed normal.

Extensive testing ruled out infection, autoimmune disease, metabolic causes, and blockage. A liver biopsy showed simple bile build-up with the tissue structure intact. She recovered fully on supportive care with ursodeoxycholic acid, a bile-acid medicine. The pattern best fits benign recurrent intrahepatic cholestasis, an inherited condition. The authors present it as the first documented case from Syria.
pmc-13264897:
Lara Rowell and a large team published a 2026 interview study on maternity care in the UK during the pandemic, seen through staff and policymaker eyes. Services were rebuilt at speed, and the study focused on care for marginalised groups, who often get a worse deal. The authors took a future-facing view to guide rebuilding.

They interviewed 21 health professionals and 20 policymakers across the four UK nations. Staff said rapid changes were hard to carry out while guarding both safety and quality. The shift to virtual care made it harder to spot who most needed in-person help. Self-monitoring and remote care suited some women but hurt those with complex medical or social needs. A lack of ethnic diversity in leadership meant guidance missed minority needs. The authors link prior unaddressed inequality to worse strain during the shock.
pmc-13264997:
Gerald Olwit and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a blistering skin disease of childhood managed without the standard lab tests in south-western Uganda. The disease, linear IgA dermatosis, is usually confirmed by a glowing antibody pattern in skin samples, tests the family could neither access nor afford. Care rested on clinical judgment alone.

The patient was a 12-year-old girl whose blister outbreaks began at age two and returned at seven and twelve, each worse than the last. Large tense blisters in rings, in a string-of-pearls pattern, covered her trunk and limbs but spared her mouth. Doctors diagnosed the disease from history, pattern, and ruling out close matches. Treatment with dapsone, steroids, antibiotics, and wound care brought marked improvement within a week. The authors stress that lack of tests should not delay treatment.
pmc-13266797:
Maryam Bader Alzamanan leads a 2026 analysis pooling trials of a jaw joint washout plus a blood-based injection. The joint is the temporomandibular joint, which links the jaw to the skull. The added injection uses platelet-rich fibrin, a gel made from the patient's own blood that may calm inflammation and aid healing.

Nine trials with 320 patients and 374 joints were pooled. Adding the injection cut pain more than control care and widened mouth opening by about five millimeters. Forward and side jaw movements also improved, though quality of life did not clearly change. A trial-check method backed the pain result. The authors still want larger trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-13267097:
Kyohei Otani wrote a 2026 review proposing a joined-up way to think about headache and mental health. Headache disorders, including migraine, are shaped by brain biology, feelings, behavior, and social life. Yet mental health care is often kept apart from headache care in daily practice, Otani argues.

The review drew on three databases for work from 1990 to 2025. Headache was strongly linked both ways with depression, anxiety, trauma, and poor sleep. Poor control of feelings and gloomy thinking about pain predicted lasting headache and disability. Otani's framework, called Psychocephalology, sorts the evidence into five linked domains. He urges routine mental health screening and team-based care to stop attacks becoming chronic.
pmc-13267297:
Stephan Masius and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a trial of a navigation aid in leg artery procedures. Doctors thread catheters through narrowed arteries using X-ray imaging that needs contrast dye. The dye and radiation carry risks for patients and staff. The Vascular Navigation PAD system aims to cut the number of X-ray runs.

Two German hospitals will enroll 160 patients with peripheral artery disease, split evenly by chance. Half get the navigation aid plus standard imaging; half get standard care alone. The main measure is how much contrast dye each procedure uses. Other measures include radiation dose, imaging time, and the number of X-ray runs. The protocol paper reports the plan only; the trial's results are not yet in.
pmc-13268397:
Roger Keller Celeste and colleagues present a 2026 study of dental coverage and gum disease across Brazil. Using the national SB Brasil 2023 survey, the team studied 7,851 adults who used public dental services. They asked whether towns having specialist dental centers, and how fully primary dental care covered the population, related to periodontal disease, meaning deep gum pockets.

Overall, about 17 percent had the disease. Towns with specialist centers showed slightly more disease, not less, though the link was weak. Full primary care coverage looked protective: towns at 100 percent coverage had the lowest disease rate, about 8 percent. The two coverage types did not interact. The authors conclude broad primary dental coverage tracks with less gum disease in smaller towns, and referral barriers deserve study.
pmc-13269597:
Yuguang Ma wrote a short research highlight in 2026 on a Nature study of quantum dot LEDs, tiny light sources for screens. Pushing these displays past 10,000 pixels per inch is key for virtual and augmented reality headsets. As pixels shrink below a micrometer, their efficiency usually collapses.

The highlighted team, led by Lihua Lin and Fushan Li, traced the loss to edge leakage from distorted electric fields inside the pixel. A precise printing method patterned pixels at up to 25,400 pixels per inch. Added nanoparticles balanced the field so light spread evenly. Red devices reached 26.1 percent efficiency with strong stability. Ma presents the work as a blueprint for sharper, thriftier micro-displays.
pmc-13269897:
Lanxin Pan and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on age-based subtypes of type 1 diabetes in children. Gut microbes, body chemicals, fats, and gene activity were profiled in 108 newly diagnosed children and 56 healthy controls. Children were grouped by onset age: under 7, 7 to 12, and 13 or over.

Each group carried its own microbe and chemical signatures. The youngest group had the highest share of B cells, a type of immune cell, at a median of 11.64 percent. The oldest group was lowest, at 5.99 percent, with more metabolic pathway activity. One gut microbe may drive B-cell growth through a fatty acid, the network analysis suggested. The authors frame the groups as distinct disease subtypes.
pmc-13270897:
Carla Huanca Challgua is lead author of a 2026 qualitative study, one based on interviews, of barriers to cervical cancer secondary prevention in Cochabamba, Bolivia. Secondary prevention means screening to find early changes and treating them before cancer develops, yet screening coverage in Bolivia stays low and uneven.

The team interviewed 30 health workers, including gynaecologists, doctors, and nurses. Workers described women's information gaps, family myths passed down, gender norms, and fear of partner violence for attending screening. Using the Quechua language in visits and offering small incentives helped draw women in. At system level, unclear rules on who should be screened also blocked access.
pmc-13270997:
Jörg Vogel is lead author of a 2026 meeting report on RNAmed, a graduate training programme for future leaders in RNA-based medicine. Funded by the Free State of Bavaria, the programme is run jointly by universities and institutes in Würzburg, Regensburg, and Munich. It trains doctoral students from basic RNA biology through to rules, ethics, and social effects.

The report covers the programme's 2025 annual retreat on San Servolo, an island in the Venice lagoon. Forty doctoral researchers, senior investigators, and guests met for three days of keynote talks, student presentations, flash talks, and a career panel. Talks featured antisense methods, circular RNAs, delivery technology, and artificial intelligence for molecule design.
pmc-13272097:
Justin Lyon is first named author on a 2026 case article on immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis. That is a disease where faulty antibody fragments build up in tissues. In the patient described, matching purple hand nodules on both hands and an enlarged tongue prompted a skin biopsy. The biopsy revealed the amyloid deposits. It led to a diagnosis of multiple myeloma, a blood cancer.

The authors stress that early recognition of typical and unusual skin signs of amyloidosis is essential. That way clinicians start prompt blood workup and treatment, improving outcomes and survival.
pmc-13272197:
Colin M. Shapiro is lead author of a 2026 clinical article on sexsomnia, sexual behaviour carried out during sleep without full awareness. He argues psychiatrists should know this entity. First described by the authors in a Canadian journal, sexsomnia is now recognised as a subtype of non-REM parasomnia. That is the family of arousal disorders that includes sleepwalking.

A recent self-reported survey put lifetime rates at roughly seven to ten percent. Past-three-month rates were about six percent. Both are higher than once believed. Forensic reports describe behaviours from self-touch to non-consensual contact and penetrative acts while asleep. The authors stress the condition arises from a primary sleep disorder. It does not arise from paraphilic interests. That distinction carries legal weight.
pmc-13272997:
Lin Cheng leads a 2026 case-control study of bone shape and second knee ligament injuries after a first reconstruction. The anterior cruciate ligament, or ACL, is often torn in athletes, and grafts can tear or the other knee can be injured. The team used CT scans from 224 patients taken within a week of surgery.

Graft rupture occurred in 16 patients, or 7.1 percent, and injury to the other knee in 22, or 9.8 percent. A smaller bony ridge height in the shin linked to graft rupture. Greater twisting of the shin bone linked to injury in the other knee. The authors identify these shape traits as independent risk factors.
pmc-13273097: Author correction notice from Sekar Tamilperuvalathan and co-authors. It concerns a paper on improving a spark-based micro-machining method for borosilicate glass with nitrogen gas help. The notice states that the reference list in the original paper contained errors. It lists incorrect reference entries that need to be replaced. The paper has now been corrected in its updated form.
pmc-13273397:
Fawaz Ahmed Prem Navaz leads a 2026 case report of a catheter fragment that traveled from a donor liver to a recipient's lung artery during transplantation. A 62-year-old woman received a liver from a brain-dead donor who had a neck-area central line in place at organ removal. Scans after surgery showed a 5 centimeter object in a lung artery branch.

All the recipient's own devices were removed intact, suggesting the fragment came from the donor, likely cut during heart removal and lodged in liver outflow. Retrieval by catheter failed due to its deep position. At six months she remained well with excellent graft function, under surveillance without blood thinners.
pmc-13273797:
Krishnamurthy and colleagues pilot a brain stimulation treatment for language loss after stroke. Their 2026 journal article tests tDCS, a weak electric current applied to the scalp. It was paired with a shortened phonomotor treatment, which rebuilds speech sounds.

The pilot enrolled only six older men with chronic aphasia. Three received active stimulation and three received sham treatment. The active group gained in producing speech sounds. Those gains held at three months. Word naming did not change in either group. The authors treat the results as early signals only. A sample this small cannot prove benefit. They call for a larger trial to test the approach.
pmc-13273997:

Survival results become with care weighed. The thorough center treats complex cases. results prove much top.

pmc-13639697:
Kawai and colleagues examined in 2026 whether heart and brain vessel disease changes how two hormone-blocking drugs perform in castration-resistant prostate cancer, a stage where standard hormone therapy has failed. The earlier ENABLE trial had found enzalutamide and abiraterone broadly equal, but patients with cardio-cerebrovascular disease are often excluded or feared harder to treat. This randomized study deliberately enrolled them and compared outcomes by disease status and drug.

Thirty-six patients had such disease, most often prior brain infarction, against 142 without. Survival measures, including time to marker progression, scan progression, and overall and cancer-specific survival, did not differ significantly between the groups, and neither drug beat the other inside either group. Side effect rates were also comparable throughout. The authors conclude both drugs remain feasible choices for patients with this history, a group clinicians often hesitate over.
