pmc-13650297: Preoperative risk stratification for pulmonar appeared in 2026. The authors made a strong case. The knowledge base retains it. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it. Its pages add to the record of the past for readers.
pmc-4580597:
Paradis, Ben, Denson, and their colleagues reviewed racism as a determinant of health in 2015. A growing body of population studies had documented health impacts of racism in recent years. That evidence had not yet been gathered into one comprehensive meta-analysis on racism itself.

The team systematically reviewed the literature and pooled results across studies. Their synthesis weighs how strongly racism is linked to poorer mental and physical health. A pooled estimate gives policy makers a firmer base than scattered single studies. The review supports treating racism as a public health issue that shapes illness and access to care.
pmc-5075697:
Rognes, Flouri, Nichols, and their colleagues presented VSEARCH in 2016, a versatile open source tool for metagenomics. VSEARCH processes and prepares nucleotide sequence data for metagenomics, genomics, and population genomics. It is multithreaded and free of charge, with its source code open to all.

The tool was designed as an alternative to USEARCH, a widely used program whose source code was not open. Open code lets researchers inspect, fix, and extend the methods they rely on. VSEARCH covers clustering, searching, and quality steps needed before analysis. It became a core free tool for labs profiling microbial communities.
pmc-7005297:
Lei Yang, Peng Shi, Gaofeng Zhao, and coauthors reviewed targeting cancer stem cell pathways in 2020. Cancer stem cells were first found in leukemia in the mid nineteen nineties. These cells can renew themselves and seed new tumor growth.

They are blamed for relapse, spread, and resistance to standard therapy. The review covers the main signaling pathways that keep such cells alive, including Wnt, Notch, and Hedgehog. Drugs aimed at those pathways are surveyed with their trial results. Killing the bulk of a tumor may not cure it if this root population survives.
pmc-7334197:
Konrad Karczewski and a very large team of co-authors published in 2020 a map of which human genes can tolerate change and which cannot. They built it from genetic variation gathered in more than one hundred forty thousand people. Where a gene almost never shows damaging changes in healthy people, that absence itself is evidence the gene does essential work.

The authors turn those patterns into a spectrum of constraint, a graded measure for gene after gene across the genome. Doctors and researchers use such measures to judge whether a rare change found in a patient is likely to cause disease. The work became a standard reference for reading human genomes in clinics and in studies of inherited illness.
pmc-8500697:
Damian Santomauro and collaborators estimated in 2021 how much the COVID-19 pandemic raised the global burden of depression and anxiety during 2020. Even before the pandemic, these two disorders were among the leading causes of health related burden worldwide. The pandemic then created conditions, from isolation to economic shock, that damage mental health on a vast scale.

The team combined data on infection rates and restrictions with surveys of symptoms, covering more than two hundred countries and territories. They calculate the extra cases of major depression and anxiety attributable to the pandemic's first year, and where the increases fell hardest. Their figures helped governments grasp that the mental health costs of the crisis rivaled many direct effects of the virus.
pmc-8728197:
Jan Meier-Kolthoff and co-authors described in 2021 a paired pair of databases built for naming and classifying bacteria and archaea from their genomes. Microbial classification now leans heavily on genome data, while the number of named species and their sequences keeps climbing steeply. Keeping names, classifications, and sequences in step has become a real challenge for database builders.

Their two resources work as a tandem: one computes a genome based classification, the other maintains the official naming record for prokaryotes. Together they let a researcher place a new genome quickly and check that its name follows the rules. The article explains how the pairing stays accurate as public repositories grow.
renfrew-witches-relation-1697:
Renfrewshire saw Scotland's last great witch trial in 1697, and an official relation prints the case. A Relation of the Diabolical Practices of the Witches of Renfrewshire sets out the charges in the Paisley affair. Seven people died for it in the end.

The charges began with a young girl, Christian Shaw, whose fits and claims named her neighbors as witches. The relation lays out the acts said to be done by hidden and evil means. Courts, clergy, and councils all had a hand in the long case. The print marks the close of large-scale witch hunting in Scotland.
robinson-children-of-the-night-1897:
Edwin Arlington Robinson published The Children of the Night in 1897, paying for the printing himself. Robinson was a poor, unknown clerk from Maine who wrote poems about a fictional town he called Tilbury Town. The book made his name among the few who read it carefully.

Richard Cory, the town's rich and envied gentleman, shocks everyone with his end. Miniver Cheevy, born too late for the age of knights, drinks and dreams his life away. Luke Havergal pleads with a lover from beyond a western gate. Robinson's plain speech and tight stanzas hide deep irony. The collection introduced one of America's most durable poetic voices.
robison-proofs-of-a-conspiracy-1797:
John Robison was an Edinburgh professor of natural philosophy who published Proofs of a Conspiracy in 1797. The book charges the Illuminati, a secret Bavarian order, and corrupted Masonic lodges with plotting the French Revolution. It became the founding text of modern conspiracy literature.

Robison claims that the order's agents entered lodges across Europe, spreading attacks on throne and altar under cover of philosophy. He writes as a Mason himself, he says, warning the brethren he still respects against the lodges he fears. His proofs, thin as later readers found them, launched a genre that has never since gone quiet.
rostand-cyrano-1897:
Edmond Rostand published Cyrano de Bergerac in 1897, his heroic comedy in verse,. The long-nosed poet-swordsman who loves from the shadows made the great romantic verse drama. Rostand wrote it in rhymed alexandrines, and its panache revived romance in a naturalist age of prose and gloom.

Cyrano, cadet of Gascony, fights duels while composing ballads and hides his love for his cousin Roxane. He feeds the handsome, tongue-tied Christian the words that win her, even letters from the siege of Arras. Roxane learns the truth only at Cyrano's death, fifteen years on, in a convent garden in falling autumn leaves. His last enemy is falsehood itself, and he dies on his feet, plume, or panache, held high to the end. The play's verve has kept it on stages and screens in every language since.
russell-day-of-vengeance-vol4-1897:
Charles Taze Russell laid out the end of the age in The Day of Vengeance, the fourth Studies in the Scriptures volume of 1897. Russell, founder of the Bible Student movement, read prophecy as a timetable. The battle of Armageddon and the close of the Gentile times stand at the book's center.

Russell taught that the old order of church and state would fall in fire, making way for God's kingdom. His followers, later known as Jehovah's Witnesses, built their hopes on such readings. The volume holds the eschatological core of the Studies series, its vision of how the world ends.
russell-foundations-geometry-1897:
An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry, published in 1897, was Bertrand Russell's first book, growing from his fellowship dissertation at Cambridge. The young Russell set out to ask what geometry assumes about space, and what philosophy can certify of those assumptions.

He examines the axioms of the new non-Euclidean geometries and argues, in Kantian spirit, that some structure of space is given in experience itself. Russell later discarded much of the book's doctrine as his logic sharpened. Even so, it shows the twenty-five-year-old already at work on his lifelong theme. Mathematics and philosophy meet here at their border.
sbe-42-atharva-veda-1897:
Maurice Bloomfield gave hymns of the Atharva-Veda English dress in 1897. The work is Book Forty-Two of the Sacred Books of the East. The Atharva-Veda is the fourth Veda of old India. Its hymns lean more to spells, cures, and home rites than the Rig Veda's songs.

Bloomfield picks a set of hymns that shows the range of the book. Charms for health, love, and luck stand by hymns of deep thought. The text gives a close view of the daily fears and hopes of old India. Bloomfield was the great Atharva man of his age.
sbe-46-vedic-hymns-2-1897:
Hermann Oldenberg gave the Vedic Hymns, Part Two, English dress in 1897. The work is Book Forty-Six of the Sacred Books of the East. The hymns come from the Rig Veda, the hymn store of old India. All of them praise one god: Agni, the god of fire.

Mandalas One to Five of the Rig Veda give the hymns in this book. Agni bears the gifts of men to the gods in the flame. He is priest, guest, and friend of the home in the old songs. Oldenberg's notes are a model of care in the Veda field.
shakespeare-romeo-and-juliet-1597:
William Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet first reached print in 1597. The play set the pattern for tales of young love ever since. In Verona, two great houses, the Montagues and Capulets, feud in the streets.

Romeo and Juliet meet at a feast and wed in secret the next day. A street brawl kills kin on both sides and exiles Romeo. A failed plan with a sleeping draught ends in a tomb of grief. Its swift verse and sad end still move crowds worldwide. Balcony and tomb scenes are known far past the stage, into song, film, and common speech.
sienkiewicz-quo-vadis-curtin-1897:
Jeremiah Curtin's translation of Henryk Sienkiewicz's Quo Vadis appeared in 1897, the first English version of the Polish novel. Sienkiewicz set his narrative in the Rome of Nero. A Roman officer's love for a Christian hostage stands at the center of a city sliding toward persecution and fire.

Vinicius pursues Lygia through feasts, prisons, and the arena, while Peter and Paul move among the hidden Christians. Nero's court, drawn in gaudy and cruel detail, prepares the great fire and the blame cast on Christians. The novel won world fame and helped win Sienkiewicz the Nobel Prize. Curtin's English carried that fame across the Atlantic.
spr-proceedings-vol12-1896-1897:
Parts thirty and thirty one, for 1896 and 1897, form volume twelve of the Proceedings. The Society for Psychical Research enters the late 1890s with its archive growing thick. Telepathy receives fresh trials and fresh doubts in equal measure. The census of hallucinations continues to shape what counts as a strong case.

Sittings with trance mediums, Piper chief among them, occupy long stretches. Investigators compare notes across sittings, hunting for patterns and leaks. Apparition stories arrive from clergy, doctors, and soldiers alike. The volume sustains the primary record of the era's great debate on survival. Few sources match its detail. It documents hope and skepticism side by side.
stahl-zymotechnia-fundamentalis-1697:
Georg Ernst Stahl, a German doctor and chemist, set out his new scheme of burning in this Latin book of 1697. Its title deals with the craft of fermentation, but its fame rests on one bold claim. Stahl held that all things that burn hold a fire stuff he named phlogiston.

When a thing burns, he said, its phlogiston flies off into the air. The scheme made sense of rust, smelting, and flame in one neat frame. Most chemists held to it for the bulk of the next hundred years, till new trials broke it.
still-autobiography-1897:
Five years before his Philosophy, Andrew Taylor Still told his own story in an Autobiography printed in 1897. Still began as a frontier doctor and served as a surgeon in the Civil War. Loss and doubt pushed him to question the medicine he had been taught.

His life story doubles as a history of osteopathy, from his first insight to the school he founded at Kirksville. He recalls patients, critics, and the slow spread of his hands-on method. Readers meet the founder in his own plain voice, and see how one man's path produced a whole new healing science.
strindberg-inferno-1897:
August Strindberg wrote Inferno in 1897, here in Claud Field's English translation of 1913 in print. The autobiographical record tells of his occult crisis in Paris, paranoia, alchemy, and spiritual breakdown in prose. He wrote it in French during the worst years of his mental torment in the 1890s.

Strindberg, alone in Paris, tries to make gold and reads secret signs in cracks and clouds. He feels pursued by unseen powers, flees to Austria and Denmark, and nears madness in cheap hotels. Swedenborg's visions guide his slow turn from occult dread toward a chastened, suffering faith in God. The prose is fevered, funny in flashes, and unlike any other memoir of a mind in crisis. It stands as the key document of the crisis that remade his art.
the-mirror-of-alchimy-1597: The Mirror of Alchimy, 1597. The alchemical mirror. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
the-revival-of-alchemy-1897: The Revival of Alchemy, 1897. The alchemical revival. This book preserves that work. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its pages add to the record of the past.
tiele-elements-science-religion-1897:
Cornelius Petrus Tiele was a Dutch scholar counted a founder of the science of religion. His Elements of the Science of Religion, published in 1897, prints his Gifford Lectures given in Edinburgh. The lectures lay out the field's morphology and ontology, its forms and its deepest question.

Morphology, in Tiele's scheme, sorts the shapes religion takes as it grows from nature worship toward ethical faith. Ontology then asks what religion is at root: man's sense of the infinite pressing on his life. Students across Europe learned the young discipline's working plan from Tiele's lectures. He writes as a believer who still insists on sorting facts first.
tob-10497:
Flavius Josephus, a Jewish historian writing in Rome around 93 AD, retold his people's story in the Antiquities of the Jews. Twenty books run from Creation to the eve of the revolt against Rome in his own lifetime. Josephus wrote partly as apology, explaining Judaism to a Greco-Roman audience that knew little about it.

Kings, prophets, and priests move through biblical history expanded with traditions and details found nowhere else. Because so many ancient sources are lost, Josephus often stands alone as evidence. The Antiquities remains our fullest ancient account of Second Temple Judaism, and a bridge between the Bible's world and the Roman Empire that destroyed the Temple.
tob-10797:
Frederick Starr surveyed Korean Buddhism after traveling in Korea, blending history with firsthand observation. Buddhism had arrived from China centuries earlier and taken root in mountain temples across the peninsula. By the early 1900s, when Starr wrote, it survived in a changed and pressured condition.

Arrival and royal patronage, decline under later dynasties, temple art, monks' lives, and popular practice all receive attention. Photographs and travel notes ground the survey in places Starr actually visited. Because English writing on Korean religion was then scarce, his book remains a rare early window on a tradition often overshadowed by its Chinese and Japanese neighbors.
trine-in-tune-with-infinite-1897:
Ralph Waldo Trine was an American writer whose In Tune with the Infinite, published in 1897, became the best-selling founding text of the New Thought movement. New Thought taught that the mind, rightly aligned, draws health and plenty from a divine supply. Trine states that faith in calm, simple chapters.

He urges readers to live in conscious union with the Infinite, letting fear and hurry fall away. Thought, in his system, is a real force that shapes body, mood, and fortune. The book shaped American metaphysical religion and still circulates among seekers of a practical, hopeful spirituality.
un-ga-res-997:
War over Egypt forced the UN General Assembly into its first emergency special session in the fall of 1956. Resolution 997, adopted on 2 November 1956, notes that Israeli forces had pushed deep into Egyptian land, in breach of the 1949 truce deal. British and French forces were also attacking Egypt, and traffic through the Suez Canal had stopped, to the harm of many states.

The Assembly urges an instant cease-fire as the first step. All forces in the fight must halt, and no more troops or arms may move into the area. The truce sides must pull back behind the truce lines, end raids across those lines, and keep the truce terms in full.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Resolution 997 (ES-I) was adopted by the General Assembly in emergency special session on 2 November 1956. It is its first response to the fighting that had broken out around the Suez Canal. With the Security Council blocked, the Assembly took up the crisis itself. It demanded an immediate halt.

The resolution urges an immediate cease-fire. It urges withdrawal of all forces behind the armistice lines, and an end to raids across them. It calls on members not to introduce military goods into the area. It asks the parties to take steps to reopen the Suez Canal on the cease-fire taking effect. It requests the Secretary-General to observe and report on compliance. The Assembly decided to stay in emergency session until its demands were met, setting the stage for a United Nations emergency force.
un-sc-res-1297: Dated 2000 in the catalog, Resolution 1297 records formal action by the United Nations Security Council. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1397:
Violence during the second Palestinian uprising forms the background to Resolution 1397, adopted on 12 March 2002. The Council voiced grave concern at the tragic events since September 2000. Recent attacks had raised the number of dead still further. In this text, for the first time, the Council set out a two-state outcome in its own words.

The resolution affirms a vision of a region where two states live side by side. Israel and Palestine would each have secure and recognized borders. The Council demanded an immediate end to all acts of violence. Terror, provocation, incitement, and destruction were all named. The Israeli and Palestinian sides and their leaders were called on to carry out the Tenet work plan. The proposals of the Mitchell Report were named as well. The goal was to bring back talks on a political settlement.
un-sc-res-1497:
Liberia's civil war brought an authorized multinational force from the Security Council on 1 August 2003. Fighting had cost countless innocent lives and was shaking the whole region. A cease-fire had been signed in Accra on 17 June 2003, but it needed outside force to hold. West African leaders of ECOWAS had brokered the truce, and the Secretary-General had asked the Council on 30 June to send a force.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorized member states to set up a multinational force in Liberia. The force would back the cease-fire and create safe conditions for aid. Its members could take all necessary measures. The Council declared itself ready to follow with a United Nations stabilization force for the transitional government. Sierra Leone's mission could give the West African advance units thirty days of support.
un-sc-res-1597:
The Yugoslav tribunal's bench rules changed in the spring of 2005. On 20 April 2005 the Security Council amended the court's statute. The change rewrote article 13 ter, on temporary ad litem judges. A list of candidates for those posts had reached the Council in February. The Secretary-General had suggested more time for nominations. The Council now granted it.

The deadline for naming ad litem judge candidates grew by thirty days. That count ran from the date of adoption. The annex to the resolution carries the new article in full. Ad litem judges let the court run more trials at once. That mattered as the tribunal worked to finish its cases on schedule. The amendment is technical, but it kept trials staffed.
un-sc-res-1697:
UNIFIL gained one month in the middle of a war on 31 July 2006. Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah had raged since 12 July. The Secretary-General's report of 22 July found the force blocked from working along the Blue Line. Lebanon had asked for six more months, but he advised one month while other options for the south were weighed. The force's mandate was about to run out.

The Council urged every party to respect the safety of UNIFIL and other United Nations staff. The force had to be allowed to resupply its posts and run search and rescue work for its own people. The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 August 2006. It stayed actively seized of the matter. The short term was a holding step: within two weeks the Council would pass resolution 1701, end the war, and rebuild the force on a far larger scale.
un-sc-res-1797:
Local elections in the Democratic Republic of the Congo gained United Nations help under a Security Council decision of 30 January 2008. The country was in its post-transition period after national polls. The Secretary-General had written in October and November 2007 to recommend that the United Nations mission, MONUC, assist with the local vote. The Council called elections central to long-term peace, reconciliation, and rule of law.

The Council authorized MONUC to help the Congolese authorities, including the National Independent Electoral Commission, organize, prepare, and run the local elections. The mission would work closely with international partners and the United Nations country team. The text is a single narrow authorization rather than a new mandate. It shows the mission shifting from keeping security toward the slower work of building elected local government across the country.
un-sc-res-1897:
Piracy off Somalia was taken up by the Security Council in Resolution 1897, adopted on 30 November 2009. Naval patrols had run for a year under earlier Council powers. Somalia's government sent letters in November 2009 agreeing to one more year. Trials for captured pirates still posed a legal puzzle for the navies involved.

The Council renews the anti-piracy powers for twelve months. States working with the Somali government may again enter its waters and use all necessary means. States are urged to sign deals with countries ready to hold captured pirates. Such deals can put law officers from those countries aboard warships, as shipriders, to ease trials. The powers apply to Somalia alone and set no general rule of law.
un-sc-res-1997:
Sudan's mission was ordered home as South Sudan was born on 11 July 2011. Khartoum's foreign minister had written on 27 May asking to end UNMIS on 9 July, the day the South took independence. The Secretary-General's report of 17 May covered the mission's close. The Council restated its pledge to the sovereignty of both Sudan and South Sudan.

The Council decided to withdraw UNMIS with effect from 11 July 2011. The Secretary-General had to complete the pullout of all uniformed and civilian staff, save those needed for liquidation, by 31 August 2011. Staff, equipment, and supplies were to pass to the new missions, UNMISS in the South and UNISFA in Abyei. Khartoum had to honor the status of forces agreement in full. Unimpeded access to United Nations premises and full freedom of movement were named in particular. A smooth handover to the two successor missions was underlined.
un-sc-res-397: The catalog's entries for 1974 include Resolution 397 of the United Nations Security Council. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-97:
Security Council Resolution 97, adopted in January 1952, dissolved the Commission for Conventional Armaments. The council had created that body in 1947 to draft plans for cutting armies and arms below atomic levels. Years of deadlock between the Western powers and the Soviet Union had left its work stalled beyond repair.

The short text closed the commission and passed the disarmament task to a new body meant to cover all arms at once. In effect, the council admitted that the old split between atomic and regular weapons no longer worked. The record shows an early UN hope fading as the arms race hardened into the Cold War pattern.
un-sc-res-997: Security Council Resolution 997 survives in the official record, and the catalog dates it to 1993. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1297, adopted on 12 May 2000, responds to renewed fighting between Eritrea and Ethiopia. The Council says it is deeply disturbed by the outbreak. It stresses that the fighting threatens peace and security and the stability of the whole subregion. It notes its serious effects on civilians. It strongly condemns the return to war.

The Council demands that both parties stop all military action at once and use no further force. It demands that substantive peace talks reopen at the earliest possible moment, without preconditions. The talks are under the Organization of African Unity, on the basis of its Framework Agreement and Modalities. It endorses the OAU communiqué of 5 May 2000. It calls on both sides to protect civilians and respect humanitarian law. It resolves to meet again within 72 hours to take steps if the fighting goes on.

For the first time, the Council said the words two states out loud for Israel and Palestine. On 12 March 2002, it adopted Resolution 1397. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. Syria held back. The vote came amid the bloodshed of the Second Intifada.

The text backs a vision of the region with two states side by side. Israel and Palestine would live within safe, agreed borders. It demands an instant halt to all acts of violence. Terror, goading, and wrecking all count. It calls on both sides to work the Tenet plan and the Mitchell Report. Those steps aimed to restart talks on a final deal. The two-state phrase became standard diplomatic language.

Liberia's civil war draws an armed response in Resolution 1497, adopted on 1 August 2003 by twelve votes to none with three abstentions. Fighting had produced a humanitarian disaster in Monrovia and was destabilizing the region. A ceasefire signed at Accra in June was not holding on its own, and West African leaders, led by Ghana and Nigeria, were preparing to send troops.

The Council authorized a multinational force to deploy to Liberia, under Chapter VII, to back the ceasefire and create conditions in which aid workers could operate safely. It also signaled that a longer UN peacekeeping mission would follow within months. The West African force landed days later, and the resolution became the legal door through which Liberia's war ended.

The Yugoslavia war crimes tribunal faced a staffing snag in 2005. Too few candidates had been nominated as temporary trial judges. Those judges, called ad litem judges, were also barred from re-election. Their first terms expired on 11 June 2005. Resolution 1597, adopted unanimously on 20 April 2005, rewrote the rules.

Acting under Chapter VII, members amended the tribunal's statute. Serving temporary judges could now stand for re-election. The nomination deadline gained thirty extra days. The annex spells out the election system. The Assembly elects twenty-seven judges from a Council list. Each serves four-year terms. The fix kept trials staffed as the Hague court worked through its remaining cases.

Resolution 1697, adopted on 31 July 2006, extends the Lebanon force for a single month while war rages around it. Fighting between Israel and Hezbollah had escalated since 12 July, and the Secretary-General's report admitted that UNIFIL, pinned down along the Blue Line, could not carry out its activities effectively. Lebanon had originally asked for six more months; the Secretary-General recommended one month while longer-term options were weighed.

The Council granted that month, to the end of August 2006. It urged all sides to keep UNIFIL troops and all UN staff safe without exception, to let the force resupply its positions, and to allow search and rescue work for its people. A wholly new mandate arrived in August.

Local elections in the Democratic Republic of the Congo are the focus of Resolution 1797, adopted on 30 January 2008. Congo had held landmark national polls in 2006 after its transition, and local elections were the next unfinished layer of the peace settlement. The Secretary-General had recommended that the UN mission, MONUC, help organize them.

The Council authorized MONUC to assist the Congolese authorities, including the national electoral commission, with organizing, preparing, and running the local polls. The work was to be done working closely with world partners and the UN country team. The resolution treats elections as central to restoring peace, reconciliation, and the rule of law after years of war.

The fight against Somali piracy is renewed by Resolution 1897, adopted on 30 November 2009. Piracy had spread into the western Indian Ocean; EU, NATO, and combined task force patrols were active, and Kenya was prosecuting captured suspects. Weak laws and limited capacity still meant some pirates were released without trial, and rising ransoms kept fuelling the trade. Somalia's government asked for another 12 months of the authorizations.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council renews for 12 months the Resolution 1846 (2008) and 1851 (2008) authorizations for cooperating states to enter Somali waters and act against piracy. It invites states to sign 'shiprider' agreements so regional law-enforcement officers can ride along and ease prosecutions. It urges states to criminalize piracy at home. It backs help for Somalia and neighbours to jail convicted pirates. The Djibouti Code of Conduct and the Contact Group's trust fund are welcomed.

Resolution 197, adopted unanimously on 30 October 1964, recommends the Republic of Zambia for membership in the United Nations. Zambia had been independent for just six days, having ended British rule as Northern Rhodesia on 24 October. Its application reached the Council almost immediately.

The whole text is the recommendation itself, addressed to the General Assembly, which holds the final vote on admissions but can act only after the Council speaks. Zambia's quick admission reflected the speed of decolonization in Africa during the 1960s, when new states joined the UN in rapid succession. The landlocked copper-producing country in southern Africa has kept its seat ever since.

Resolution 1997, adopted on 11 July 2011, winds up the United Nations Mission in Sudan, UNMIS. Sudan's foreign minister had written to say his government wanted the mission ended on 9 July, the day South Sudan became independent. The Secretary-General reported on the mission's close, and two new missions, for South Sudan and for Abyei, were taking shape.

The Council decides to withdraw UNMIS effective 11 July 2011 and asks that all uniformed and civilian staff, apart from those winding the mission down, be out by 31 August 2011. Staff, gear, and supplies are to move to the new missions, UNMISS and UNISFA. Sudan is asked to honor the status of forces deal in full until the last staff leave. Options for UN support in Blue Nile and Southern Kordofan are also requested.

Qatar ended its status as a British-protected state in September 1971. Oil had made the small Gulf peninsula rich. Independence brought a swift UN application. Resolution 297 was adopted unanimously on 15 September 1971. The Council acted at its 1578th meeting, less than two weeks after independence.

The members recommended Qatar's admission to the General Assembly. The Assembly seated Qatar within the week. Gulf neighbors Bahrain and Oman joined the UN the same season. Together they shifted the region's diplomacy away from London. For Qatar, membership was the legal seal on sovereignty. The one-sentence text hides a busy year in which Britain's Gulf treaties all came to an end.

A young African state sought its seat at the United Nations in 1976, the year after its independence from Portugal. Resolution 397 deals with the application of the People's Republic of Angola. The Council examined the application and voted on it. Thirteen votes backed the recommendation, with one abstention. The Council recommended to the General Assembly that Angola be admitted to membership in the United Nations. The recommendation ended the new state's wait for a seat.

One of the UN's first disarmament bodies died by this single sentence. The Commission for Conventional Armaments had been created in the UN's early years. It worked on plans for limiting armies and non-nuclear weapons. By 1952 the General Assembly had judged the effort stalled. Its resolution of 11 January 1952 pointed the way out.

Resolution 97, adopted on 30 January 1952, dissolves the Commission outright. It follows the Assembly's recommendation, cited in the text. No debate details survive in the record. The move closed a chapter of early Cold War arms talks. Disarmament work shifted to new forums. The Council had helped launch the Commission's work in 1949; five years on, it signed the body's end.

Forces of Rwanda's former regime were preparing attacks from camps in neighboring countries in 1995. Raids into Rwanda were growing. The United Nations Assistance Mission for Rwanda, called UNAMIR, was still in the country after the genocide of 1994. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 4 June 1995, set out its future. Resolution 997 was adopted unanimously on 9 June 1995.

The Council extended UNAMIR until 8 December 1995, but shrank it at the same time. Its troops would fall to 2,330 within three months and to 1,800 within four. The observers and civilian police stayed at the same level. The mission's tasks shifted toward helping refugees return home and rebuilding trust. States near Rwanda were told to stop arms from reaching the Rwandan camps on their soil. The arms ban of Resolution 918 was also confirmed, for anyone supplying fighters who would use the weapons inside Rwanda.
virgil-aeneid-dryden-1697:
Virgil wrote the Aeneid in Latin in the last years before Christ. John Dryden gave it English verse in 1697, and his version ruled for a hundred years. Dryden, then England's famed poet, used crisp heroic couplets throughout.

Aeneas flees burning Troy and sails toward a new home in Italy. Gods thwart and aid him, and Dido's love ends in grief and fire. Wars in Italy test his duty to the gods and his son. Dryden's lines made Rome's epic a classic of English poetry too. Pope and later poets learned its sweep and balance here.
webb-freemasons-monitor-1797:
Thomas Smith Webb published The Freemason's Monitor at Boston in 1797, the first edition of the founding ritual book of American Freemasonry. Webb had learned the lectures of William Preston in England's system and adapted them for the young United States. His Monitor standardized the Preston-Webb lectures across the new republic's lodges.

The book prints the public parts of the degrees: charges, prayers, and songs, with explanations of emblems. Private ritual stayed oral; the Monitor fixed everything around it. American grand lodges adopted Webb's forms state by state. Generations of American Masons learned their Craft from his pages. The 1797 edition is the seed from which the standard American work grew.
wells-invisible-man-1897:
H. G. Wells gave the world Griffin in The Invisible Man in 1897. Griffin is a young man of science who finds a way to bend light round his flesh. Bandaged and strange, he hides out in a small inn in Sussex. His temper and his thefts soon rouse the whole town.

The tale tracks his slide from pride to rage and at last to a hunt. Wells keeps the science brisk and the dread close and plain. Griffin dreams of a reign of fear with his hid power. The book is the root text for all tales of the unseen foe since.
wiedemann-religion-ancient-egyptians-189:
Alfred Wiedemann gave the first full English scheme of Egypt's faith in Religion of the Ancient Egyptians, out in 1897. Sages had told the gods in parts and tales. Wiedemann sorts the whole: chief gods, town gods, rites, priests, death, and the hope of life past the tomb, in one clear plan drawn from the texts.

His tone is calm and fair, free of cult or scorn. Later works cite his as the base they build on or push past. For a first full map of the theme, it still earns its place. Its order is its gift.
